The northern Red Sea from Rabigh to the Sinai Peninsula escaped most of the bleaching and the mortality of the last couple of decades. Destroyed and critical reefs are only 6% of the total (Wilkinson 2004) because of its high latitude and very deep water extending close to shore, and wind induced upwelling. If these factors continue they are likely to contribute to survival of northern Red Sea species into the future. The southern Red Sea did not escape recent bleaching events and the Gulf of Aqaba and the Hurghada regions are affected by numerous direct impacts from coastal development and industry.

Genetics studies have, however, demonstrated the wide degree of differentiation of Red Sea populations from other Indian Ocean and Indo-West Pacific populations, consistent with a low level of gene exchange between the Red Sea and elsewhere. This relative isolation means that recovery following regional scale disturbance that decimates populations in the Red Sea may be compromised. For Red Sea endemics such disturbances would prove catastrophic.

threats:
In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide and a major cause of reef deterioration (Weil et al. 2006). The numbers of diseases and coral species affected, as well as the distribution of diseases have all increased dramatically within the last decade (Porter et al. 2001, Green and Bruckner 2000, Sutherland et al. 2004, Weil 2004). Coral disease epizootics have resulted in significant losses of coral cover and were implicated in the dramatic decline of acroporids in the Florida Keys (Aronson and Precht 2001, Porter et al. 2001, Patterson et al. 2002). In the Indo-Pacific, disease is also on the rise with disease outbreaks recently reported from the Great Barrier Reef (Willis et al. 2004), Marshall Islands (Jacobson 2006) and the northwestern Hawaiian Islands (Aeby 2006). Increased coral disease levels on the GBR were correlated with increased ocean temperatures (Willis et al. 2007) supporting the prediction that disease levels will be increasing with higher sea surface temperatures. Escalating anthropogenic stressors combined with the threats associated with global climate change of increases in coral disease, frequency and duration of coral bleaching and ocean acidification place coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific at high risk of collapse.

Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities.

The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual species is not known.
population:
This is an uncommon species.

There is no species specific population information available for this species. However, there is evidence that overall coral reef habitat has declined, and this is used as a proxy for population decline for this species. This species is particularly susceptible to bleaching, disease, and other threats and therefore population decline is based on both the percentage of destroyed reefs and critical reefs that are likely to be destroyed within 20 years (Wilkinson 2004). We assume that most, if not all, mature individuals will be removed from a destroyed reef and that on average, the number of individuals on reefs are equal across its range and proportional to the percentage destroyed reefs. Reef losses throughout the species' range have been estimated over three generations, two in the past and one projected into the future.

The age of first maturity of most reef building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999) and therefore we assume that average age of mature individuals is greater than eight years. Furthermore, based on average sizes and growth rates, we assume that average generation length is 10 years, unless otherwise stated. Total longevity is not known, but likely to be more than ten years. Therefore any population decline rates for the Red List assessment are measured over at least 30 years. See the Supplementary Material for further details on population decline and generation length estimates.
range: In the Indo-West Pacific, this species is found in the northwest Indian Ocean and Arabian/Iranian Gulf. This species is found in the Rodrigues (Fenner et al. 2004) and Mauritius (Pillay et al. 2002).
conservationActions:
All corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. Parts of the species’ range fall within Marine Protected Areas.

Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in taxonomy, population, abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration action; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management. Artificial propagation and techniques such as cryo-preservation of gametes may become important for conserving coral biodiversity.

rationale: Virtually nothing known about population numbers, trends or ecology, hence listed as Data Deficient.
habitat: Unknown.
threats: Unknown.
population: Unknown.
range: Endopsammia pourtalesi is an endemic species from the Galápagos Archipelago; known only from the type locality, west of Baltra; depth unknown (Wells 1983, Cairns 1991, Reyes-Bonilla 2002).
conservationActions: Present in one protected area in the ETP region: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). Included with corals in CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Prior to 1984, this coral was recorded in 2 to 43 m depth from Caleta Tagus (Isabela), and Gardner Island and Devil's Crown (Floreana) (Glynn and Wellington 1983, Cairns 1991). The species was extremely abundant at Tagus Cove (approx. 13% mean cover of reef surface at 15 m depth). All colonies known prior to the 1982-83 El Niño event have apparently since disappeared, although a few colonies of the species have been detected at two sites - Cousins and Gordons Rocks in the past decade (P. Humann pers. comm. to C.P. Hickman), with these colonies apparently now also lost. Estimated decline since 1982 (generation length is >10 years): >90% (Edgar and Garske 2005). The threat of El Niño has not ceased, hence if it is still extant, there is likely to be continuing decline in the range of this species.
habitat: R. wellingtoni occurs on under rock ledges, overhangs and ceilings of caves; at depths of 2 to 45 m (Wells 1983, Cairns 1991, Hickman 2005, P. Humann pers. comm. to C.P. Hickman).
threats: Despite no specific information on the thermal tolerance limits of R. wellingtoni, the dramatic reduction in its distributional range immediately after the 1982-83 El Niño event suggests that this species is particularly sensitive to thermal anomalies.
population: Before the 1982-83 ENSO (El Niño) event, Glynn and Wellington (1983) reported R. wellingtoni was most abundant (approx. 13% of mean surface coverage) at 15 m depth at Tagus Cove, Isabela. After the 1982-83 El Niño event most R. wellingtoni colonies were destroyed, except for colonies at Cousins and Gordons Rocks (Hickman 2005). P. Humann (pers. comm. to C.P. Hickman) observed and photographed one colony at Cousins and another one at Gordons Rocks in 1993; and in the late 1990s he took a photograph at the Gordons Rocks' colony. Witman and Smith (2003) reported R. wellingtoni inside their permanent photo quadrats at Gordons Rocks in 1999 and in 2000. Since then, R. wellingtoni has not been observed at Gordons Rocks, Cousins or anywhere else, despite targeted searches.
range: Rhizopsammia wellingtoni is an endemic species from the Galápagos Archipelago, Ecuador; only known from Tagus Cove, Isabela; Cousins, Santiago; Daphne Islet and Gordons Rocks, Santa Cruz; Gardner Islet (near Floreana) and Devil's Crown, Floreana (Well 1983, Cairns 1991, Reyes-Bonilla 2002, Hickman 2005, P. Humann pers. comm. to C.P. Hickman).
conservationActions: Inside one protected area in the ETP region: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). Included with corals in CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Prior to 1984, recorded from Playa Prieta (Floreana), Caleta Iguana and Punta Vicente Roca (Isabela), Santiago, Gardner Island (Española) and Pinzón (Glynn and Wellington 1983, Cairns 1991). Since the 1982-83 El Niño, the only sightings are a few colonies observed at Cousins Rocks (Santiago; P. Humann pers. comm. to P. Glynn) and Isla Gardner (Floreana; A. Chiriboga pers. comm.). The species is presumed to have been widespread and not uncommon prior to 1983 because it was recorded at six sites during a time of very little underwater survey activity. Colonies subsequently disappeared from all six known sites at the time of the 1982-83 El Niño, and despite intensive searches the species is recently only known from two sites, hence the species is now extremely rare. At one of the two sites where it was observed in the past decade, the species has not been seen since 2001, leaving only a single confirmed site. Thus, decline since 1982 is estimated to exceed 80% (generation length is >10 years). The threat of El Niño has not ceased.
habitat: T. floreana occurs in cryptic habitats; on ceilings of caves, ledges and rocks overhangs (Wells 1983, Hickman 2005). T. floreana has been reported to occur at depths of 2 to 46 m depth (Wells 1983, Cairns 1991, Hickman 2005, A. Chiriboga pers. comm., P. Humann pers. comm. to C.P. Hickman).
threats: Despite a lack of information on the thermal tolerances of T. floreana, the dramatic reduction in its distribution immediately after the 1982-83 El Niño event suggests that this mortality resulted from the event. Presumably climate change is an additional threat.
population: Before 1983 T. floreana was known from Caleta Iguana, Isabela; Buccaneer Cove, Santiago; Cousins near Santiago; Pinzón, Playa Prieta, Floreana, and Gardner Islet near Floreana (Wells 1983, Cairns 1991). However, after the 1982-83 ENSO (El Niño) event, T. floreana was not reported from any site until the early 1990s; when P. Humann observed and photographed three colonies at Cousins, near Santiago (P. Humann pers. comm. to C.P. Hickman). According to P. Humann (pers. comm. to C.P. Hickman), he observed these colonies yearly until 2001, but has not seen them since. Despite targeted searches throughout the Archipelago, the only colonies found during the past decade were located at Gardner Islet, near Floreana in 2004 (A. Chiriboga pers. comm.).
range: Tubastraea floreana is a rare endemic species to the Galápagos Archipelago, only known from a small number of sites: Playa Prieta, Floreana; Caleta Iguana, Isabela; Gardner Islet, near Floreana; Pinzón Island; Buccaneer Cove, Santiago, and Cousins, near Santiago (Wells 1983, Cairns 1991, Hickman 2005).
conservationActions: Inside one protected area in the ETP region: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). Included with corals in CITES Appendix II.

habitat: F. daphnense was collected at 101 m depth (Cairns 1991). Little else is known.
threats: Unknown.
population: Unknown.
range: Flabellum daphnense is known only from one specimen, the holotype; collected at Daphne Mayor, near Santa Cruz, Galápagos, Ecuador (Cairns 1991, Reyes-Bonilla 2002).

Included with corals in CITES Appendix II.

threats: Unknown.
population: Unknown.
range: Pseudocyathoceras avis is an endemic species within the ETP region; found only in the Galápagos Archipelago off Española and Floreana Islands (Cairns 1991, Cairns et al. 1999, Reyes-Bonilla 2002).
conservationActions: Present in one protected area in the ETP region: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). habitat: According to Cairns (1991) C. solida occurs at depths of 373 to 488 m (depth range from 488 to 1,160 is questioned in Cairns 1991). Little else is known.
threats: Unknown. This species has a limited range and slow growth rates and therefore could be intrinsically at risk from future threats.
population: Unknown.
range: Caryophyllia solida is an endemic species from the Galápagos Archipelago; only reported from three locations, southeast of Fernandina Island; north of San Cristóbal (questioned location, see Cairns 1991), and north of Santiago Island (Cairns 1991, Reyes-Bonilla 2002).
conservationActions: Included in one protected area: Ecuador: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). conservationActions: Recorded from one protected area: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). population: Unknown.
range: Crispatotrochus galapagensis is an endemic species from the Galápagos Archipelago. Reported from the southwest side of Fernandina Island; off Tagus Cove, Isabela Island; north of Floreana Island; off Santa Cruz Island, and off Roca Redonda (Cairns 1991, Reyes-Bonilla 2002).
conservationActions: Present in one protected area: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). Included with corals in CITES Appendix II.

rationale: Recorded as isolated colonies at only three sites on one island (i.e., Punta Albemarle, Punta Vicente Roca and Caleta Iguana). Extensive underwater surveys across Galápagos between 2000 and 2006 have revealed the presence of this species at only two sites. Although assessed here as Vulnerable using the D2 criterion associated with small range size and potential threat from the effects of El Niño, there is also concern that populations of P. isabela have declined in recent decades, as is evident for other local coral species. The population status of the type subpopulation from Punta Albemarle is unknown, although the species has not been sighted in recent searches in that region. The subpopulation from Punta Vicente Roca (sighted in 2003), has not been subsequently seen; despite this location having been surveyed since. While this evidence for decline may suggest listing as Endangered under criteria A or B, the paucity of records for this species makes it difficult to have any degree of confidence in population trends and therefore it is more tenable to assess it as Vulnerable under the D2 criterion which does appear to be well supported by the available evidence.
habitat: In recesses or caves with subdued light (Hickman 2005), reported at depths of 10 to 23 m (Cairns 1991, Hickman 2005).
threats: Unknown. Presumably El Niño and climate change.
population:
P. isabela is an uncommon species (Hickman 2005), only recorded from three sites at Isabela Island (viz. Punta Albemarle, Punta Vicente Roca and Caleta Iguana). The population status of the type subpopulation from Punta Albemarle is unknown, although the species has not been sighted in recent searches in that region.

The subpopulation from Punta Vicente Roca (sighted in 2003), has not been seen subsequently, despite this location having been surveyed seasonally since that time (Chiriboga, Hickamn and Edgar pers. comms.). In addition, another small colony was sighted in 2004 at Caleta Iguana, Isabela during underwater searches (Chiriboga, Hickman and Edgar pers. comms.).
range: Polycyathus isabela is an endemic species for the ETP region, present only around the Galápagos Archipelago. Occurrence known from Punta Albemarle (14 m, holotype); Punta Vicente Roca (10 m), and Caleta Iguana (11 m) at Isabela Island (Wells 1983, Cairns 1991, Reyes-Bonilla 2002, Hickman 2005).
conservationActions: Present in one protected area in the ETP region: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). Included with corals in CITES Appendix II.

habitat: D. johnsoni has been reported from depth ranges of 373 to 462 m (Cairns 1991). Little else is known.
threats: Unknown.
population: Unknown.
range: Dendrophyllia johnsoni is endemic to the Galápagos Archipelago, only recorded from two locations; off Santa Cruz Island and from a seamount to the north of Santiago Island (Cairns 1991).
conservationActions: Present in one protected area in the ETP region: Galápagos Marine Reserve (IUCN category VI); Galápagos Archipelago Particularly Sensitive Area (PSSA); Galápagos Island World Heritage Site (UNESCO N (i)(ii)(iii)(iv), and Galápagos Island Man and Biosphere Reserve (UNESCO). Included with corals in CITES Appendix II.

rationale: The species is known only from the western Mediterranean Sea, where it has been observed from four sites. Little information is available on its abundance, population status, or habitats and ecology. There are no known species-specific threats, but threats to coral habitats may also be impacting this species. Therefore, this species is listed as Data Deficient. Further research on the distribution, population status, and ecology is recommended.
habitat: This species has been only observed on three occasions. It has been found growing on rocks, calcareous algae, tunicates, coralligenous bottoms and axes of gorgonians in shallow waters (Weinberg 1986, Silvestre 1987, López-Gonzalez and García-Gómez 1994).
threats: <span lang="EN-US">There is no knowledge about the threats to this species.
population: There is no information available on the population abundance of this species.
range: Clavularia carpediem is known from a small number of records in the western Mediterranean Sea. It has been reported from the Alboran Sea from three sites; north of Cabo Negro, near M'diq, Morocco (Weinberg 1986), the seamount Seco de los Olivos/Chella Bank in Almeria, and from 'la Atunara' (in the Strait of Gibraltar) in Cádiz Province, Spain (López-González and García-Gómez 1994). It has also been recorded from off the Columbretes Islands, province of Castellón (Spain) (Aguilar et al. 2008).
useTrade: The species is not utilized.
conservationActions: The species is present in the Natural Park of Estrecho in Spain. At present, there is no conservation plans for this species. Further research on the distribution, population status, and ecology is recommended.

rationale: Clavularia crassa is widespread in most of the Mediterranean Sea (Betti 2012) from the Straits of Gibraltar to the eastern Aegean Sea, although there are no records from North Africa or the Levantine basin. Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large overall population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
habitat: In the east Mediterranean basin (Aegean Sea), Clavularia crassa is common in algae communities from 0 to 15 meters depth (Vafidis et al. 1994, Morri et al. 2000), while in the Adriatic Sea and around the Balearic Islands, it is relatively common between 15-35 m depth (Kružić 2007).
threats: Clavularia crassa could be impacted by organic pollution and habitat destruction due to coastal development. Changes in algae communities could also impact the species.
population: Off the Italian coast, Clavularia crassa has been observed at maximum densities of 2,000 polyps/m2 (Betti 2012). In the Alboran Sea (south of the Iberian Peninsula), this species is also common (Ocaña et al. 2000, Cebrian and Ballesteros 2004).
range: Clavularia crassa is widespread in most of the Mediterranean Sea (Betti 2012) from the Straits of Gibraltar to the eastern Aegean Sea, although there are no records from North Africa or the Levantine basin. It is present in the Aegean Sea (Vafidis et al. 1994); the Sea of Marmara (Vafidis et al. 1994); the Adriatic Sea (e.g., Kružić 2007, Betti 2012); the southern Tyrrhenian Sea-Sicily Channel and the Ligurian Sea (Betti 2012); the western Mediterranean basin, including the Balearic Islands (Martí et al. 2005, Gili et al. 1989), and the Alboran Sea (Ocaña et al. 2000, Cebrian and Ballesteros 2004).
useTrade: The species is not known to be utilized.
conservationActions: It is necessary to improve knowledge of Clavularia crassa biology and ecology. Knowledge of the aspects like population dynamics and reproduction in the Mediterranean are vital to apply future management measures.

rationale: M. edwarsi is listed as Data Deficient due to it being a rare species, although it can be locally abundant in some sites. Although it is found in a range of habitats, each of these habitats are susceptible to various threats, and it is possible that these are resulting in a population decline which may be sufficient to trigger a threatened category, where more detailed information available. It is easily overlooked in coralligenous assemblages so possibly its distribution is larger than originally thought. More efforts are needed to know its distribution, its biology and ecological requirements.
habitat:
It is commonly found on rocky bottoms at depths between 2 and 15 m but can reach down to 40 m. It colonizes habitats made by the remains of shells and stones, rocky walls and coraligenous outcrops and it has also been reported in green algae crops (Oceana 2006). In all these habitats, it is often possible to find a lot of other colonies nearby, except in coraligenous outcrops where the colonies are more disperse and are less dense.

It prefers well illuminated areas. In the Alboran Island, M. edwarsi is able to form important concentrations of colonies in the shallow waters of horizontal rocky areas (Ocaña  pers. obs. 2013). Very little is known about its reproduction but ova have been observed in May (Weinberg 1977) June (Giordano et al. 2012), July (Templado et al. 2002, Ocaña pers. obs. 2013 at Strombolichio) and September (Gili 1982) giving the idea that it has seasonal spawning, probably linked to the moon phases or the increase of seawater temperature (Giordano et al. 2012). The embryos are joined by a mucous secretion to the adult colonies similarly to other species of Anthozoa.
threats: There is no information about specific threats to M. edwardsi but  the deteriorating water quality in coastal marine environments and the expanding coastal urbanization with the associated discharge of insufficiently treated sewage, will have direct effects on the shallow waters communities and coraligenous outcrops where the populations of M. edwardsi are distributed. Moreover, shallow populations maybe affected by anchorage from boats. It is likely to also be impacted by fishing activities due to its occurrence in coraligenous outcrops.
population: Very little information is available about the population density of this species. However it is known that Maasella edwardsi is present in important populations around the Columbretes Islands, Alboran Island and Strombolichio (near Stromboli Island) (Ocaña pers. obs. 2013).
range:
Maasella edwardsi is an endemic species from the Mediterranean and has been recorded in the Adriatic Sea, Thyrrenian and Ionic Sea (Fava and Ponti 2007, Castellato and Stefanon 2008) and the Northern and western Aegean sea and Dardanelles (Özalp and Ates 2015, Özalp and Ates 2015b) as well as other Western Mediterranean areas (Weinberg 1977, Weinberg and Ocaña 2003, Fava and Ponti 2007).

It is present in Banyuls sur Mer (France), Alberes, Gulf di Marsiglia, Golfo di Napoli, Cargano, Chioggia and Porto Cesareo (Italy). In Italy, the species also occurs in Strombolicchio, a small volcanic islet close to the island of Stromboli, off the north coast of Sicily.

In the Spanish coast, the species was previously observed at Medes and west Columbretes Islands (Gili 1982, García-Carrascosa et al. 1987, Templado et al. 2002), Murcia (Calvín 1995), Granada coast (Ocaña Martín et al. 2000), Algeciras Bay (López-González 1993), Alborán Island  (Aguilar et al. 2008, Moreno 2006) and the Ceuta region (Ocaña and Serrais 2004, Ocaña et al. 2009). 

It was previously erroneously recorded at Britain, and on the Atlantic coast of France.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: There is not enough information about the species to develop conservation proposals and even to judge if they are necessary. Most of the known populations of M. edwardsi are located in protected areas. More research on distribution, ecology and threats is needed for this species.

rationale: Although this species has been recorded quite widely in the Mediterranean, in most of the localities where it has been found there was evidence of damage from fishing activities. This is suspected to be causing a population decline, but with the data currently available it is not possible to quantify the rate. As a result, this species is presently assessed as Data Deficient.
habitat: It is commonly found between 40-200 m depth (Carpine and Grasshof 1975). However it has also been sighted around 500-800 m depth (Angeletti et al. 2014, Mastrototaro et al. 2010). Deeper colonies at 1,000 m has being described but the identification is doubtful (Cartes et al. 2009). The species is always found on hard substrata, including coralligenous formations (Grinyo et al. 2012, Bo et al. 2011a, Aguilar et al. 2009).
threats: Fishing activities, mainly trammel nets and longline fishing, are most probably the main threat to this species. In most of the sites where the species has been recorded, damage from fishing activities has been evident (Bo pers. comm. 2014).
population: In the St. Eufemia Gulf in Calabria (Italy), population density of Paramuricea macrospina reaches 1-13 colony per m2. A similar density is suspected in the Balearic Islands (Spain), but there is not yet published information confirming this (Gili pers. comm. 2014). Its population trend is unknown, but based on the main threats and observed disturbances, it is suspected to be in decline.
range: This is a Mediterranean endemic species. Paramuricea macrospina seems abundant in Corsica but it can be also found in the French coast of the Gulf of Lions, Pantelleria Island in the Strait of Sicily, Tyrrhenian coast of Napoli, Adriatic and Aegean seas as well as Tunisia (Carpine and Grasshoff 1975). More recently, the species has also been found in the Spanish waters in Catalonia (Gili 1981) Chella Bank in the Alboran Sea (Aguilar et al. pers. obs.2014) and Balearic Islands (Grinyó et al. 2012, Cartes et al. 2009; Aguilar et al. 2008), in different Italian sites in the Ligurian Sea (Balduzzi et al. 1994), Thyrrenian coast (Bo et al. 2011a, 2011b, 2012), Adriatic (Angeletti et al. 2014) and Ionian Seas (Mastrototaro et al. 2010, Vertino et al. 2010). It has also been observed in Malta (Mifsud et al. 2008), Greece (Koukouras 2010) and in Turkey, from Balikci Island in the Marmara sea (Topçu and Öztürk 2013).
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: There is not any conservation action in place for this species. It is unknown whether Paramuricea macrospina occurs in marine protected areas. Better protection of coralligenous communities from destructive fishing practices and more research on the species' distribution, population and threats is needed to assure species conservation.

rationale: No population information is available for this species; even very little information about threats might be inferred from its habitat of occurrence. Therefore this species is listed as Data Deficient. More research on the distribution of this species is highly recommended, as well as ecological and population studies, to allow the evaluation of its conservation status. This species should be re-evaluated when these data become available.
habitat: Bunodeopsis strumosa is an anemone characteristic of brackish waters of muddy sands in sheltered areas. It is a species commonly found in leaves of seagrasses, in particular Zostera noltii, Cymodocea nodosa (Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995) and Ruppia sp. (Martínez-Garrido pers. comm. 2013). In Marseille, it occurs on Posidonia oceanica leaves in littoral lagoons. It can be also found in the surface of macroalgae and bryozoans or even attached on hard substrata (Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995). Over winter time, when the sea surface temperature lowers to 10ºC, this anemone retracts into the substratum (Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995). The species seems to withstand moderate organic pollution (Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995).
threats: Because the common association of Bunodeopsis strumosa with marine phanerogams (Posidonia oceanica, Zostera noltii, Cymodocea nodosa, Ruppi spp.), it is expected that its threats are those of seagrasses. Therefore, habitat destruction due to anchoring and recreational activities might be the main threats for the species at present.
population: There is no information available. However, quite dense populations have been described from Thermaikos Gulf (Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995). In the locality of Mar Menor (Murcia, Spain), it has also been found in high abundance, attached to Rhuppia spp. leaves at shallow (0-3 m) waters depths (Martínez-Garrido pers. comm. 2013).
range:
In the Mediterranean, the presence of Bunodeopsis strumosa  has been documented in Mar Menor and Granada coast (Spain); Banyuls, Marseille and Nice (France); Villafranca and Gulf of Naples (Italy), Portobello (Croatia) and the Ionian Sea (Corfu and Lefkada islands, Greece) as well as Thermaikos Gulf (Aegean Sea, Greece) (Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995, Martínez-Garrido pers. comm. 2013). Recently, it has also been reported in Turkey (Çinar et al. 2014).

Bunodeopsis strumosa has also been reported in the Canary islands (Ocaña and Den Hartog 2002).
useTrade: This species is not used for commercial purposes.
conservationActions: Information on the distribution of the species, its ecology, life history and population status are needed to better evaluate its conservation status. There is a need for experimental studies to assess the resistance of these anemones to the predicted changes in seawater temperatures due to climate change.

rationale: This coral is known from a small number of scattered sites in the Mediterranean Sea. It is assessed as Data Deficient in view of the absence of information on its population size and trend, status, and threats.
habitat: <span lang="EN-US">This species is found in the infralittoral and circalittoral zones between 10-50 m depth in caves, overhangs and shaded cliffs (Zibroiwius 1980, Kružić 2008, Ocaña and Brito 2013). The observations of the colonies along the Eolian islands (Ocaña and Brito 2013) describe that some populations can form dense macro bio-structures where other marine organisms occupy the rest of the dead skeleton. Extra-calicinal budding is the most common reproduction pathway from a laminar expansion, and intra-calicinal division has been only observed scarcely in the basal plate form. According to Zibrowius (1980) the larvae use the dead corallum calices to settle.
threats: No published data are available on threats to this species.
population:
Very little is known of the population density of this species. The only information available is from a study undertaken around Mljet Island in the south Adriatic Sea, where population density at 37 m depth reached 15 colonies/m2 and at 44 m depth 20 colonies/m2 (Kružić 2008).

Ocaña and Brito (2013) recorded that this species is very common in the Aeolian Archipelago (islands of Lipari, Vulcano, Salina and Strombolichio) along the vertical walls of the islands encrusting from 10 to 50 m depth. Normally small polyps groups were observed inside crevices or under slopes, but also growing directly on the vertical walls.
range: The coral Cladopsammia rolandi is endemic to the Mediterranean Sea. Its occurrence is rare, but is recorded from Spain (the Sea of Alboran; Ocaña et al. 2000), Malta, in the southwestern coasts of Algeria and Tunisia, the central Mediterranean area (eastern coast of Sicily, Gulf of Naples and Gulf of Taranto), the Aeolian Islands, and north of Sicily (Zibrowius 1980, Ocaña and Brito 2013). C. rolandi has also been found off the island of Chios, in the eastern Aegean Sea (Vafidis et al. 1997), in the South Adriatic, south of Lastovo Island and southwest of Mljet Island (Kružić 2008). Its presence in the Adriatic Sea (south Croatia), is the northernmost finding in the Mediterranean Sea, due probably to the inflow of the sea surface currents in the eastern side of the Adriatic Sea (Kružić 2008). This new finding should not be considered evidence of recent colonization, but records of previously overlooked coral populations (Kružić 2008).
useTrade: The species is not utilized.
conservationActions: There are no conservation actions currently in place for this species. It is unknown if the species occurs in any protected area, but it may occur in the Mljet national park in Croatia. Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in population abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats; identification, establishment of new protected areas and expansion of existing sites.

rationale: A. cari is a rare shallow-water species known from the Mediterranean. More efforts are needed to know its distribution, its biology and ecological requirements. Impacts of coastal disturbances (e.g., eutrophication, coastal development) are unknown, but likely to have negative impacts on this species. Therefore, this species is assessed as Data Deficient.
habitat: Actinia cari is usually found in the shallow infralittoral zone as a member of the biocoenosis of photophylic algae, often attached to bare stones and rocks (Pax and Müller 1962, Schmidt 1972, cited in Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995). However, it may occur to a depth of at least 20 m, as demonstrated by a specimen found in the Adriatic Sea, attached to the stalk of a colony of Alcyonium palmatum adriaticum (Kükenthal, 1906) (Chintiroglou and den Harto 1995). A. cari shows variability in the colour and form of the rings. The sexes are separate, the female is oviparous with no records of individuals brooding young internally (Schmidt 1972, cited in Perrin et al. 1999).
threats: There is no information about specific threats to A. cari although the deteriorating water quality in coastal marine environments and the expanding coastal urbanization with the associated discharge of insufficiently treated sewage, will have direct effects on the shallow water communities where the populations of A. cari are distributed.
population: Very little information is available about the population density of this species.
range:
Actinia cari is a rare species, known only from the Mediterranean. It has been reported from the Gulf of Naples, but Schmidt (1972, cited in Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995) failed to find it there in the early 1970s and suggested a decline of the species in the western Mediterranean. The species was later recorded from the Catalan coast including Medes Island, Spain (Gili 1982).

Most records are from the Adriatic Sea (Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995). The species was recently reported for the first time from the Aegean Sea (Evian Island) by Ates (1990, cited in Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995) in Zakinthos, western Greece.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: There is not enough information about the species to develop conservation proposals and even to judge if they are necessary. More efforts are needed to know its distribution, its biology and ecological requirements.

rationale: <span lang="EN-US">The species has been recorded mainly from the western Mediterranean and the Adriatic, and recently from the Aegean Sea. It is listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presence in marine protected areas, and the lack of evidence of threats affecting it.
habitat: Cibrinopsis crassa typically lives on hard substrata in rocky holes, under stones and on Posidonia oceanica meadows (Kružić 2007). The general depth range of the species lies between 3 and 100 m (Weinberg 1998).
threats: There are no known widespread threats.
population: Population density and trends of Cribrinopsis crassa in the Mediterranean are currently unknown, but the species is generally considered not to form dense populations (Weinberg 1998). It has been reported as quite common in the Adriatic Sea (Kružić 2007).
range: Cribrinopsis crassa is considered a Mediterranean endemic (Chintiroglou et al. 1997). It has been reported mostly from the western part and the Adriatic (Schmidt 1972, Gili 1981, Chintiroglou et al. 1997, Ocaña et al. 2000, Kružić 2007), whereas its presence in the Aegean Seas has been recently confirmed (Antoniadou and Chintiroglou pers. obs. 2014).
useTrade: The species is not utilized.
conservationActions: There are no conservation actions in place for this species. The species is present in several marine protected areas.

rationale: There are limited data on the distribution of Paranemonia cinerea and baseline information on its population status are absent. The species is assessed as Data Deficient in view of the limited information on its distribution, population size and trend, status, and threats.
habitat: It is a typical brackish water species that tolerates well large temperature and salinity variations. Paranemonia cinerea lives attached on Zostera leaves or other marine plant species and performs vertical migrations depending on season.
threats: Habitat degradation due to urbanization (desiccation or deterioration of lagoon for urbanization) and pollution (solids, domestic, industrial waste into lagoon environment) are the main threats to the species.
population: The only available data refer to Kune lagoon in Albania, reporting five individuals per 0.2 m2 (Boncagni et al. 2009), whereas the species' average abundance has been estimated from nine Adriatic lagoons and three Tyrrhenian ones as 0.03 and 0.72 respectively (Munari and Mistri 2008).
range:
The species Paranemonia cinerea is known from several brackish coastal Mediterranean lagoons, mainly along the Adriatic Sea and the Tyrrhenian Sea (Gravina et al. 1989, Ates 1992, Marzano et al. 2003, Munari and Mistri 2008, Boncagni et al. 2009, Hartog and Ates 2011, Macali et al. 2013). It seems therefore that these coastal lagoons represent an important geographic site, crucial for the species’ sustainability. 

The first report of this species from the Aegean Sea (Chintiroglou et al. 1992) was a misidentification (Chintiroglou and Hartog 1995). However, the species has been found thereafter around Lesvos Island and its presence has been confirmed at this site (Chintiroglou et al. 1997). In Spain, it has been observed in the Delta el Ebro (Castellón, Spain) and Mar Menor (Murcia) (Casado-Amezúa et al. 2014). It has also been reported from the Vlora Gulf in Albania (Maiorano et al. 2011) and the Salses-Leucate Lagoon in France (Carlier et al. 2009).
useTrade: The species has been reported among the edible sea anemone species that used to be found in the market and consumed in Venice (Marino 1985).
conservationActions: There are no active conservation measures for the species, neither baseline information about its populations. Actions needed are closely related with habitat preservation (i.e., seaweeds, Zostera seagrass). More efforts are needed to know its distribution, its biology and ecological requirements.

rationale: Paranemonia vouliagmeniensis is endemic to one site (two locations as the two habitat types would be impacted differently by the threats) in a small karst lagoon, Lake Vouliagmeni, in Greece. The lake is exploited as a spa area for bathers all year round, receiving large numbers of bathers from late spring to early autumn. Although the use of sun-cream is forbidden by the management body of the lake, recursive maintenance works take place in the lagoon that severely affect the species’ population, especially considering young recruits which are directly killed when flora is removed by the lake, whereas larger individuals suffers from trampling. The extent of occurrence is less than 8 km2, and the area of occupancy is estimated to be around 4 km2. Although the population has not been continuously monitored, a 50% reduction has been assessed during the last decade, which is a severe cause of concern. As a result of the extremely restricted distribution, presence in just two locations, and continuing decline in quality of habitat, it is assessed as EN B1ab(iii)+2ab(iii).
habitat: Paranemonia vouliagmeniensis lives in both hard (natural and artificial) and soft substrata (mixed sediments composed mainly by sand, gravels and pebbles, algae and meadows), at depths ranging from 0.10 m to 11 m showing an aggregated pattern of dispersion (Chintiroglou et al. 2000). Its lifespan has been estimated as approximately five years (Anagnostou et al. 2013) with an extended reproduction period lasting from winter till late spring. It feeds on small crustaceans and gastropods (Chintiroglou et al. 2008). The species follows two different migrations during its life cycle: during the first one young individuals (juveniles) migrate to deeper waters for better feeding and protection and to avoid intra-specific competition, whereas during the second one the reverse pattern is observed as larger, mature individuals leave the algae on which they have been previously settled and migrate towards the shallower part of Lake Vouliagmeni (Chintiroglou et al. 1996, 2000). No predators have been observed in the lagoon.
threats: Human activities (tourist development, as the area is used as a resort) or unforeseen disasters are the main threat for the species. Its population trends have been negatively correlated with anthropogenic activities (Chintiroglou et al. 2000, Anagnostou et al. 2013). Regular maintenance works are conducted in Lake Vouliagmeni, including the cleaning of the sea bottom by removing the flora in spring-summer for aesthetic reasons for the bathers, thus destroying the appropriate habitat of young individuals, and directly killing them when flora is removed by the lake. Larger individuals suffer also from trampling. Gravel and sand are spread as pathways for bathers, also impacting the species.
population:
The species forms dense populations in small depths and in various substrata types. Its population density has been estimated to vary annually from 68.1 ± 33.9 to 87.8 ± 50.8 individuals/m2 in the shallow sites (0.10-3 m) living attached on mixed soft substrata sediment and on artificial hard substrata, and from 35 to 180 individuals/5 l of algae in the deeper sites (3-10 m), where it lives settled on the alga thalli (Chintiroglou et al. 2000).

According to monthly data collected in 2011-2012 the species population density has been reduced by more than 50% from previous records (Anagnostou et al. 2013).
range: The species Paranemonia vouliagmeniensis is known from a single site, namely Lake Vouliagmeni (Attiki), a geological karst formation in the coastal area of Attika, Greece (Doumenc et al. 1987, Chintiroglou et al. 2000, 2008, Anagnostou et al. 2013). Accordingly, this tectonic lagoon presents an important geographic site, crucial for the species’ sustainability.
useTrade: The species is not utilized.
conservationActions:
There are no active conservation measures for the species. It has been assessed as vulnerable VU D2 in the Red List of Greece (Legakis and Maragos 2009). The Management Body of the Lake intend to implement a monitoring program in the near future.

Actions needed are closely related with regulations on maintenance works for bathers (removal of flora and sand input) and also, appropriate monitoring of P. vouliagmeniensis populations on an annual basis or at least per generation length (five years) to obtain time-series abundance data for the species.

rationale: The worldwide distribution of Segonzactis hartogi is restricted within deep silty or sandy-silty bottoms in Aegean Sea but there is not much information. Therefore it is listed as Data Deficient in view of the absence of information on its population size and trend, status, and threats.
habitat: Segonzactis hartogi lives in soft sediments composed by silt, at depths ranging from 80 m to 800 m (Vafidis and Chintiroglou 2002). There is no information on the species ecological requirements.
threats: Bottom fishery is the main threat for the species over its entire distributional range.
population: The species' population has not been estimated; only four specimens have been so far collected (Vafidis and Chintiroglou 2002).
range: The species Segonzactis hartogi is distributed only within the Aegean Sea, at silty bottoms and in depths ranging from 80-800 m (Vafidis and Chintiroglou 2002). Only four (4) specimens have been collected so far, two (2) from mount Athos at 750 and 800 m depth on a silty bottom, and two other from Ios island at 80 m depth on sandy-silty bottom. As the species lives exclusively in the Aegean Sea, it is an important geographic site, crucial for the species’ sustainability.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: There are no active conservation measures for the species. Actions needed are closely related with bottom-trawling fisheries regulations that should be implemented as well as the development of a monitoring for S. hartogi populations in order to obtain information on its status and trends.

rationale: The species has been recorded mainly from the western Mediterranean and the Adriatic, being very rare in the Aegean Sea; AOO and EOO cannot be estimated precisely. It's listed as Data Deficient in view of the absence of information on its population size and trend, status, and threats.
habitat: The species Phymanthus pulcher lives typically on biogenic substrata. Occasionally near Posidonia meadows and in coralligenous biocoenosis; it has been also reported among main inhabitants of Ophiothrix populations and to co-occur with Cerianthus membranaceous (Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995). The general depth range of the species lies between 15 and 70 m.
threats: The threats to this species are unknown. As it is a cold-water species, it may be affected by global warming.
population: Population density and trends of Phymanthus pulcher in the Mediterranean are currently unknown, but the species is generally considered to be rare.
range: The species Phymanthus pulcher is considered a Mediterranean endemic. It has been reported from the western basin, the Adriatic, and the Aegean Sea (Gili 1981, Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995, Chintiroglou et al. 1997, Vafidis et al. 1997, Ocaña et al. 2000, Kruzic 2007). It is generally considered rare, forming isolated populations.
useTrade: This species is not utilized.
conservationActions: There are no active conservation measures for the species. It is present in some protected areas (e.g., Telascica Nature Park, Mljet). more research on distribution, ecology and threats is needed for this species.

rationale:
Crassophyllum thessalonicae is endemic to the Aegean Sea in the Mediterranean basin, where it is known from the Thermaikos Gulf. This locality comprises two locations, as one part is subject to trawling pressure and the other is not. The extent of occurrence is larger than 100 km2, but the area of occupancy is estimated to be around 60 km2, as the species lives deeper than 30 m depth and requires silty soft substrata. The area of occupancy is estimated to have reduced as a result of intense bottom trawl fishery, apart from the northern part of Thermaikos Gulf which constitutes a protected area as bottom trawling is prohibited. The AOO is expected to further decline and the quality of habitat is severely impacted from fisheries and also, from urbanization and pollution (Thermaikos Gulf is one of the most severely impacted coastal areas of Greece).

Due to its restricted distribution, presence in two locations, and continuing decline in quality of habitat, it is assessed as Endangered (B1ab(ii,iii)+2ab(ii,iii)).
habitat: This rare sea-pen lives on mixed sediments composed of silty and muddy biogenic bottoms, at depths ranging from 30 m to 60 m, at the northern part of the outer Thermaikos Gulf (Vafidis and Koukouras 1991, Fryganiotis et al. 2011). There is no information on the species' ecological requirements.
threats: Bottom fishery is the main threat for the species. A large part of its distributional range is heavily impacted by commercial otter trawl, and several colonies are caught as by-catch during the trawling open fishing season (bottom trawling takes place from 1st October to 31 May according to Greek and EU laws). This effect is continuous and affects current and future population trends. According to the Hellenic Statistical Authority, trawl fishery provides 27% of the annual catch of the Hellenic fisheries, whereas 12% of the above percentage derives from Thermaikos Gulf. These figures are indicatives of the intensive fishing activity taking place within the Gulf (Fryganiotis et al. 2013).
population: The species' population has been estimated over its distributional area using bottom trawling fisheries data. Its population density ranges from 0.5 to 4 colonies/20 km (Fryganiotis pers. comm. 2014). Population trends have not been quantitatively estimated continuously, and the existing information is only from observations in 2005 and 2006, suggesting a southward trend distribution, probably because of the trawling intensity (the northern area of Thermaikos has been closed to bottom trawling for over 30 years). However, as the remainder of its distribution area is heavily exploited using bottom trawling, its population is expected to be severely impacted, and a declining trend can be assumed, though no strategic survey dedicated on C. thessalonicae populations has been so far conducted to accurately estimate its natural stocks and population trends.
range: The species Crassophyllum thessalonicae is endemic to the Mediterranean Sea, with a very restricted distribution. It is exclusively recorded from the Thermaikos Gulf in a shallow-water embayment in the northwest Aegean Sea. This makes the specific geographic area crucial for the species’ sustainability (Vafidis and Koukouras 1991, Fryganiotis et al. 2011). The AOO is estimated at 60 km2.
useTrade: The species is not utilised.
conservationActions: There are no active conservation measures for the species. The species is partially protected at the inner, northern, part of Thermaikos Gulf, where bottom trawling is prohibited. Actions needed are closely related with bottom-trawling fisheries regulations that should be implemented, after appropriate monitoring of C. thessalonicae populations is implemented to obtain a baseline time-series abundance data for this rare sea-pen.

rationale: The most important known threat for this species is extensive reduction of coral reef habitat due to a combination of threats. Specific population trends are unknown but population reduction can be inferred from estimated habitat loss (Wilkinson 2004). It has a small, disjunct range and is a uncommon. It is found in very shallow waters and therefore may be more susceptible to bleaching. Therefore, the estimated habitat loss of 10% from reefs already destroyed and those at critical stage within its range is the best inference of population reduction (Wilkinson 2004). This inference of population reduction over three generation lengths (30 years) does not meet the threshold of a threat category and this species is Least Concern. However, because of predicted threats from climate change and ocean acidification it will be important to reassess this species in 10 years or sooner, particularly if the species is also observed to disappear from reefs currently at the critical stage of reef degradation.
habitat: The species occurs in very shallow, wave exposed habitats. The maximum size is 25 cm.
threats:
In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide and a major cause of reef deterioration (Weil et al. 2006). The numbers of diseases and coral species affected, as well as the distribution of diseases have all increased dramatically within the last decade (Porter et al. 2001, Green and Bruckner 2000, Sutherland et al. 2004, Weil 2004). Coral disease epizootics have resulted in significant losses of coral cover and were implicated in the dramatic decline of acroporids in the Florida Keys (Aronson and Precht 2001, Porter et al. 2001, Patterson et al. 2002). In the Indo-Pacific, disease is also on the rise with disease outbreaks recently reported from the Great Barrier Reef (Willis et al. 2004), Marshall Islands (Jacobson 2006) and the northwestern Hawaiian Islands (Aeby 2006). Increased coral disease levels on the GBR were correlated with increased ocean temperatures (Willis et al. 2007) supporting the prediction that disease levels will be increasing with higher sea surface temperatures. Escalating anthropogenic stressors combined with the threats associated with global climate change of increases in coral disease, frequency and duration of coral bleaching and ocean acidification place coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific at high risk of collapse.

Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities.

The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual species is not known.
population:
The species is uncommon.

There is no species specific population information available for this species. However, there is evidence that overall coral reef habitat has declined, and this is used as a proxy for population decline for this species. This species is particularly susceptible to bleaching, disease, and other threats and therefore population decline is based on both the percentage of destroyed reefs and critical reefs that are likely to be destroyed within 20 years (Wilkinson 2004). We assume that most, if not all, mature individuals will be removed from a destroyed reef and that on average, the number of individuals on reefs are equal across its range and proportional to the percentage destroyed reefs. Reef losses throughout the species' range have been estimated over three generations, two in the past and one projected into the future.

The age of first maturity of most reef building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999) and therefore we assume that average age of mature individuals is greater than eight years. Furthermore, based on average sizes and growth rates, we assume that average generation length is 10 years, unless otherwise stated. Total longevity is not known, but likely to be more than ten years. Therefore any population decline rates for the Red List assessment are measured over at least 30 years. See the Supplementary Material for further details on population decline and generation length estimates.
range: In the Indo-West Pacific, this species is known from Guam, American Samoa, Fiji, the Great Barrier Reef, Palau and the Marianas (Fenner pers. comm.).
conservationActions:
All corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. Parts of the species’ range fall within Marine Protected Areas.

Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in taxonomy, population, abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration action; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management. Artificial propagation and techniques such as cryo-preservation of gametes may become important for conserving coral biodiversity.

rationale: The most important known threat for this species is extensive reduction of coral reef habitat due to a combination of threats. Specific population trends are unknown but population reduction can be inferred from estimated habitat loss (Wilkinson 2004). It is widespread and common throughout its range and therefore is likely to be more resilient to habitat loss and reef degradation because of an assumed large effective population size that is highly connected and/or stable with enhanced genetic variability. Therefore, the estimated habitat loss of 20% from reefs already destroyed within its range is the best inference of population reduction since it may survive in coral reefs already at the critical stage of degradation (Wilkinson 2004). This inference of population reduction over three generation lengths (30 years) does not meet the threshold of a threat category. However, this species is susceptible to bleaching and is collected for the aquarium trade, therefore it is listed as Near Threatened. However, because of predicted threats from climate change and ocean acidification it will be important to reassess this species in 10 years or sooner, particularly if the species is also observed to disappear from reefs currently at the critical stage of reef degradation.
habitat:
This species is found on exposed reef fronts and where currents are strong. Pocillopora eydouxi occurs in most reef environments, especially exposed reef fronts and at sits with strong currents; this coral also occurs on coral communities on rocky substrata (Hickman 2005). It has been reported from 2 m to at least 20 m depth, but commonly occurs between 5-10 m (Guzmán et al. pers. comm.). It may form large stands. The maximum size is over 1 m across.

P. eydouxi is capable of building reef frameworks; in Santa Elena, Costa Rica, a 50 m² reef is composed exclusively of P. eydouxi (Cortes and Jimenez 2003). Additionally, at La Azufrada and Playa Blanca in Gorgona Island, Colombia, P. eydouxi forms fringing reef frameworks with large dense colonies (Zapata and Vargas-Ángel 2003). Moreover, according to Guzmán (pers. comm.), at least one reef in Colombia is formed from 100% cover of P. eydouxi.

Amongst the reef building corals in the Eastern Tropical Pacific region, pocilloporid species have the highest growth rates (Guzmán and Cortes 1993). Reported growth rates of Pocillopora eydouxi range between 2.1 and 3.9 cm per year at Bahia Culebra, Costa Rica (Jiménez and Cortés 2003). Guzmán and Cortés (1993) reported growth rates from 3.1 cm per year in Galápagos to 3.32 cm per year in Costa Rica.

Pocilloporid corals, presumably including P. eydouxi, are generally amongst the strongest coral competitors with relatively high rates of calcification (Glynn 2001). However, coral species exhibiting high rates of calcification usually have relatively high mortality rates (Glynn 2000). Pocilloporid corals also usually predominate at shallow depths (1-15 m). Amongst the reef building corals in the Eastern Tropical Pacific region, pocilloporid species have the highest growth rates (Guzmán and Cortes 1993). They are the principal framework builders on Panamanian reefs (Glynn 2001).

Pocillopora species are preyed on by at least nine groups of consumers. These vary in their consumption patterns, but include:

a) Species that bite off colony branch-tips: pufferfishes (Arothron), parrotfishes (Scaridae), filefishes (Monacanthidae) (Glynn 2002).

b) Species that scrape skeletal surface: hermit crabs (Trizopagurus, Aniculus, and Calcinus) (Glynn 2002).

c) Species that remove tissues but leave the skeleton intact: gastropods (Jenneria pustulata and Quoyula sp. (Glynn 2002)), buterflyfishes, angelfishes, damselfish (Stegastes acapulcoensis), and Acanthaster planci (Glynn 2002).

d) Species that abrade tissues and skeleton: Eucidaris galapagensis (Glynn 2001).

Jenneria and Acanthaster can kill whole, relatively large (approx. 30 cm in diameter) colonies of Pocillopora (Glynn 2002). Pocilloporid species can have crab (Trapezia sp.) and alpheid shrimp as mutualistic symbionts that protect the coral from the attack of the crown-of-thorns sea star A. planci (Glynn 2001).
threats:
This species exhibited high bleaching and mortality in the 1998 bleaching event in Palau (Brunno et al. 2001).

Pocilloporid species as well as other major reef building corals within the Eastern Tropical Pacific region (Porites, Pavona, Gardinoseris) catastrophically declined in the Galápagos Archipelago and Cocos Island after 1983. Recovery observed since that time was in large part nullified by the 1997-98 ENSO event (Glynn 2000). According to Glynn et al.(1988), pocilloporid coral mortality in the eastern Pacific was high, ranging from 51% at Caño Island to 76-85% in Panama and 97-100% in the Galápagos Islands (Glynn et al. 1988).

Glynn (1994) suggests that the sea urchin Eucidaris galapagensis (syn. E. thouarsii) provides important biotic control of pocilloporid reef development. This urchin is the most persistent corallivore in the Galapagos Islands, where it is often observed grazing on pocilloporid corals (Glynn 2001).

Overfishing is probably responsible for some ecological imbalance on coral reefs that could prolong recovery from other disturbances (Glynn 2001). Moreover, Edgar et al.(unpublished manuscript) reported that over-exploitation of sea urchin predators (lobsters and fishes), along with ENSO, has a major effect in the condition and distribution of corals in the Galapagos Islands, by increasing the grazer and bioerosion pressure on corals.

Coral mortality associated with phytoplankton blooms has been reported from Caño Island, Costa Rica, and Uva Island, Panama, in 1985; where mortality of pocilloporid species (especially P. capitata and P. elegans) was in the order of 100% and 13% respectively at 3 m depth (Guzmán et al. 1990).

According to Glynn (2001), pocilloporid coral harvesting is an important threat in the Eastern Tropical Pacific region, specially along the continental coast. This activity has virtually eliminated pocilloporid corals from Acapulco (Mexico), Bahia Culebra (Costa Rica), Taboga Island (Panama), and parts of the coast of Ecuador (Glynn 2001). Nevertheless, this activity is now largely excluded from Costa Rica and Panama (Guzmán pers. comm.).

The total number of corals (live and raw) exported for this species in 2005 was 1,498.

Bryant et al. (1998), based on four anthropogenic factors (coastal development; overexploitation and destructive fishing practice; inland pollution and erosion, and marine pollution), estimated a high threat to coral reefs along the coasts of Costa Rica, Panama and Colombia. High levels of siltation caused by accelerated coastal erosion have degraded coral reefs in Costa Rica, Colombia and Ecuador (Glynn 2001)

Other threats include: a) predation principally by Acanthaster and Jenneria (Glynn 2002, 1994, 2000), and b) harvesting for the curio trade, an activity that has virtually eliminated pocilloporid corals from Acapulco (Mexico), Bahia Culebra (Costa Rica), Taboga Island (Panama), and parts of the coast of Ecuador (Glynn 2001).

According to Glynn et al. (1988), pocilloporid coral mortality in the eastern Pacific was high, ranging from 51% at Caño Island to 76-85% in Panama and 97-100% in the Galapagos Islands (Glynn et al. 1988). However, following this high coral mortality, numerous pocilloporid recruits have been observed at some sites in Costa Rica, Panama and the Galapagos Islands (Glynn unpublished data in Glynn et al. 1991). Apparently, Pocillopora eydouxi populations have been recovering in recent years (Guzmán et al. pers. comm.), following the severe coral mortality associated with recent ENSO events (1982-83 and 1997-98) and red tides.

In the Galápagos Islands, pocilloporid communities were well developed off northeastern San Cristobal, Espanola and Floreana Island until the 1980s (Glynn 1994, 2003), but disappeared following the 1982-83 ENSO event, with minimal coral recruitment since (Glynn 2003).

Acanthaster planci, the crown-of-thorns starfish, has been observed preferentially preying upon corals of the genus Acropora (Colgan 1987). Monospecific stands of this species are particularly vulnerable to disease outbreaks (Willis and Page pers. comm.). Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) (Acanthaster planci) are found throughout the Pacific and Indian Oceans, and the Red Sea. These starfish voracious predators of reef-building corals, with a preference for branching and tabular corals such as Acropora species. Populations of the crown-of-thorns starfish have greatly increased since the 1970s and have been known to wipe out large areas of coral reef habitat. Increased breakouts of COTS has become a major threat to some species, and have contributed to the overall decline and reef destruction in the Indo-Pacific region. The effects of such an outbreak include the reduction of abundance and surface cover of living coral, reduction of species diversity and composition, and overall reduction in habitat area.
