Recommended conservation measures include population surveys to monitor the effects of collecting for the aquarium trade, especially in Indonesia.

rationale: This widely distributed coral species is common. It has experienced global-level declines due to major threats from disease and bleaching as well as other secondary anthropogenic-related threats. Based on underwater surveys in many localities across its range, it has undergone an inferred global population decline of 50% or higher over the past three generations (30 years) and is therefore listed as Endangered A2bce. The current rates of mortality are exceeding growth and recruitment and threats are increasing in magnitude. Due to the extreme longevity, low rates of recruitment and regeneration of lesions as well as long generation time, scope for recovery of populations of this species is limited. If current trends continue, this species may warrant listing in a higher Red List category.
habitat:
This species occurs in semi-protected reef environments and is frequently a dominant species of lagoons and upper reef slopes. It usually displays a massive, columnar-lobate and encrusting morphology where it grows upward forming a clonal copy known as a rammet and leaving naturally an area of calcium carbonate with no live tissue at its basal area (Veron 2000, Edmunds 2015). This species also exhibits high phenotypic plasticity. Its unique morphology makes it relatively easy to identify when large colonies are present. However, smaller juvenile colonies could be easily mistaken with other species of this genus, as coralites are fairly similar. The minimum coralite diameter ranges from to a maximum of 2.5 mm to 3.8 mm (Coral Trait Database 2020). Colonies tend to be yellowish or brownish and exhibit a range of Symbiodinium clades, dominated by clade C (77%), clade D (14%), clade B (7%) and clade A (2%) and a diverse range of subclades reported in Coraltraits.org.

This is a hermaphroditic broadcast spawner during synchronous events in the summer. This species shows high variability in skeletal density (from 1.2 to 2.4 g cm-3), extension rates (from 0.5 to 1.7 mm yr-1) and calcification rates (from 0.4 to 0.75 g cm-2 y-1); some of the variability could be the result of measurements taken in experimental versus in situ conditions (Coral Trait Database 2020). Species in this genus are known for having low larval recruitment rates and moderate regeneration capabilities (Meesters et al. 1994, Cróquer et al. 2002). Overall, the lifespan of this species was found to be 53 to 95 years (Booker et al. 2019).

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
In 2014, an outbreak of a coral disease termed Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD) was reported off the coast of Miami-Dade County and has since spread along Florida and to some reefs in the Caribbean. At least 44% of Florida’s reef-building corals have been affected (Florida Department of Environmental Protection 2019). The pathogen causing the disease is unknown. This species is highly susceptible to SCTLD, with reported colony prevalence ranging from 8% to 77% in Florida during 2015-2018 (Precht et al. 2016, Hayes 2019), and ~10% in the Mexican Caribbean in surveys conducted in 101 sites along 450 km from 2018 to 2020 (Alvarez- Filip et al. 2019, L. Alvarez-Filip pers. comm. 2020). Up to September 2020, there have been no reports of SCTLD epizootic events in Cuba, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Venezuela, and the Dominican Republic (Roth et al. 2020). In 2021, an SCTLD outbreak impacted the east northern coast of the Dominican Republic, including Samana Bay, Galeras and Terrenas (A. Croquer, S. Zambrano, A. Reyes and K. Samuel pers. obs. 2021). SCTLD represents a threat to this species due to: (1) its rapid spread across individual colonies; (2) high mortality rate; (3) rapid spread between reefs; (4) high infection rate (Pratte and Richardson 2014, Dahlgren 2020); and (5) overall change of the coral-associated microbiota (Meyer et al. 2019). This species is also vulnerable to Black Band, White Plague, Dark Spot, and Yellow Band diseases and to bleaching. 

Other threats include predation by Sparisoma viride (Stoplight Parrotfish), hurricane damage, and loss of habitat at the recruitment stage due to algal overgrowth and sedimentation, as well as localized impacts due to bioerosion by sponges and other organisms, and other diseases. This species is also threatened by oil spills which have produced significant mortalities and long-lasting chronic effects in Panamanian reefs (Guzmán et al. 2020). Local threats such as uncontrolled anchoring produce injuries and fragmentation on larger colonies which may increase susceptibility to disease.

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, (i) temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, (ii) severity of ENSO events and storms, and (iii) ocean acidification. The most recent, and first, multi-year global bleaching event (spanning hundreds of kilometres or more) was from 2014 to 2017. Nearly 30% of reefs suffered mortality level-stress, more than 50% of affected reef areas were impacted at least twice, and some locations experienced almost complete coral cover loss (Blunden et al. 2018, Vargas-Angel et al. 2019, Eakin et al. 2019). The average interval between bleaching events is now more than 50% less than before, preventing full reef recovery (Hughes et al. 2018).

Coral disease has also emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide and is a major cause of reef deterioration (Weil et al. 2006, Richards et al. 2008, Maynard et al. 2015). As noted in Walton et al. (2018), in addition to thermal stress, increased coral disease prevalence and mortality can be linked to reduced water quality (Bruno et al. 2003) and clarity (van Woesik and McCaffrey 2017), nutrient enrichment (Vega Thurber et al. 2013), dredging associated sedimentation (Pollock et al. 2014, Miller et al. 2016), and plastic pollution. Based on a survey of 159 reefs in the Asia-Pacific region, the likelihood of disease increases 20-fold when corals are in contact with plastic (Lamb et al. 2018). Increased coral disease levels on the Great Barrier Reef were correlated with increased ocean temperatures (Boyett et al. 2007) supporting the prediction that disease levels will be increasing with higher sea surface temperatures.

Localized threats to this species include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, resort development, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, marine debris, and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual coral species is not known, however, more than 60% of the world’s reefs are immediately threatened by local pressures (http://www.wri.org/project/reefs-at-risk; Bridge et al. 2013).
population:
This is a common species that is often the most abundant coral from 1-10 m depth. This species showed strong population differentiation among Puerto Rico, lower Florida Keys and the Yucatan Peninsula populations (Severance and Karl 2006). Populations of this species have been genetically differentiated into three regions in the greater Caribbean: eastern (Lesser Antilles, Venezuela and Curaçao), western (the Bahamas, Cuba, Belize and Cayman Islands) and central (Jamaica, Honduras, Nicaragua, Colombia, Puerto Rico, British Virgin Islands and Dominican Republic) (Foster et al. 2012). The population structure between Belize and Honduras is attributed to an ephemeral salinity gradient that could act as a temporary barrier of low salinity that may reduce the survival of larvae moving from Honduras to Belize (Foster et al. 2012).

Populations of this species are generally dominated by medium size to very large colonies. In shallow areas, it can grow and create continuous large colonies. In the Mexican Caribbean, it has an average minimum size that ranges from 4 to 309 cm2 and maximum sizes of 3,366 to 4,370 cm2 (Hernández-Landa et al. 2020) and in some reefs, like Puerto Morelos, colonies as large as three metres in diameter can be found. In southwest Gulf of Mexico reefs, this species is widespread and common and it can be the dominant coral species. In a study conducted in 2014, the relative abundance of this species ranged among reefs from 1 to 21%, and colony densities from 0.03 to 1.2 col m-2 (Mean: 0.2; SD: 0.3) (E. Jordán-Dahlgren pers. comm. 2020).

In Venezuela, this species is conspicuous across the oceanic islands and along the western and central coast, where it contributes the bulk of cover in some reefs (Miyazawa et al. 2020). In Cuba, this species was reported among the most abundant species in coral communities located at depths of 5-18 m in Maria la Gorda, where it represented 11% of the colonies recorded (Caballero et al. 2007). In the Dominican Republic, this species represents the major reef builder across several sites of  the southeastern coast (Cortés-Useche et al. 2019, Reef Check Report 2019), particularly within MPAs that show the greatest alfa and beta diversity of the island.

Off Curaçao, the combined current abundance of Montastraea annularis/faveolata (Orbicella annularis/faveolata) (in terms of percentage bottom cover) is 3.14% (SD: 3.76, n=145 sites in 2015 at 10 m depths (Waitt Institute 2017), off Aruba: 1.45% (SD: 2.76, n=53 sites in 2019) (Carmabi unpubl. data). Off Curaçao, a decline in population sizes occurred as historic cover (1973) was 24.2% (Nagelkerken 1979, Nagelkerken et al. 2005). The abundance of this species declined from 14.1% in 1973 to 9.8% in 2005 off Bonaire (de Bakker 2019). Recruitment rates are extremely low and no juveniles were ever observed off Curaçao (Bak and Engel 1979, Vermeij et al. 2011). Bonaire and Curaçao have some of the least degraded reefs in the Caribbean (Jackson et al. 2014) and the decreases in adult abundance and low recruitment under favorable conditions indicate that population persistence in this species is likely even more compromised in other locations.

Live coral cover of this species is greatly variable throughout its range. Data from the CARICOMP project shows that cover of this species ranged from 1 to 27% among the fore-reefs of several Caribbean countries from 1993 to 2006. During this period, different trends were recorded. This includes massive mortality of reefs dominated by this species (e.g. Morrocoy National Park massive mortality; Villamizar 2000, Labboy-Nieves et al. 2001) and large decline for this species in reefs of La Parguera (e.g. Turrumote and Media Luna; E. Weil pers. comm. 2008) to stability in reefs of Trinidad and Tobago (A. Croquer et al. in prep. 2021).

The cover of this species can also fluctuate greatly in time in a single reef. On the leeward side of the island of Bonaire, Dutch Caribbean, this species was found to be dominant, representing an average of 12% cover over a period of ~15 years (Steneck et al. 2019). However, this species had a decline over several years due to hurricane and bleaching events in Bonaire, yet seven years post disturbance this species recovered to ~13% cover, similar to pre-disturbances conditions (Steneck et al. 2019).

In the last 30 years, there has been a severe decline in the overall cover and abundance of this species in several parts of the Caribbean. For example, 90% of the cover of the species was lost in the coastal waters off Jamaica from 1980 through 1994 (Hughes 1994). Off the coast of eastern Puerto Rico, declines in cover were recorded at between 40 and 60% (Hernández-Delgado 2005), at around 40% off southeastern Puerto Rico (E. Weil pers. comm. 2008), 50% off Mona Island (Bruckner and Bruckner 2006), and 72% in St. John, US Virgin Islands, between 1988 and 1999 (Edmunds and Elahi 2007). Dustan and Halas (1987) observed a 31% decline in cover of the annularis complex on Carysfort Reef (Key Largo) between 1975-1982, with a 21% decline in colony size.

After the mass bleaching events of 2005 and 2010, reductions in the coral cover of this species of up to 40% were recorded in Venezuela (Del Mónaco et al. 2012) and other Caribbean countries (Brandt and McManus 2009). In Panama, a study from 2002-2013 measured the long-term impacts of bleaching events in the reproductive capacity of this species and recorded a lower spawning rate of 79% and 95% of this species right after the bleaching events in 2005 and 2010 respectively (Levitan et al. 2014). Demographic simulations conducted for this species in Culebra Island, Puerto Rico, predicted a 54% decline in the next 100 years if bleaching continues to occur (Hernández-Pacheco et al. 2011). Off the northern coast of Belize, declines up to 90% were recorded for this species (Burke et al. 2004). Recruitment failure for this species (1977-1993) has been described in Jamaica (Hughes and Tanner 2000). Long term data sets are rare for other locations, so the possibility that recruitment failure has also occurred elsewhere is high.

In Mexico, species within this genus remained as major reef builders after the acroporid die-off in the 1980s, in reefs of the southwest Gulf of Mexico, the Campeche Bank and the Caribbean. In the Campeche Bank and the Caribbean, the populations of this species decreased in the last two decades in many areas mainly due to diseases (e.g. yellow band, white plague) and bleaching impacts (Harvell et al. 2007). Of high concern is that remnant populations are currently rapidly succumbing to a recent emergent outbreak of Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2019). In the southwest Gulf of Mexico, populations of species in this genus have been less affected by diseases and bleaching events compared to the Caribbean (Jordán-Garza et al. 2017).
range: This species is distributed in the western Atlantic from the Flower Garden Banks in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico and Mexico (Veracruz) to south Florida and the Bahamas southward throughout the Caribbean to Trinidad and Tobago. It also occurs in Bermuda. The depth range is 0.5-82 metres (Reed 1985).
useTrade: According to the CITES Trade Database, there is practically no international trade in this species.
conservationActions:
All corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. In Mexico, this species is listed as 'Endangered' (SEMARNAT 2010). In U.S. waters, it is illegal to harvest corals for commercial purposes. 

This species is present in several marine protected areas (MPAs). In the U.S., it is present in many MPAs, including Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, Biscayne National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Buck Island Reef National Monument and Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary. It is also present in Hol Chan Marine Reserve (Belize), Exuma Cays Land, Sea Park (Bahamas), and in several MPAs in the Mexican Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico. Studies conducted in the southwest Gulf of Mexico from 2010 to 2017 recorded this species in three MPAs, with percentage occurrences of 89% in the Sistema Arrecifal Lobos-Tuxpan (9 reefs), 85% in the Sistema Arrecifal Veracruzano (20 reefs) and 6% in the Sistema Arrecifal Los Tuxtlas (33 reefs) (Jordán-Garza et al. 2017).

Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in taxonomy, population, abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration actions via sexual propagation and/or micro fragmentation techniques; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management. Assisted propagation and techniques such as cryo-preservation of gametes may become important for conserving coral biodiversity. The coral biorepository in Mexico (Coralium-UNAM) includes cryopreserved Orbicella annularis sperm.

rationale: This widely distributed species is common. Global level, species-specific population data are limited; however, coral reefs have declined globally and are expected to continue rapidly declining due to increasing severe bleaching conditions under temperature stress caused by climate change as well as a variety of other threats. Our species-specific vulnerability traits analysis indicates this species is moderately susceptible to major threats related to coral reef degradation (e.g., disease and bleaching). We applied two analytical approaches involving two different global coral datasets and the species’ distribution map as proxies to infer population decline. Based on global coral cover monitoring data, this species experienced an inferred decline of <20% over the past three generations, or since 1989. Based on the projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) conditions via both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios of global climate model data, this species is inferred to decline by less than 25% over the next three generations, or by 2050. This species is therefore listed as Least Concern.
habitat:
Both the zooxanthellate (Madracis pharensis f. luciphila) and the azooxanthellate form (Madracis pharensis f. pharensis, likely a different species) are found in cryptic habitats (e.g. in crevices, caves, under ledges) in fore reef and deep reef environments, and also in silty, back reef lagoon environments. The zooxanthellate form (Madracis pharensis f. luciphila) is found across large depth gradients but common in deep-water fore reef environments below 25 m where it appears more on exposed surfaces on the reef bottom with a maximum depth recorded of 99 m (Reed 1985).

The diagnostic character that distinguishes M. pharensis from other Madracis in the Caribbean is the presence of paliform lobes in front of the main septa. In the original description of the two forms of M. pharensis from Jamaica, Wells (1973) used the colony form as the main distinguishing character, so he referred to expanding, laminar, or encrusting sheets as M. pharensis f. luciphila, while encrusting stolon-like ribbons, with infrequent nodular proliferations, and lucifugous as the typical form M. pharensis f. pharensis. These two forms were thought to be ecomorphs of the same species with morphological differences driven by light exposure (Fenner 1993). Later, the divergence in response to light was linked to different degrees of genetic exchange within the M. pharensis/decactis complex in habitats of varying complexity (Vermeij et al. 2007).

In other Madracis species, genetic splits have been found based on their ecological distribution, with shallow water species (M. mirabilis and M. decactis) clustering in the same clade, while deep water or depth generalist species forming a second clade (M. senaria, M. carmabi and M. formosa) (Frade et al. 2008). This species represents an exception: genetic analyses revealed that M. pharensis specimens cluster together with their depth-congenerics from shallow and deep reef habitats (with threshold about 23-24 m), rather than with their conspecifics (Frade et al. 2010). This genetic differentiation also matches exactly with the symbiont type harboured: Breviolum ITS2 type B7 in the shallows (< 25 m depth) and B15 in the deep habitats (>25 m depth), representing ecological zonation of this species’ symbionts (Frade et al. 2008). The genotype B15 dominates the deeper symbiont populations associated with M. pharensis f. luciphila all the way down to the host’s lower limit of distribution of  >90 m depth (Bongaerts et al. 2015).

This is a hermaphroditic brooding species. Oocyte development typically begins in June and precedes the development of spermaries. Mature gametes, male and female, are present from September to November when seawater temperatures reach their yearly maximum (Vermeij et al. 2004). This species releases azooxanthellate larvae (0.027-0.029 mm3 in size) in small numbers over multiple months each year from April to December with maximum releases from September to November and whereby spawning intensity fluctuates highly at a daily scale. On average, this species (on Curaçao) releases 0.04 planula per day per cm2 adult tissue. Larval release is not related to a moon-phase. Different colour morphs differ in the percentage of gravid colonies, not in the number of larvae produced per tissue area (Vermeij et al. 2003, 2004).

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
There are no major threats known, and the deeper zooxanthellate form has not been reported to bleach.

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide and a major cause of reef deterioration (Weil et al. 2006). The numbers of diseases and coral species affected, as well as the distribution of diseases have all increased dramatically within the last decade (Green and Bruckner 2000, Porter et al. 2001, Sutherland et al. 2004, Weil 2004). Coral disease epizootics have resulted in significant losses of coral cover and were implicated in the dramatic decline of acroporids in the Florida Keys (Aronson and Precht 2001, Porter et al. 2001, Patterson et al. 2002). Escalating anthropogenic stressors combined with the threats associated with global climate change of increases in coral disease, frequency and duration of coral bleaching and ocean acidification place coral reefs at high risk of collapse.

Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual coral species is not known.
population:
This species is common, but occurs in low abundances throughout its range. It can be abundant on structurally complex reefs with high availability of cryptic habitats. Densities up to 8 individuals per projected square meter of reef area have been reported from the Southern Caribbean (Vermeij and Bak 2003). 

Abundance estimates for the genus Madracis typically are <1% benthic cover in most locations (González-Rivero et al. 2019; 2020). For example, extensive surveys across 108 reefs from 12 Caribbean countries (158,000 m2 photographed) in 2013 detected Madracis spp. in 5% of meter-square photo quadrats. Mean abundances in terms of percent cover per reef were 0.39% ±3.00 SD. Percent cover estimates ranged from 0.003% ± 0.085 SD in the Bahamas (where Madracis spp. were observed in just 0.2% of quadrats) to 3.002% ± 8.341 in Curaçao where it was found in 26% of quadrats on the fore reef. Other localities where the percentage of benthic cover for Madracis spp. have been estimated: Turks and Caicos (0.004±0.077%), St. Vincent (0.043±0.965%), St. Eustatius (0.009±0.154%), Mexico (0.018±0.195%), Guadeloupe (0.079±1.081%), Bonaire (1.287±4.410%), Bermuda (0.006±0.090%), Belize (0.021±0.266%), Aruba (1.277±5.811%) and Anguilla (0.004±0.086%) (González-Rivero et al. 2019, Catlin Seaview Survey dataset).

Species-specific, global level population information is limited. However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hughes et al. 2018). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.     

Approach 1: Future population trend

The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that corals are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022). 

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is poorly understood and varies by species and locality (van Hooidonk et al. 2013, Logan et al. 2014). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells.

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2030 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2034 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2059 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2072 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on 1°C of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is moderately susceptible to bleaching. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the understanding that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and is expected to decline at a faster global rate than species that also or primarily occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Atlantic, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in the Mediterranean Sea (Flecha et al. 2015). Therefore, this species is inferred to experience a projected global level decline of less than 25% by the year 2050, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario.  

Approach 2: Past population trend

Coral reef monitoring data was also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the five Caribbean subregions (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range in the Caribbean. Sufficient estimates of coral cover loss are not available for the part of the range extending beyond the Caribbean (i.e. eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean); therefore, for the purposes of estimating global level decline per this Red List assessment, an assumption of 'no change' was applied for that area.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered nine species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 5-99 m and is predominately found at depths greater than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered common, overall population is not highly fragmented, does occur off-reef, is moderately susceptible to disease, does not recover well from bleaching or disease and is moderately susceptible to bleaching, it is overall inferred to be moderately susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 50% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a global level decline of <20% since 1989, or over the past three generations.
range:
This species is distributed in the western Atlantic from North Carolina, U.S. to Florida, Bermuda, throughout the Gulf of Mexico and the Bahamas southward throughout the Caribbean to Trinidad and Tobago. The form M. pharensis f. pharensis is also known from the eastern Atlantic (Azores, Cape Verde Islands and Canary Islands), and Mediterranean (Cairns and Zibrowius 1997, see discussion in Cairns 2000: 44-45), although genetic and morphological characteristics strongly suggest the ecotypes are in fact a different species than the Caribbean zooxanthellate form M. pharensis f. luciphila (Benzoni et al. 2018). The depth range is 5-99 m (Reed 1985) but the species usually occurs from 5-30 m. 

There is another azooxanthellate Madracis form referred to as M. sp. cf M. pharensis that has been recorded in various Pacific localities (see Benzoni et al. 2018), including the Philippines and Fiji (Cairns and Zibrowius 1997), the Galapagos (Wells 1983, Cairns 1991, Hickman 2008), and in the Gulf of California, Mexico (Reyes Bonilla et al. 1995, Cairns and Zibrowius 1997). Reyes Bonilla et al. (1995) and Benzoni et al. (2018) suggest based on skeletal morphology that the Pacific form may be a distinct species. Here we treat this non-reef-building coral in the Pacific as distinct from M. pharensis.
useTrade: This species is not utilized. Atlantic reef corals are not part of the international trade for the aquarium industry (B. Hoeksema pers. comm. 2022).
conservationActions:
All corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. In U.S. waters, it is illegal to harvest corals for commercial purposes. Parts of the species’ range overlaps with marine protected areas (MPAs). In the U.S., this species is present in many MPAs, including Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, Biscayne National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Buck Island Reef National Monument and Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary. It is also present in Hol Chan Marine Reserve (Belize), Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park (Bahamas). In Colombia, this species occurs in protected areas in the Tayrona Natural Park, Rosario and San Bernardo Natural Park, and the Deep-Sea Corals Natural Park (Santodomingo et al. 2007, Reyes et al. 2010). 

There is a need for more quantitative information on the status of this species because of its occurrence in cryptic habitats, deep water and low abundance (R. Aronson, W. Precht, J. Moore, E. Weil and A. Bruckner pers. comm. 2008).

Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in taxonomy, population, abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration action; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management. Artificial propagation and techniques such as cryo-preservation of gametes may become important for conserving coral biodiversity.

rationale: This species is widely distributed and rare. Global level, species-specific population data are limited; however, coral reefs have declined globally and are expected to continue rapidly declining due to increasing severe bleaching conditions under temperature stress caused by climate change as well as a variety of other threats. Our species-specific vulnerability traits analysis indicates this species is moderately susceptible to major threats related to coral reef degradation (e.g., disease and bleaching). We applied two analytical approaches involving two different global coral datasets and the species’ distribution map as proxies to infer population decline. Based on global coral cover monitoring data, this species experienced a suspected decline of less than 25% over the past three generations, or since 1989. Based on the projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) conditions via both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios of global climate model data, in combination with the species’ depth range, distribution and bleaching vulnerability, this species is suspected to decline by less than 25% over the next three generations, or by 2050. It is listed as Least Concern. The change in status from the previous assessment reflects updated declines calculated from improved data on modeled coral cover loss and projected date of annual severe bleaching, along with improved knowledge of species traits.
habitat:
This species occurs in shallow reef environments on the back and foreslope of the reef and in lagoons. 

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
The major threats are global warming and predation. The bleaching of coral reefs, which has become increasingly frequent since the 1970s, is related to the ongoing rise in ocean in temperatures as a result of global climate change. Bleaching events, leading to coral mortality, are predicted to become more frequent and severe.

Other more localised threats include coral removal and harvesting, disturbance by fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, storms, and human recreation and tourism activities.

However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, Donovan et al. 2021). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.

The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is little understood and varies by species and locality (Bay et al. 2017, Matz et al. 2020, Logan et al. 2021). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells.

The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Approach 2: Past population trend
Coral reef monitoring data were also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the 37 subregions of the Indo-Pacific (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered 11 species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 3-40 m and is predominately found at depths greater than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered rare, overall population is not restricted or highly fragmented, does not occur off-reef, is highly susceptible to disease, has a moderate recovery potential from bleaching or disease, has a low susceptibility to crown-of-thorns starfish, is moderately susceptible to bleaching, has a relatively higher susceptibility to the impacts of ocean acidification (Kornder et al. 2018), did not have >10,000 pieces exported annually in the aquarium trade between 2010-2019, it is overall suspected to be moderately susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. It is commonly found from 3-11 m, rarely from 12-15 m, in the South China Sea and Gulf of Siam (Titlyanov and Titlyanova 2002). The sizes of small, medium and large colonies of this species had decreased significantly (up to >50%) along the Great Barrier Reef from 1995/1996 to 2016/2017 (Dietzel et al. 2020). This species, once common, has been decimated in the Chagos Archipelago (Sheppard et al. 2020). This is a brooder and therefore has a smaller sexual reproductive output and limited dispersal capacity (Z. Richards pers. comm. 2008). This species is sensitive to ocean acidification; increased pCO2 leads to lower coral calcification (Iguchi et al. 2014). Under high CO2 concentrations (550 and 1000 ppm pCO2), the growth of this species is significantly impeded, probably owing to reduced aragonite levels (Yusuf et al. 2019). 

The growth of this species is very sensitive to temperature (Anderson et al. 2017, Razak et al. 2017; 2020). Skeletal density of this species declined linearly and significantly at a rate of 1.2% yr-1 between 2002 and 2012 at an offshore reef (Myrmidon Reef) of the central Great Barrier Reef (GBR), Australia. The collection of this species for the aquarium trade may lead to overharvest and localised reductions in abundance, especially for populations of naturally rare species (Bruckner and Borneman 2006). However, the wild collection of corals is highly selective and considered low impact in the long-term relative to other activities such as coral mining and dynamite fishing (Green and Shirley 1999, Pratchett et al. 2020).

We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2035 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2039 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2062 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2071 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0–30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on no level of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is highly susceptible to bleaching. For widespread species, the final estimate of decline was further adjusted by excluding the proportion of cells within its range that were expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 after 2050 (three generation lengths), in order to account for the potential resilience of species to the asynchronous variability of bleaching events that occur across the Indo-Pacific. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Pacific, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in high-latitude reefs (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of at least 62% by the year 2050, or three generations in the future, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario. 

Approach 2: Past population trend
Coral reef monitoring data were also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the 37 subregions of the Indo-Pacific (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered 11 species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 0-40 m and is predominately found at depths less than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered common, overall population is not restricted or highly fragmented, does not occur off-reef, is highly susceptible to disease, does not recover well from bleaching or disease, has a high susceptibility to crown-of-thorns starfish, is highly susceptible to bleaching, has a relatively higher susceptibility to the impacts of ocean acidification (Kornder et al. 2018), did not have >10,000 pieces exported annually in the aquarium trade between 2010-2019, it is overall suspected to be highly susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 80% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a suspected global level decline of 11% since 1989, or over the past three generations.
range:
This species is found in the southwest and northern Indian Ocean, the central Indo-Pacific, Australia, Southeast Asia, Japan, the East China Sea, the oceanic west Pacific, Micronesia (Z. Richards pers. comm. 2008) and American Samoa (C. Wallace and D. Fenner pers. comm. 2008). 

The depth range is 0-40 m, but the species primarily occurs from 1-15 m (Muir et al. 2015, L. DeVantier pers. comm. 2024).
useTrade: This species is moderately traded for aquaria, with 1,000-10,000 pieces being collected from the wild and exported annually between 2010-2020 (CITES 2021).
conservationActions: All stony corals (Order: Scleractinia) are listed on CITES Appendix II, and under Annex B of the European Union Wildlife Trade Regulations. Moreover, several countries (e.g., India, Israel, Jordan, Djibouti, Fiji and the Philippines) at various stages have banned either the trade or the export of CITES II listed species, which includes all stony corals. Other countries such as Indonesia, trade maricultured corals, with quotas, production limit and regulations in place to ensure the trade is sustainable.

rationale: This species occurs on shallow, rocky substrate and has a relatively small range off West Africa. In general, little is known on its population and ecology as well as its potential susceptibility to bleaching, which is a globally pervasive threat to corals. This species, which is very patchily distributed, may also be impacted by other local threats, but the limited research conducted on coral reefs of West Africa causes these impacts to be poorly understood in general. It is therefore listed as Data Deficient with a recommendation to conduct coral research and develop bleaching monitoring programs in the West African region. Taxonomic research is also needed to resolve questions in the Oculinidae family.
habitat:
This species occurs on rocky foreshores and shallow, well-lit horizontal rock surfaces. It has also been observed in estuaries and a nearly landlocked mangrove channel near Libreville (Laborel 1974). 

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
The relative vulnerability of this species to bleaching is unknown, but it could possibly be impacted. The lack of coral reef research or monitoring of bleaching in the West African region causes its susceptibility to bleaching to be poorly understood (B. Hoeksema and F. Nunes pers. comm. 2022).  

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification. In addition to global climate change, corals are also threatened by a number of localized threats. Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual coral species is not known.
population: This species is uncommon. It was observed as covering <5% of the benthos in photo-quadrat surveys conducted off São Tomé Island (Maia 2018). Note that while the species listed in Maia’s 2018 PhD thesis is Schizoculina africana, this has been corrected to Schizoculina fissipara in the paper published in Marine Ecology (Maia et al. 2018). Schizoculina africana is rare in São Tomé (Laborel 1974), and was not observed during the expedition to São Tomé conducted by Floeter and colleagues (F. Nunes pers. comm. 2022).
range:
This species is distributed in the eastern Atlantic off West Africa from Sierra Leone to Angola, including the São Tomé and Príncipe Islands. It is not present in Senegal or the Cape Verde Islands. The depth range is 0-10 metres (Laborel 1974). 

This species is patchily distributed across its relatively limited range as it only settles on rocky substrate and does not occur in the long stretches of sandy or sediment-rich coastlines influenced by the presence of outflows and estuaries associated with the Niger, Volta and Congo Rivers that are located along West Africa. Spatial data are not available to estimate an area of occupancy (AOO) at this time, but AOO may be limited and should be estimated in future assessments of this species if data become available (F. Nunes pers. comm. 2022).

Genetic studies are needed to resolve taxonomic questions in the Oculinidae family (Leydet and Hellberg 2015), which may affect the inferred distributions of Schizoculina africana and its congener, Schizoculina fissipara.
useTrade: This species is not utilized. Atlantic reef corals are not part of the international trade for the aquarium industry (B. Hoeksema pers. comm. 2022).
conservationActions:
All corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. Parts of the species’ range overlaps with marine protected areas (MPAs).

Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in taxonomy, population, abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration action; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management. Artificial propagation and techniques such as cryo-preservation of gametes may become important for conserving coral biodiversity.  

Genetic studies are needed to resolve taxonomic questions in the Oculinidae family (Leydet and Hellberg 2015).

rationale:
This coral species is primarily found in the Mediterranean Sea, with a small number of records in adjacent parts of the eastern Atlantic (Morocco and Portugal). In the Mediterranean Sea, the species is widespread and can be locally abundant. It can form extensive banks, but also occurs as scattered, non-reef forming colonies.

This is a long lived, colonial species with an estimated generation length of 30 years. The most extensive populations described to date, inhabiting the Adriatic Sea and Columbretes Islands, have been reported to have severely declined during the past decades, impacted by a range of threats. Over the nine-year period from 2003 to 2012, the population in the Columbretes Islands declined by 55-80%. Other subpopulations have also declined, including the Gulf of La Spezia, Dardanelles (Marmara Sea, Turkey) and Cyprus, although quantitative measures of declines are not available. Although declines cannot be measured over the past three generation lengths (~90 years), the main threat to this species, which is global climate change resulting in warming seawater temperatures, is expected to continue and perhaps worsen, in the near future. Populations can recover from the mortality events through a recently discovered survival and recovery strategy called rejuvenescence and the establishment of new colonies by recruitment. However, the recruitment rate for this long-lived species is extremely low and it is not able to compensate for the increasing mortality rates. While, although rejuvenescence has shown to be an effective recovery mechanism, the increased frequency and intensity of warming events most probably outpace the recovery capacity of the species. Within a three generation length period that includes the past and present, it is inferred that the population will decline by at least 55% to perhaps as high as 80%, as has been documented in the banks at the Columbretes Islands. Although these declines nearly reach the threshold for Critically Endangered, the non-reef forming colonies throughout the Mediterranean Sea are persisting at present levels of mortality. Therefore, this species is assessed as Endangered A4bc.

Continuous monitoring of the species populations is highly recommended. This species should be re-evaluated in five years to include additional information and to determine the effects of continued or increased threats from climate change and direct anthropogenic impacts.
habitat:
This species occurs on a wide range of reef substratum, a range of depths (commonly from 5 to 40 m depth), and hydrodynamic conditions (Zibrowius 1980). In Cyprus, the species occurs from 1-5 m depth (L. Hadjioannou pers. comm. 2015), whilst in several western Mediterranean localities, such as the Medes Islands and Cap de Creus, the species is commonly found below 20 m depth in dim light conditions (Kersting 2013). The capacity of the species to tolerate a range of environments and to withstand seasonal abiotic factors such as temperature and light, typical of temperate seas as the Mediterranean, is probably related to the ability of this species to regulate autotrophy and heterotrophy depending on the environmental light conditions, as suggested by Hoogenboom et al. (2010). Preferred environmental conditions appears to include lower concentrations of calcite and phosphate and areas with lower wave height and complex coastlines (Chefaoui et al. 2017). The species occurs in both clear waters as well as quite turbid waters (D. Kersting pers. comm. 2022).

This species may occur in a wide range of reef habitats, from shallow photophilic communities to circalittoral assemblages, however, the equilibrium between hydrodynamic protection and high water exchange through strong currents seems to enhance the development of extensive populations, such as in the Mjlet National Park and Columbretes Islands (Kružić and Benkovic 2008, Kersting and Linares 2012). 

Early studies considered high prevalence of macroalgae to be a limiting factor in the development of this coral (e.g., Peirano et al. 1998, Rodolfo-Metalpa et al. 1999). However, the coral has been shown to be able to successfully compete with macroalgae in some localities, such as in Illa Grossa Bay where algal cover is high and most of the coral colonies and banks occur within the infralittoral photophilic algal community (Kersting and Linares 2012, Kersting 2013). In this sense, it is remarkable that many of the populations in the NW Mediterranean (e.g., Formentera, Menorca, Columbretes Islands) thrive among well-developed shallow algal communities, showing either neutral or even positive relationships and, in some cases, the coral facilitates the development of population of certain perennial long-lived algal species (Kersting et al. 2017a, Pons-Fita et al. 2020; 2021). These studies show a predominant concurrence of corals and macroalgae in these areas. In other localities, such the Adriatic and Marmara seas, the presence of invasive algae (mainly Caulerpa racemosa) has been observed to impact the growth of the species (Kružić and Požar-Domac 2007, B. Özalp pers. comm. 2014).

Sexual reproduction of this species has been recorded in situ in the Adriatic Sea (Kružic et al. 2008), where the coral has been described as hermaphroditic at colony and polyp levels. Spawning has been observed to occur coinciding with increasing summer water temperature and correlated with the lunar cycle. Eggs are released by the polyps in a mucus coating that binds them together as clumps of eggs, while sperm are freely released (Kružic et al. 2008). In the western Mediterranean, histological analyses have shown that this species is gonochoric (Kersting et al. 2013c). Spawning time has been observed to differ significantly between the Adriatic Sea and the western Mediterranean; in the former, spawning was observed at the beginning of summer, coinciding with rising seawater temperatures (Kružic et al. 2008), whilst in the western Mediterranean, spawning seems to occur at the end of the summer coinciding with the cooling of seawater temperature (Kersting et al. 2013c). These notable differences between these two regions should be further investigated.

Based on average sizes and growth rates of the species, we assume that average generation length is 30 years. Average longevity is not known, but is likely to be more than 100 years. In the Adriatic Sea and Columbretes Islands, colonies of up to 300 years of age have been described.
threats:
This is a long-lived species with slow life history dynamics (low recruitment and natural mortality rates) and limited dispersal capability (Kersting and Linares 2012, Kersting et al. 2014b, López-Márquez et al. 2019; 2021); thus, significant impacts to its mortality rates may easily overcome its capacity to recover through recruitment exacerbating the long-term impacts from climate change (Kersting et al. 2014b). However, the species exhibits some survival strategies, including rejuvenescence, that increases recovery from major mortality events over a subsequent period of several years. Although, the predicted increased frequency of heat waves will likely reduce the effectiveness of this strategy (Kersting and Linares 2019).

Mass mortalities of this species related to seawater warming and summer heat waves have been reported in several Mediterranean localities (Perez et al. 2000, Rodolfo-Metalpa et al. 2005, Garrabou et al. 2009, Kružić et al. 2012, Kersting et al. 2013b, L. Hadjioannou pers. comm. 2015). Increasing seawater temperature in shallow waters as well as short times recorded between mortality events have severe consequences for the viability of the affected populations of this species. These populations also show a dramatic decrease in biomass, along with a very slow recovery. Seawater temperatures recorded during the summer of 2003 were the warmest in the past 30 years (Garrabou et al. 2009). During these years, not only were temperatures high, but the warm and stable conditions lasted for an unusually long time (more than one month). In the case of the Columbretes Islands population, a positive correlation between temperature and mortality rates in colonies of this species was observed over this period (Kersting et al. 2013b). These recurrent mortalities are expected to affect over 50% of the colony cover in this area during the next decade (Kersting et al. 2013b). Severe impacts from increasing heat waves are expected to continue in the Mediterranean as climate change progresses (Galli et al. 2017, Cramer et al. 2018, Garrabou et al. 2019).

An experimental study showed that the presence of turf-forming invasive algae (i.e., Womersleyella setacea) could act in synergy with warming and increase the mortality rates of this species (Kersting et al. 2015). The presence of the invasive algae Caulerpa cylindracea has been reported in Mjlet National Park (Kružić et al. 2012), Columbretes Islands (Kersting et al. 2014a) and Dardanos region (B. Özalp pers. comm. 2013), and the spread of this invasive algae over the most important known populations of this coral is concerning. In the case of Columbretes Island population, another invasive algal species has been also observed, Lophocladia lallemandii. No lethal effects derived from C. cylindracea and L. lallemandi invasions have been detected in the population of this species in the Columbretes Islands as the adult colonies successfully compete with the algae. However, sublethal effects derived of the algal invasion on other stages of the life cycle of this species, such as recruitment and juvenile survival cannot be disregarded (Kersting et al. 2014a). The invasive alga C. cylindracea is also present in C. caespitosa populations in some areas of the Dardanos region have been significantly impacted by the invasive algae C. cylindracea, which occurs at shallow depths to 18 m. In this area, in some instances, colonies previously impacted by warming-induced necrosis are completely covered by the algae, and a more intensive study is being undertaken at this site to distinguish between the potential damage of increasing seawater temperature and algae coverage of the colonies (B. Özalp pers. comm. 2013). Blooms of benthic mucilaginous aggregates, which are composed of different algal species and organic matter, cause necrosis and reduced colony density and cover in this species and may represent an additional serious threat (De Biasi et al. 2021).

Negative impacts resulting from eutrophication have been described in some populations of this species (e.g., Croatia and Cyprus; Kružić and Požar-Domac 2007, L. Hadjioannou pers. comm. 2015); however, the species survives in both nutrient-rich and nutrient-poor conditions (Hadjioannou et al. 2019). Anthropogenic activities such as industrial and sewage discharges, trawling and other fishing activities and coastal development have caused a major decline in the eastern Adriatic Sea. Trawling and dredging are probably the most destructive impacts currently affecting marine bioconstructors, including this species, resulting in physical damage to coral colonies and habitat destruction. Small-scale line fisheries, such as in the Dardanelles Strait, cause localised impacts as a result of boat anchors. High sedimentation rates due to beach replenishing or dredging may cause the collapse of colonies. Although, increased water turbidity may be accompanied by an elevation of the deepest limit of distribution of this coral (Carbonne et al. 2021). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Atlantic, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in the Mediterranean Sea (Flecha et al. 2015). This species may have some resiliency to the threat from ocean acidification and further study is warranted (Carbonne et al. 2021).
population:
This species is part of the recent fossil history of the Mediterranean Sea. Since the Pliocene, it has been the only species that develops monospecific reef-like structures in the Mediterranean Basin. The oldest fossil records of banks of this species are those described by Aguirre and Jiménez (1998) from the Upper Pliocene shallow marine deposit of the Almería-Nijar basin (southeastern Spain). This coral species became very common in some Quaternary peri-Mediterranean basins and diverse Holocene and Pleistocene fossil banks have been described from several areas (e.g., Cuerda et al. 1986, Fornós et al. 1996, Kühlmann et al. 1996, Bernasconi et al. 1997). Furthermore, Laborel (1987) mentioned the existence of extensive dead banks of this species (dated around 2,500-3,000 years ago) on the coasts of Tunisia and Corsica.

Though this species has occurrences across most of the Mediterranean basin, the majority of its global population occurs in 10 banks and 21 beds distributed across the northern Mediterranean (Chefaoui et al. 2017). Only in a very few cases have populations of this species been described in terms of cover, distribution, health status and population dynamics (Schiller 1993; Peirano et al. 2001; Kružić and Benkovic 2008; Kersting and Linares 2012; Kersting et al. 2013b, 2014b, 2017a, 2021a,b). Following the available information, the most important sites for this species in terms of colony cover and extent are in Mjlet National Park (Croatia, Adriatic Sea; Kružić and Benkovic 2008) and the Columbretes Islands Marine Reserve (Spain, NW Mediterranean; Kersting and Linares 2012). Nevertheless, as exploration efforts increase, other important populations have been discovered and described during the last years (e.g., Kersting et al. 2017a, 2021a,b). According to the most recent Red List assessment (Casado de Amezua et al. 2015), information on both population size and trend was only available for the population of Illa Grossa Bay (Columbretes Islands, NW Mediterranean; Kersting and Linares 2012; Kersting et al. 2013a, 2014b). Detailed information on population size and/or structure is also available for populations of the Adriatic coasts in the islands Prvić, Pag and Iz and in the Mjlet National Park as well as for the populations inhabiting the Marmara Sea (B. Özalp pers. comm. 2013).

Population genetic studies conducted in the western Mediterranean basin (Casado-Amezúa et al. 2014) suggest that populations of this species are highly dependent on self-recruitment. Although, the genetic connectivity among the populations seems to be related to sporadic dispersal events. These features indicate a reduced resilience of the populations mainly driven by the high levels of self-recruitment. A population genetics study conducted in Cyprus and Greece reported low genetic connectivity between populations separated by only 11 km (López-Márquez et al. 2021). Genetic differentiation among localities in the Adriatic and northern Ionian Seas was also relatively low (López-Márquez et al. 2019).

Columbretes Islands, Spain subpopulation: The population of this species in Illa Grosa Bay (Columbretes Islands) is formed by a combination of banks and separate colonies (beds) with a highly aggregated distribution between 5 and 30 m depth. The cumulative cover area of this species in the bay was estimated to be approximately 2,900 m2. Regarding the growth rates obtained for this population (~ 2.5 mm year-1), some of the coral colonies in the Columbretes could reach ages up to 300 years (Kersting and Linares 2012). Cover of this species in Illa Grossa Bay declined by 55-80% due to recurrent mortalities related to warming and extreme summer water temperatures (Kersting et al. 2013b). This climate-induced necrosis has been recorded over nine summers from 2003 to 2012, in two mortality periods (2003-2006 and 2008-2012). The first mortality period, and especially the summer of 2003, triggered high necrosis in this population, while impacts over the second period were milder. This indicates that extreme hot summers, such as in 2003, have a significant negative impact on this population. Furthermore, the summer of 2003 had delayed effects in the following summers resulting in an increase in the recorded necrosis rates, even if seawater temperature showed mild thermal anomalies (Kersting et al. 2013b). Given these results and the increase in frequency and persistence of extreme events projected for the 21st century in the Mediterranean Sea (Déqué et al. 2007, Diffenbaugh et al. 2007), recurrent mortality episodes could likely be repeated and will impact this species, which, due to its slow life history dynamics, will most likely not be able to cope with elevated mortality rates (Kersting et al. 2014b). Monitoring of this species has been continuous since 2002 in the Columbretes and analyses of these data indicate that about 38% of colonies impacted by the last major mortality event caused by warming showed clear signs of recovery several years later through the process of rejuvenescence (Kersting and Linares 2019). However, Kersting and Linares (2019) state that complete recoveries through rejuvenescence might take up to 10 years. Therefore, while rejuvenescence is an affective survival and recovery mechanism, its rate will be easily outpaced by the increased frequency and intensity of warming events (Kersting and Linares 2019). This population is also being impacted by two invasive algae (Caulerpa cylindracea and Lophocladia lallemandii). Even if no lethal effects of these algae have been detected for this species in Columbretes, sublethal effects derived of the algal invasion on other stages of its life cycle, including recruitment and juvenile survival, cannot be disregarded (Kersting et al. 2014a), as well as potential synergies with warming impacts (Kersting et al. 2015).  

Adriatic Sea subpopulation: The most extensive population of the species occurs in Veliko Jezero (Mljet National Park, southern Adriatic) at 6-18 m depth, where the bank has a large area coverage of 650 m2 (Kružić and Pozar-Domac 2003). Average coral growth rate has been estimated on a range of 1.92-4.19 mm/year; and the age of the banks has been estimated to be 46-312 years (Kružić and Pozar-Domac 2002). Three other banks of the species have been described in the Adriatic Sea. The banks close to Prvić Island (Kvarner region, North Adriatic Sea) occur between 11-19 m depth and cover an area of about 190 m2. Its average growth rate has been estimated in 3.08 mm/year, and the age of the bank is estimated as 194 years. The bank near Pag Island (central Adriatic), occurs between 15-21 m depth and covers an area of 120 m2. Its average coral growth rate has been estimated as 3.06 mm/year and the estimated age of the bank is 294 years (Kružić and Benković 2008). A bank near Iz Island (central Adriatic) has been described as occurring between 12-16 m depth and covering an area of 150 m2 (Kružić and Požar-Domac 2007). Anthropogenic activities such as industrial and sewage discharges, trawling and other fishing activities and coastal works development have caused a major decline of this species in the eastern Adriatic Sea. A negative correlation has been observed in this population between sea surface temperature and coral carbonate density (Kružić et al. 2012), indicating an attenuation of calcification probably due to inhibition of the photosynthetic process carried out by zooxanthellae at higher temperatures. During 1954-1958, high input of phosphates into the seawater decreased coral growth on the Mljet coral bank in the Veliko Jezero Lake. This event was related to the experimental fertilization of Mljet’s Veliko Jezero Lake in 1953, in which, around 17 tons of phosphates (117 kg/hectare) were discharged into the lake. During the summers of 1997 and 1998, the increased temperatures caused polyp necrosis in 10% colonies at the Mljet bank (Kružić et al. 2012). During 2001-2005 more than 90% of colonies of this species in the bank near Iz Island died potentially due the increase of nitrites and nitrates concentrations from nearby tuna farms. This increase in nutrients enhanced phytoplankton and macroalgal blooms, thus decreasing the light available for the benthic communities. Increased levels of nutrients also led to higher levels of filamentous algae. Monitoring of a population in Boka Kotorska Bay in the southeastern Adriatic in 2018 reported high prevalence of mortality (Mačić et al. 2019).

Marmara Sea subpopulation: Populations in the Dardanelles and Marmara Sea are formed by beds of colonies varying from 8-96 cm diameter. The colonies occur at 2-23 m depth and the total spreading area that colonies cover in the Dardanos region is 27 m2. In the Soğandere region, the total area is 3 m2. The total coverage for other areas is less than 2 m2 (B. Özalp pers. comm. 2013). According to observations conducted in late 2013 (B. Özalp pers. obs.), the necrosed extent of the colonies is about 50% of the colony area. It is thought that the physico-chemical conditions and the seasonal abnormal changes contribute to this problem. Although short-term surveys indicate an increase in necrosis, more extensive scientific investigation focusing on population dynamics and colony condition and regular monitoring of ecological features need to be undertaken (Casado de Amezua et al. 2015).

Information on smaller subpopulations: Beds of this species in the Gulf of La Spezia (northern Tyrrhenian Sea) in the localities of Fiascherino Bay, Punta Bianca and Bocca di Magra are mainly formed by colonies within a range of 20-65 cm in diameter (Periano et al. 1999). The age of colonies from this population range from 9-63 years old. A bank of this species has been recorded in the Gulf of La Spezia (Morri et al. 2000), however, no population information is available. A three-year monitoring study of colonies at Fiascherino Bay during the 1997-1999 period indicated that about 50% of the colonies were completely dead by 1999 (Rodolfo-Metalpa et al. 2005), and this mortality is attributed to an increase in seawater temperature during the summer period. A severe mortality event was observed in 2017 following a heat wave on the Ischia coast of western Italy in the Tyrrhenian Sea and this resulted in a loss of 20% of colonies of this species (Gambi et al. 2018).

The percentage live cover of this species declined by 85% on Meloria Shoals off the Tuscany coast of Italy after an extensive bloom of benthic mucilaginous aggregate in 2019 (De Biasi et al. 2021). Monitoring studies of populations in Cyprus indicate that some beds were heavily impacted by warming events in 2010 and 2012, with a high percentage of necrosed colonies (Jiménez et al. 2016). A storm event in 2015 damaged about 7% of the colonies at a monitored site off Cyprus (Hadjioannou et al. 2016).

Populations around Medes Islands and Cap de Creus (NW Mediterranean Sea) comprise disperse colonies. These populations have started to be impacted by climate-induced mortalities during the past 5-10 years, while no invasive species are affecting them (D. Kersting and C. Linares pers. comm. 2022). Large spreading banks of the species have been found in the Balearic Islands in the locality of Cap Blanc (Mallorca, 36 m depth, R. Aguilar pers. comm. 2014), as well as in Banyuls in France (Romans pers. comm. 2014). Two recent studies assessed the main traits of populations of this species along the coasts of Menorca (Balearic Islands), as well as their health status and threats (Kersting et al. 2021a,b). These authors show that the species is present in most of the studied localities throughout the island, showing average cover values between 1 and 5%, but reaching up to 12% of cover in some localities, where colonies up to 150 cm in diameter were described.
