rationale: This widely distributed, reef-building species is particularly susceptible to bleaching, disease and disturbances. The estimated generation length is 10 years. It is assessed as Critically Endangered A2bce, based on an inferred population decline of greater than 80% over the past 30 years. The primary causes of this decline include disease and climate change (major bleaching events) as well as other human-related impacts. Although the current population is persisting in some areas, the current population trend appears to be in punctuated decline (i.e., there are places where populations continue to decrease and others where there seems to be moderate or localized recovery). Restoration of this species, mostly by asexual propagation, is an ongoing and growing effort across much of the species' range. Whether mortality continues to exceed growth and recruitment or not, this species requires immediate investigation and monitoring.
habitat:
This species is found in shallow, tropical reef ecosystems, favouring upper to mid-reef slopes and lagoons in areas with moderate to low wave exposure (Aronson and Precht 2001a,b). In southeast Florida, this species clusters along topographic features termed ridge crests (D’Antonio et al. 2016).

In the few areas where there are high densities of the species, density-dependent effects between the coral and fish communities may only manifest themselves at high densities of this coral species (Huntington et al. 2017), although experimental density manipulations with this species indicate a reduction in species health and survival (Ladd et al. 2016, Goergen and Gilliam 2018).

A low rate of larval recruitment has been considered the norm for this species in the Caribbean (Knowlton et al. 1990) and recruitment by sexual reproduction is limited (Vargas-Angel et al. 2003). Nonetheless, according to a study by Vargas-Ángel et al. (2003) off Fort Lauderdale, Florida, this species does invest considerable energy in gamete production and release and proposed that local sexual recruitment may be limited by: (1) reduced fertilization success due to asynchronous spawning, (2) transport of reproductive products away from local population, (3) pre- and post-settlement mortality and predation. It is also possible that the unusual egg membrane characteristics observed may compromise fertilization success.

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
In general, the major threat to corals, including this species, are global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification (Richards et al. 2008). The most recent, and first, multi-year, global bleaching event (spanning hundreds of kilometres or more) occurred from 2014 to 2017. Nearly 30% of coral reefs suffered mortality-level stress, more than 50% of affected reef areas were impacted at least twice, and some locations saw almost complete coral cover loss (Eakin et al. 2010, 2019; Blunden et al. 2018; Vargas-Angel et al. 2019). The average interval between bleaching events is now more than 50% less than before, preventing full reef recovery (Hughes et al. 2018).

Given the current rates of growth and recruitment of this species, together with storm frequency, natural species recovery is unlikely unless the large-scale issues of climate change and ocean warming, which affect the intensity and frequency of disease and predation, are addressed (Goergen et al. 2019). The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual coral species is not known (Richards et al. 2008). However, more than 60% of the world’s reefs are immediately threatened by local pressures (http://www.wri.org/project/reefs-at-risk; Bridge et al. 2013). This species is highly sensitive to climate change, although it can exhibit some level of adaptability (Foden et al. 2013). In the La Parguera Natural Reserve on the southwest coast of Puerto Rico, this species showed overall higher mortality due to temperature anomalies and disease compared to Acropora prolifera (Weil et al. 2020). Human impacts have been found to be responsible for widespread loss of acroporids in the Caribbean since the 1950s (Cramer et al. 2020).|

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide, a major cause of reef deterioration, and may be as likely to cause mortality as bleaching in the coming decades (Weil et al. 2006, Richards et al. 2008, Maynard et al. 2015). According to Walton et al. (2018), in addition to thermal stress, increased coral disease prevalence and mortality can be linked to reduced water quality (Bruno et al. 2003) and clarity (van Woesik and McCaffrey 2017), nutrient enrichment (Vega Thurber et al. 2013), sedimentation associated with dredging (Pollock et al. 2014, Miller et al. 2016), and plastic pollution. Based on a survey of 159 reefs in the Asia-Pacific region, the likelihood of disease increases 20-fold when corals are in contact with plastic (Lamb et al. 2018). Surveys conducted across the Caribbean region from 2004 and 2005 showed low prevalence of White Band Disease for this species, probably associated with its limited distribution and abundance (Croquer and Weil 2009, Weil and Croquer 2009). White-band disease (WBD) is believed to be the primary cause for the region-wide Caribbean acroporid decline during the 1980s (Aronson and Precht 2001a,b) and is still ongoing (Williams and Miller 2005). To date, only 6% of the remaining populations of this species have been shown to be resistant to WBD (Volmer and Kline 2008).

Coral disease epizootics have resulted in significant losses of coral cover and were implicated in the dramatic decline of acroporids in the Florida Keys (Aronson and Precht 2001, Porter et al. 2001, Patterson et al. 2002, Richards et al. 2008). In 2014, an outbreak of a coral disease termed Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD) was reported off the coast of Miami-Dade County and has since spread along Florida and to reefs in the Caribbean. At least 44% of Florida’s reef-building corals have been affected, although controlled studies in Florida show that SCTLD from susceptible species does not transmit to Acropora spp. (Florida Department of Environmental Protection 2019).

In the Indo-Pacific, disease outbreaks have also been reported from the Great Barrier Reef (GBR; Willis et al. 2004), Marshall Islands (Jacobson 2006) and the northwestern Hawaiian Islands (Aeby et al. 2006). Increased coral disease levels on the GBR were correlated with increased ocean temperatures (Willis et al. 2004), supporting the prediction that disease levels will be increasing with higher sea surface temperatures. However, a recent study shows that major declines of this species from pre-human values first occurred during the 1960s, decades before disease outbreaks (Cramer et al. 2020).

Other major threats include thermal-induced bleaching, rapid tissue loss (Williams and Miller 2005, Miller et al. 2014), storms (Goergen et al. 2019), and predation by Stegastes planifrons (Three-spot Damselfish; Precht et al. 2002, Acropora BRT 2005, Schopmeyer and Lirman 2015), Hermodice carunculata (Bearded Fireworm; Miller et al. 2014), and Coralliophyllia spp. (coralivorous snail; Johnston and Miller 2014, Bright et al. 2015). Localized threats to corals include hurricanes, fisheries and overfishing, human development (industry, settlement, resort development, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, marine debris and human recreation and tourism activities. Restricted genetic flow across the Caribbean has been identified as a major problem for population recovery of the species (Baums et al. 2005, Vollmer and Palumbi 2007).
population:
Historically, this species was found in high abundance and cover on many reefs across the Greater Caribbean, Florida and Gulf of Mexico (Davis 1982, Bruckner 2002, Acropora Biological Review Team 2005). Overall, decline of critical reefs in the Caribbean region has been 38% (according to Wilkinson 2004); however, much higher population reductions for this species have been reported as it is particularly susceptible to disease, bleaching, and environmental disturbances. From the late 1970s to 1980s, an unprecedented disease event caused an 80–98% decline in cover, abundance, and occupied range of this species (Davis 1982, Aronson and Precht 2001). Other reports have validated major declines in the Florida Keys, Jamaica (Crabbe 2016), Dry Tortugas, Belize, St. Croix (Acropora Biological Review Team 2005) and Puerto Rico (Weil et al. 2003).

In most regions, little to no recovery of this species has occurred, leaving populations geographically isolated in low colony abundance (Miller et al. 2002, Acropora Biological Review Team 2005). There have been signs of recovery in some areas at pre-existing sites, particularly after the Caribbean-wide bleaching event of 2005 (Eakin et al. 2010, Crabbe 2016). In the Florida reef tract, there has been sporadic recovery, although long-term trends tend towards a decline (Walker et al. 2012, Goergen et al. 2019). Sporadic recovery has also occurred in the Dominican Republic since 2008 (Drury et al. 2016, Kitchen et al. 2020, Yetsko et al. 2020). Examples where patches persist into recent times occur in the following areas: Belize (Busch et al. 2016), Dominican Republic (Lirman et al. 2010), Florida (Vargas-Ángel et al. 2003, Walker et al. 2012, Lidz and Zawada 2013, D’Antonio et al. 2016, Miller et al. 2016, Goergen et al. 2019), Honduras (Keck et al. 2005), Jamaica (Idjadi et al. 2006, Crabbe 2014), Mexico (Vega-Zepeda 2007, Larson et al. 2014), Puerto Rico (Mercado-Molina et al. 2015, Lucas and Weil 2016, Weil et al. 2020), US Virgin Islands (Nylander-Asplin 2018), and Venezuela (Martinez 2015, Miyazawa et al. 2020).

This species is in a critical condition throughout the Colombian Caribbean reefs (García-Urueña and Garzón-Machado 2020). In the Morrocoy National Park on the central west coast of Venezuela, this species was not sighted during the last three years of a coral research project (Yranzo et al. in prep.). Diving schools in this area and associates of the San Esteban National Park (a protected area close to Morrocoy) indicate this species has not been sighted since 2002 (Santana pers. comm.). Based on these results and observations, it is likely that this species is locally extinct. The largest populations in Venezuela occur along the oceanic reefs such as the Archipelago de las Aves, Los Roques (Miyazawa et al. 2020) and La Orchila, and it has been reported from the central coast of Venezuela (La Cienaga) all the way down to the eastern coast (e.g. Rodríguez and Rojas-Suárez et al. 2008). In Los Roques, extensive surveys conducted across 107 sites between 2014 and 2015 showed evidence of widespread distribution, with limited numbers of extensive patches and predominance of scattered patches (Martinez 2015).
range: This species is distributed in the western Atlantic from Mexico (Veracruz), southern Florida (Broward County) and the northern Bahamas (Abaco) south to Trinidad and Tobago, including the insular and coastal reefs of Barbados, Venezuela, Aruba, Curaçao, Bonaire and Colombia. rationale: This species is widespread and common. habitat:
This species is common on reef slopes and vertical walls, inhabiting most reef environments (Veron et al. 2016). It can form large plates of up to 1 m in diameter.  

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
This species is easily bleached, but has high resilience (Ng et al. 2020, Khen et al. 2023).

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide with increases in numbers of diseases, coral species affected, and geographic extent (Ward et al. 2004, Sutherland et al. 2004, Sokolow et al. 2009). Outbreaks of coral diseases have damaged coral reefs worldwide with the most widespread, virulent, and longest running coral disease outbreak currently occurring on the Florida Reef Tract and throughout the Caribbean. The disease, stony coral tissue loss disease, has been ongoing since 2014 (Precht et al. 2016) and has devastated affected reefs along Florida (Walton et al. 2018, Williams et al. 2021) and throughout the Caribbean (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2019, Kramer et al. 2019). Numerous disease outbreaks have also occurred in the Indo-Pacific (Willis et al. 2004, Aeby et al. 2011; 2016), Indian Ocean (Raj et al. 2016) and Persian Gulf (Howells et al. 2020). Escalating anthropogenic stressors combined with the threats associated with global climate change of increases in coral disease, frequency and duration of coral bleaching and ocean acidification place coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific at high risk of collapse. 

Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual species is not known.
population:

Species-specific, global level population information is limited. However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, Donovan et al. 2021). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.     

Approach 1: Future population trend
The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is little understood and varies by species and locality (Bay et al. 2017, Matz et al. 2020, Logan et al. 2021). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2035 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2039 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2062 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2070 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where the onset of ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0-30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on 1°C of adaptation is lower given this species is not primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is moderately susceptible to bleaching. For widespread species, the final estimate of decline was further adjusted by excluding the proportion of cells within its range that were expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 after 2050 (three generation lengths), in order to account for the potential resilience of species to the asynchronous variability of bleaching events that occur across the Indo-Pacific. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Pacific, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in high-latitude reefs (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of less than 25% by the year 2050, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario. 

Approach 2: Past population trend
Coral reef monitoring data were also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the 37 subregions of the Indo-Pacific (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered 11 species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 1-50 m and is predominately found at depths greater than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered common, overall population is not restricted or highly fragmented, does not occur off-reef, is highly susceptible to disease, does recover well from bleaching or disease, has a low susceptibility to crown-of-thorns starfish, is moderately susceptible to bleaching, has a relatively higher susceptibility to the impacts of ocean acidification (Kornder et al. 2018), did not have >10,000 pieces exported annually in the aquarium trade between 2010-2019, it is overall suspected to be moderately susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 50% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a suspected global level decline of less than 25% since 1989, or over the past three generations.

rationale: This species has a restricted range in New Caledonia and has an estimated area of occupancy (AOO) of less than 2,000 km² but greater than 500 km². In general, this species is relatively rare, but can be found in high densities in some localities. It is susceptible to major threats from habitat degradation due to sediment runoff from terrestrial mining activities. It is also moderately susceptible to impacts from bleaching events. It is assessed as Vulnerable B2ab(iii).
habitat:
This species inhabits mostly hard substrata in silty and muddy habitats in sheltered bays and turbid, inshore lagoons with a unique coral assemblage. It attaches to hard substrates surrounded by metal-rich sediment and is more abundant on natural rock than on artificial substrates (Gilbert et al. 2015). This species appears to be tolerant of high turbidity and metal-rich environments. Individuals have been observed in relatively high densities in Grande Rade, a harbor from New Caledonia known to be polluted with high concentrations of iron, nickel, chromium, and manganese from a nearby nickel industry (Gilbert et al. 2015). Other fungiids are known to shed sediment, even when completely buried (Bongaerts et al. 2012), and so this species may use a similar mechanism to tolerate such environmental conditions (Gilbert et al. 2015). The maximum size is 7 cm diameter (Hoeksema 1989). 

While there is some information regarding the age in which corals reach sexual maturation, it is largely based on measurements of size as a proxy for age (Harrison and Wallace 1990), which can be problematic in modular animals because of processes such as partial mortality and fission (Hughes and Jackson 1980). Nonetheless, it appears that many brooding coral species tend to reach puberty at about 1-2 years of age, which is much earlier than many broadcast-spawners that become reproductive at 3-8 years or more (Harrison and Wallace 1990, Wallace 1999). Therefore, we assume that the average age of mature individuals on a given reef is greater than eight years. Furthermore, based on average sizes and growth rates, we assume that the average generation length is 10 years, unless otherwise stated. Total longevity is not known for any coral, but likely to be more than ten years. Therefore, any population decline rates for the Red List assessment are measured over at least 30 years.
threats:
The main threat to this species is mining activities causing sedimentation and habitat degradation. It is also moderately susceptible to bleaching. Predation from the crown-of-thorns on this species has not been reported. Predation by Acanthaster spp. may threaten this species by reducing its abundance, however, it is unclear to what degree (Lohe 2020). Based on disease surveys conducted in 2015 in New Caledonia, there were little disease impacts found in Fungiidae species (Aeby et al. 2015).

Another critical threat for this species, like for most coral species, is the extensive degradation and reduction of coral-reef habitat because of a combination of local and global threats (Hughes et al. 2017, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Donovan et al. 2021). The increasing threats from climate change are being further compounded by additional local stressors, such as pollution and overfishing (Knowlton and Jackson 2008, Lamb et al. 2018, MacNeil et al. 2019, Donovan et al. 2021). There is some evidence that this species has reduced vulnerability to thermal stress, however, the 2016 bleaching event affected two thirds of the Caledonian reefs (Meadows 2014, Lohe 2020). Bleaching can lead to coral mortality, which reduces coral cover, and hence reducing effective coral population as well as the disruption of coral reproduction and diminishment of coral recruitment, and therefore population turnover. 

Generally, the biggest threat to the persistence of corals is climate change (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Hughes et al. 2017, Sully et al. 2019), and more specifically - ocean warming and marine heatwaves that are leading to an increase in the frequency and intensity of events of anomalously high water temperatures (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2019, Laufkötter et al. 2020). Under anomalously high temperatures, the symbiotic relationship between corals and their photosynthetic symbionts is disrupted, and many corals begin to bleach (Glynn 1996, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 1999, Warner et al. 1999, Loya et al. 2001). Mass bleaching events resulting from thermal stress have become increasingly common in the last two decades and may lead to widespread coral mortality and changes in overall reef community over large areas (Loya et al. 2001, Graham et al. 2015, Hughes et al. 2018, Safaie et al. 2018, Stuart-Smith et al. 2018, McClanahan et al. 2019, Sully et al. 2019).

Superimposed on thermal stress and bleaching are additional stressors that can either directly threaten corals or exacerbate coral mortality after thermal stress (Kennedy et al. 2013, MacNeil et al. 2019, Abelson et al. 2020, Donovan et al. 2021, Knowlton et al. 2021). Moreover, in some localities, increased amounts of outbreaks of the corallivorous sea star, crown of thorns, can cause substantial damage to the reef, contributing to the overall decline and reef destruction (Saponari et al. 2015, Pratchett et al. 2017).

ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2033 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2037 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2061 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2069 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. This species occurs in all types of reef environments from the shallow subtidal to 70 m depth (Goreau and Wells 1967), and is most common at 5-15 m depth. This species does well in areas with high turbidity and sedimentation, as it is capable of removing a wide range of sediment sizes (Hubbard and Pocock 1972). This species is able to succeed in heavy regimes of sedimentation and turbidity.

This is a gonochoric broadcasting species with a sex ratio of 1:1 that has one reproductive cycle per year in the late summer (August-September) (Soong 1990). Its eggs measure around 0.8 x 0.3 mm in diameter and lack zooxanthellae. Colony shapes range from hemispherical to flat; irregular surfaces may be caused by periods of death and subsequent overgrowth and by extensive boring (Budd 1980). Puberty size is reached at sizes larger than 100 cm2 (Soong 1993).

This is a slow growing species, reported to increase in diameter between 1.5 and 9.3 mm per year (Huston 1985). Mean growth rate of small colonies derived from sexual reproduction (4.0 ± 0.6 mm yr-1) can be 2.5-fold greater than that of small ramets which were estimated to be ~100 years older (1.6 ± 0.5 mm yr-1) (Elahi and Edmunds 2007). Growth rate has been found to decrease significantly with depth (Huston 1985).

Size-frequency distributions are generally strongly skewed towards small size classes (Lewis 1997, Elahi and Edmunds 2007), with mean diameters generally being less than 1 m, although some colonies can reach diameters up to 5 m (Lewis 1997). Partial mortality in this species can be substantial and variable among reefs. Lewis (1997) found that partial mortality of this species in reefs of Barbados was positively correlated with colony size.

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Sea-level rise is another potential threat, especially in areas where hard-bottom communities are replaced by soft substrates. The most recent, and first, multi-year, global bleaching event (spanning hundreds of kilometres or more) was from 2014 to 2017. Nearly 30% of reefs suffered mortality level-stress, more than 50% of affected reef areas were impacted at least twice, and some locations saw almost complete coral cover loss (Blunden et al. 2018, Vargas-Angel et al. 2019, Eakin et al. 2019). The average interval between bleaching events is now more than 50% less than before, preventing full reef recovery (Hughes et al. 2018). In Belize, for example, Baumann et al. (2019) recorded a decline in skeletal extension rates of this species over the past century in nearshore colonies and suggested that it was driven primarily by the combined effects of long‐term ocean warming and increasing exposure to higher levels of land‐based anthropogenic stressors.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide and is a major cause of reef deterioration (Weil et al. 2006, Richards et al. 2008, Maynard et al. 2015). As noted in Walton et al. (2018), in addition to thermal stress, increased coral disease prevalence and mortality can be linked to reduced water quality (Bruno et al. 2007) and clarity (van Woeski and McCaffrey 2017), nutrient enrichment (Vega Thurber et al. 2013), dredging associated sedimentation (Pollock et al. 2014, Miller et al. 2016), and plastic pollution. Based on a survey of 159 reefs in the Asia-Pacific region, the likelihood of disease increases 20-fold when corals are in contact with plastic (Lamb et al. 2018). Increased coral disease levels on the Great Barrier Reef were correlated with increased ocean temperatures (Willis et al. 2004) supporting the prediction that disease levels will be increasing with higher sea surface temperatures.

Since 2014, populations of this species declined significantly due to Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease in some reefs in southeast Florida (42%; Lunz et al. 2017) and since 2018 colonies of this species affected by this disease were also recorded along the Mexican Caribbean with prevalence ranging from 26 to 58% among sites (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2019). Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD) represents one of the greatest threats to this species due to: (1) its rapid spread across individual colonies, (2) high mortality rate, (3) rapid spread between reefs, and (4) high infection rate (Pratte and Richardson 2014, Dahlgren 2020). The pathogen causing the disease is unknown. To September 2020, there have been no reports of SCTLD epizootic events in Venezuela, the Dominican Republic, and the Lesser Antilles (A. Croquer pers. comm. 2020). This species is also affected by black band disease, dark spot disease, and white plague.

Century‐scale growth records of inner and outer reef corals across ~200 km of the Florida Keys Reef Tract, using skeletal cores showed that this species sustained extension and calcification rates over the past century but has experienced a long‐term reduction in skeletal density, regardless of reef zone; the significant reduction in skeletal density may indicate underlying vulnerability to present and future trends in ocean acidification (Rippe et al. 2018).

Other localized threats include habitat loss, fisheries and overfishing, human development (industry, settlement, resort development, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, marine debris and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual species is not known, however, more than 60% of the world’s reefs are immediately threatened by local pressures (http://www.wri.org/project/reefs-at-risk; Bridge et al. 2013).

Although exhibiting high rates of recruitment, new recruits may sustain high mortality due to algal overgrowth. Localized mortality may take place due to bio-erosion from endolithic sponges, and ship groundings (R. Aronson, W. Precht, J. Moore, E. Weil and A. Bruckner pers. comm. 2008).
population:
This species is common in most reef environments in the Caribbean, the Gulf of Mexico, Florida, the Bahamas, and Bermuda, at low to moderate abundances. In certain localized areas, this species can be the most abundant coral. In North Carolina’s Onslow Bay (the northernmost site of this species), only small size (<10 cm) colonies occur, scattered in patches on mostly Miocene calcareous quartz sandstone flat outcrops (not forming a reefal framework) at depths of 20 to 40 m (Macintyre 2003). However, it is intermediately susceptible to stony coral tissue loss disease and moderately susceptible to bleaching. In Caribbean reefs, it is abundant in fore reefs and common in other reef environments. 

In Puerto Morelos Reef, Mexican Caribbean, the density of this species ranged from 0.8 to 2.4 col m2 in 2016 (R. Rodríguez-Martínez pers. comm. 2020).

On Curaçao, its current abundance (in terms of percentage bottom cover) is 0.683% (SD: 0.641, n=145 sites in 2015 at 10 m depths (Waitt Institute 2017), on Aruba: 0.32% (SD: 0.39, n=53 sites in 2019) (Carmabi unpubl. data). On Curaçao, a decline in population sizes occurred as historic cover (1973) was 7.1% (Nagelkerken 1979, Nagelkerken et al. 2005). The abundance of this species declined from 4.3% in 1973 to 3.1% in 2005 on Bonaire (de Bakker 2019). Recruitment rates increased between 1973 and 2005, i.e. from 0.08 to 1.05 individuals per m2 on average in Curaçao (Bak and Engel 1979, Vermeij et al. 2011). Bonaire and Curaçao still possess some of the least degraded reefs left in the Caribbean (Jackson et al. 2013) and the decreases in adult abundance under favourable conditions indicate that population persistence in this species is likely even more compromised in other locations. The increase in recruitment under favourable conditions indicates that population increases in this species are possible.

Localized declines of this species have been reported (Bell et al. 1994), but no major global-level declines have been observed (R. Aronson, W. Precht, J. Moore, E. Weil and A. Bruckner pers. comm. 2008). In some reefs in the Caribbean, the relative abundance of this species has increased as a result of the mortality of acroporids and other dominant reef corals (e.g. Mexican Caribbean; Estrada-Saldivar et al. 2019). In Cuban reefs, it is the most consistently abundant coral species in all reef sites (González-Díaz et al. 2018). Specific population information provided by Nunes et al. (2011), indicate a possible population expansion at least in the São Tomé population, West Africa, and that the species is able to maintain gene flow among populations separated by as much as 2,000 km along the coast of Brazil. On a larger scale, Pax-C gene indicate that populations of this species in São Tomé (West Africa) had lower average gene diversity than populations in the Caribbean and Brazil (Nunes et al. 2011).

Recent population declines have been reported recently due to Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease, with colony losses of 42% in parts of the Florida Reef Tract in 2016 (Lunz et al. 2017), and ranging from 26 to 58% in the Mexican Caribbean coast from 2018 to 2020 (Alvarez- Filip et al. 2019, L.  Alvarez-Filip pers. comm. 2020).

Species-specific, global level population information is limited. However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hughes et al. 2018). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.     

Approach 1: Future population trend

The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that corals are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022). 

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is poorly understood and varies by species and locality (van Hooidonk et al. 2013, Logan et al. 2014). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells.

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2030 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2034 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2059 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2072 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on no level of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is highly susceptible to bleaching. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the understanding that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and is expected to decline at a faster global rate than species that also or primarily occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Atlantic, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in the Mediterranean Sea (Flecha et al. 2015). Therefore, this species is inferred to experience a projected global level decline of at least 80% by the year 2050, or three generations in the future, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario. 

Approach 2: Past population trend

Coral reef monitoring data was also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the five Caribbean and three Brazil subregions (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ entire range (except for the São Tomé and Príncipe Islands).

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered nine species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 1-70 m and is predominately found at depths greater than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered common, overall population is not highly fragmented, does not occur off-reef, is moderately susceptible to disease, is moderately susceptible to Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD), does recover well from bleaching or disease and is highly susceptible to bleaching, it is overall inferred to be moderately susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 50% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a global level decline of <20% since 1989, or over the past three generations.
range:
This is an amphi-Atlantic species (Nunes et al. 2011). In the western Atlantic, it occurs from Onslow Bay, North Carolina in the U.S. between latitudes 33°30’ and 34°39’ (Macintyre and Pilkey 1969, Macintyre 2003) southward to Florida, Bermuda, the Flower Garden Banks and Mexico (Tamaulipas) to the Florida Middle Grounds in the Gulf of Mexico, and the Bahamas southward throughout the Caribbean to 18°02′16″S 38°40′02″W on the Abrolhos Bank, Bahia, Brazil. The first Brazilian record was based on a single specimen from the C. Hartt collection deposited at the NMNH (Neves et al. 2016), and since then, Nunes et al. (2011), based on allele frequencies, indicate that this species also occurs in Abrolhos (Bahia State), João Pessoa (Paraíba State) and Fortaleza (Ceará State), all on the northeastern Brazilian coast. Nunes et al. (2011) also confirmed the occurrence of this species in São Tomé e Príncipe, Africa at  0°20′00″N and 6°44′00″E. Records of Siderastrea glynni, which is a synonym of S. siderea and previously thought to be endemic to Pacific Panama, is now understood to represent unintentionally introduced live colonies of S. siderea from the Caribbean to the Pacific side of the Isthmus of Panama in the 1980s (Glynn et al. 2016).

useTrade: This species is not utilized. Atlantic reef corals are not part of the international trade for the aquarium industry (B. Hoeksema pers. comm. 2022).
conservationActions:
All corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. In U.S. and Brazilian waters, it is illegal to harvest corals for commercial purposes.

Parts of this species' distribution overlaps with several marine protected areas (MPAs). In the U.S., it is present in many MPAs, including Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, Biscayne National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Buck Island Reef National Monument and Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary. It is also present in Hol Chan Marine Reserve (Belize), Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park (Bahamas). In Brazil, this species is reported from the Baia de Todos-os-Santos State Protected Area, Abrolhos National Marine Park, Environmental Protecte Area of the Ponta da Baleia and Extractive Reserve of Corumbáu. In Mexico, it is found in all MPAs in the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico. In Costa Rica, it is present in Cahuita National Park and in the Gandoca-Manzanillo National Wildlife  Refuge (Araya-Vargas and Nova-Bustos 2017). In Colombia, this species is present in the Tayrona National Park (Carvajalino 2017).

Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in taxonomy, population, abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration action; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management. Artificial propagation and techniques such as cryo-preservation of gametes may become important for conserving coral biodiversity.

Our species-specific vulnerability traits analysis indicates this species is moderately susceptible to major threats related to coral reef degradation (e.g., disease and bleaching). We applied two analytical approaches involving two different global coral datasets and the species’ distribution map as proxies to infer population decline. Based on global coral cover monitoring data, this species experienced a suspected decline of less than 25% over the past three generations, or since 1989. Based on the projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) conditions via both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios of global climate model data, in combination with the species’ depth range, distribution and bleaching vulnerability, this species is suspected to decline by at least 47% over the next three generations, or by 2050. Since the species qualifies for a higher category under the projected decline, we therefore list it as Vulnerable A3ce. The change in status from the previous assessment reflects updated declines calculated from improved data on modeled coral cover loss and projected date of annual severe bleaching, along with improved knowledge of species traits.
habitat:
This species is found in shallow tropical reef environments, especially intertidal reef flats. It is commonly found from 3-15 m, rarely from 1-2 m and deeper from 18-20 m, in the South China Sea and Gulf of Siam (Titlyanov and Titlyanova 2002). It has also been recorded on mesophotic reefs (Bridge et al. 2012). It can form large fields of over 1 m across. 

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.

In general, species from this genus are considered to have higher bleaching vulnerability and moderate recovery (Khen et al. 2023). Like many branching corals, this species is highly susceptible to bleaching and with severely reduced populations and even local extinction of the species occurring following bleaching events (Loya et al. 2001, van Woesik et al. 2011, McClanahan and Muthiga 2014). In Watamu Marine National Park, Kenya, this species was present prior to severe bleaching in 1998 (Lemmens 1993), but has not been found since, suggesting it is locally extinct (Cowburn et al. 2018).

The collection of this species for the aquarium trade may lead to overharvest and localised reductions in abundance, especially for populations of naturally rare species (Bruckner and Borneman 2006). However, the wild collection of corals is highly selective and considered low impact in the long-term relative to other activities such as coral mining and dynamite fishing (Green and Shirley 1999, Pratchett et al. 2020). 

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide with increases in numbers of diseases, coral species affected, and geographic extent (Ward et al. 2004, Sutherland et al. 2004, Sokolow et al. 2009). Outbreaks of coral diseases have damaged coral reefs worldwide with the most widespread, virulent, and longest running coral disease outbreak currently occurring on the Florida Reef Tract and throughout the Caribbean. The disease, stony coral tissue loss disease, has been ongoing since 2014 (Precht et al. 2016) and has devastated affected reefs along Florida (Walton et al. 2018, Williams et al. 2021) and throughout the Caribbean (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2019, Kramer et al. 2019). Numerous disease outbreaks have also occurred in the Indo-Pacific (Willis et al. 2004, Aeby et al. 2011; 2016), Indian Ocean (Raj et al. 2016) and Persian Gulf (Howells et al. 2020). Escalating anthropogenic stressors combined with the threats associated with global climate change of increases in coral disease, frequency and duration of coral bleaching and ocean acidification place coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific at high risk of collapse.

Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual species is not known.
population:

range:
This species is found in the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Raghunathan and Venkataraman 2012), the southwest and central Indian Ocean, the central Indo-Pacific, the Marshall Islands (Richards and Beger 2013), tropical Australia, China (Xin-Qing et al. 2013), southern Japan and the South China Sea, the oceanic West Pacific, and the central Pacific.

conservationActions: All stony corals (Order: Scleractinia) are listed on CITES Appendix II, and under Annex B of the European Union Wildlife Trade Regulations. Moreover, several countries (e.g., India, Israel, Jordan, Djibouti, Fiji and the Philippines) at various stages have banned either the trade or the export of CITES II listed species, which includes all stony corals. Other countries such as Indonesia, trade maricultured corals, with quotas, production limit and regulations in place to ensure the trade is sustainable. Having timely access to national-level trade data from CITES is valuable for monitoring trends for this species. Consideration of the suitability of species for aquaria should also be included as part of fisheries management, and population surveys should be carried out to monitor the effects of harvesting alongside other population trends.

However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, Donovan et al. 2021). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.     

Approach 1: Future population trend
The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is little understood and varies by species and locality (Bay et al. 2017, Matz et al. 2020, Logan et al. 2021). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2035 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2038 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2062 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2070 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where the onset of ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0-30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on 1°C of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is moderately susceptible to bleaching. For widespread species, the final estimate of decline was further adjusted by excluding the proportion of cells within its range that were expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 after 2050 (three generation lengths), in order to account for the potential resilience of species to the asynchronous variability of bleaching events that occur across the Indo-Pacific. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Pacific, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in high-latitude reefs (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of less than 25% by the year 2050, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario.

The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range.

The numbers of diseases and coral species affected, as well as the distribution of diseases have all increased dramatically within the last two decades (Porter et al. 2001, Green and Bruckner 2000, Sutherland et al. 2004, Weil 2004). Coral disease epizootics have resulted in significant losses of coral cover and were implicated in the dramatic decline of acroporids in the Florida Keys (Aronson and Precht 2001, Porter et al. 2001, Patterson et al. 2002). As environmental conditions continue to change, it is predicted that conditions on temperate reefs will become favourable for coral diseases and thermodependent bacteria (Bally and Garrabou 2007, Brodnicke et al. 2019) and the geographical range of tropical coral diseases will extend (Vergés et al. 2019).

There is evidence that overall cover of Acropora has declined in many regions, including Australia (Hughes et al. 2020, Dietzel et al. 2020), French Polynesia (Moritz et al. 2021), Mauritius (Elliott et al. 2018), Thailand (Yeemin et al. 2013), Chagos Archipelago (Head et al. 2019), Lakshadweep Archipelago (Yadav et al. 2018), Indonesia (Cleary et al. 2014), Japan (Hongo and Yamano 2013), Taiwan (Kuo et al. 2012), Persian Gulf (Riegl et al. 2018) and these genus-level declines indicate global-level declines are highly likely for all Acropora species (with the possible exception of tabular Acropora which have been shown to recover quickly after disturbance; Johns et al. 2014, Mellin et al. 2019, Richards et al. 2021). Coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, Donovan et al. 2020). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.     

Approach 1: Future population trend
The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is little understood and varies by species and locality (Bay et al. 2017, Matz et al. 2020, Logan et al. 2021). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2039 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2043 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2065 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2075 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0–30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on no level of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is highly susceptible to bleaching. For widespread species, the final estimate of decline was further adjusted by excluding the proportion of cells within its range that were expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 after 2050 (three generation lengths), in order to account for the potential resilience of species to the asynchronous variability of bleaching events that occur across the Indo-Pacific. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Pacific, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in high-latitude reefs (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of at least 57% by the year 2050, or three generations in the future, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario. 

Approach 2: Past population trend
Coral reef monitoring data were also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the 37 subregions of the Indo-Pacific (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered 11 species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 1-30 m and is predominately found at depths greater than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered rare, overall population is not restricted or highly fragmented, does not occur off-reef, is highly susceptible to disease, does not recover well from bleaching or disease, has a high susceptibility to crown-of-thorns starfish, is highly susceptible to bleaching, has a relatively higher susceptibility to the impacts of ocean acidification (Kornder et al. 2018), did not have >10,000 pieces exported annually in the aquarium trade between 2010-2019, it is overall suspected to be highly susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 80% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a suspected global level decline of less than 25% since 1989, or over the past three generations.

This species is found in the central Indo-Pacific, and north, west and south Australia, the Philippines, the Andamans, Banggai (D. Fenner pers. comm. 2008), Malaysia, the Marshall Islands, Papua New Guinea and west Thailand (Wallace et al. 2012).

Furthermore, several countries (India, Israel, Somalia, Djibouti, Solomon Islands and the Philippines) at various stages have banned either the trade or export of CITES II listed species, which includes all stony corals, since 1999 (UNEP 2020). habitat:
This species occurs in most reef environments and also exists in back reef shallow platforms with Thalassia turtle grass beds and attached to mangrove prop roots (Weil 1992). It can be found growing on and directly adjacent to mangrove prop roots in Florida (Kellogg et al. 2020) and in the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef off Belize (Finnerty et al. 2019).

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
This species is sensitive to climate change (Foden et al. 2013). From 2005 to 2009, this species was seldom observed bearing active signs of diseases but predation was a frequent condition described across several Caribbean countries (Croquer and Weil 2009, Weil et al. 2009, Weil and Croquer 2009). In 2014, an outbreak of a coral disease termed Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD) was reported off the coast of Miami-Dade County and has since spread along Florida and to reefs in the Caribbean. At least 44% of Florida’s reef-building corals have been affected (Florida Department of Environmental Protection 2019). This species has been reported to be susceptible to SCTLD in reefs off Mexico in 101 sampled sites along 450 km since 2018 (L. Alvarez-Filip pers. comm. 2020). In the Indo-Pacific, disease outbreaks have also been reported from the Great Barrier Reef (GBR; Willis et al. 2004), Marshall Islands (Jacobson 2006) and the northwestern Hawaiian Islands (Aeby et al. 2006). Increased coral disease levels on the GBR were correlated with increased ocean temperatures (Boyett et al. 2007) supporting the prediction that disease levels will be increasing with higher sea surface temperatures.

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification (Richards et al. 2008). The most recent, and first, multi-year, global bleaching event (spanning hundreds of kilometres or more) was from 2014 to 2017. Nearly 30% of reefs suffered mortality level-stress, more than 50% of affected reef areas were impacted at least twice, and some locations saw almost complete coral cover loss (Blunden et al. 2018; Vargas-Angel et al. 2019; Eakin et al. 2010, 2019). The average interval between bleaching events is now more than 50% less than before, preventing full reef recovery (Hughes et al. 2018). 

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide, a major cause of reef deterioration, and may be as likely to cause mortality as bleaching in the coming decades (Weil et al. 2006, Richards et al. 2008, Maynard et al. 2015). As noted in Walton et al. (2018), in addition to thermal stress, increased coral disease prevalence and mortality can be linked to reduced water quality (Bruno et al. 2003) and clarity (van Woesik and McCaffrey 2017), nutrient enrichment (Vega Thurber et al. 2013), dredging associated sedimentation (Pollock et al. 2014, Miller et al. 2016), and plastic pollution. Based on a survey of a 159 reefs in the Asia-Pacific region, the likelihood of disease increases 20-fold when corals are in contact with plastic (Lamb et al. 2018).

Localized threats to corals include hurricanes, fisheries and overfishing, human development (industry, settlement, resort development, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, marine debris and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual coral species is not known (Richards et al. 2008). However, more than 60% of the world’s reefs are immediately threatened by local pressures (http://www.wri.org/project/reefs-at-risk; Bridge et al. 2013).

Severe challenges causing population loss have arisen from a variety of anthropogenic and environmental factors including overfishing, destructive fishing practices, coral bleaching, marine heat spots, ocean acidification, sea-level rise, algal blooms, agricultural run-off, coastal and resort development, marine pollution, increasing coral diseases, algal overgrowth and sedimentation, predation by snails, mortality by endolithic sponges, ship groundings, anchor damage, trampling and marine debris, invasive species, hurricane/cyclone damage, pollution from domestic, urban and industrial sources, sedimentation, changing dynamics of native species, and damage caused by human recreation and tourism activities and development (e.g. Albright et al. 2010; Williams and Miller 2012; Fogarty 2012; Rogers and Muller 2012; van Woesik et al. 2014; Kuffner and Toth 2016; Pawlik et al. 2016; Frölicher et al. 2018; Beck et al. 2018; Crabbe 2014, 2019).

Localized declines are associated with: loss of habitat at the recruitment stage due to algal overgrowth and sedimentation; predation by snails; mortality by endolithic sponges; ship groundings, anchor damage, trampling, and marine debris. The long-term threat of reduced skeletal integrity due to ocean acidification is of particular concern due to the species' presence in wave-swept environments. Shallow-water populations are susceptible to typical threats such as pollution, burial by sediment, hurricane damage, and predation by Sparisoma viride (Stoplight Parrotfish), and loss of habitat due to coastal development, dredging, and beach renourishment, which have caused localized declines.

conservationActions:
All corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. In U.S. waters, it is illegal to harvest corals for commercial purposes.  

Parts of this species' distribution overlaps with several marine protected areas (MPAs). In the U.S., it is present in many MPAs, including Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, Biscayne National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, and Buck Island Reef National Monument. Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in taxonomy, population, abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration action; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management.
