Species-specific, global level population information is limited. However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, Donovan et al. 2021). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.     

Approach 1: Future population trend
The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is little understood and varies by species and locality (Bay et al. 2017, Matz et al. 2020, Logan et al. 2021). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2026 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2024 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2050 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2057 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0–30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on no level of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is highly susceptible to bleaching. For widespread species, the final estimate of decline was further adjusted by excluding the proportion of cells within its range that were expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 after 2050 (three generation lengths), in order to account for the potential resilience of species to the asynchronous variability of bleaching events that occur across the Indo-Pacific. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Pacific, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in high-latitude reefs (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of at least 77% by the year 2050, or three generations in the future, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario.

Coral reef monitoring data were also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hughes et al. 2018). Approach 1: Future population trend
The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is poorly understood and varies by species and locality (van Hooidonk et al. 2013, Logan et al. 2014). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2028 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2030 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2056 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2067 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0–30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on 1°C of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is moderately susceptible to bleaching. For widespread species, the final estimate of decline was further adjusted by excluding the proportion of cells within its range that were expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 after 2050 (three generation lengths), in order to account for the potential resilience of species to the asynchronous variability of bleaching events that occur across the Indo-Pacific. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of less than 25% by the year 2050, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario.

Coral reef monitoring data were also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ entire range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered 11 species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 5-20 m and is predominately found at depths greater than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered rare, overall population is not restricted or highly fragmented, does not occur off-reef, is moderately susceptible to disease, does not recover well from bleaching or disease, has a low susceptibility to crown-of-thorns starfish, is moderately susceptible to bleaching, has an unknown susceptibility to the impacts of ocean acidification (Kornder et al. 2018), did not have >10,000 pieces exported annually in the aquarium trade between 2010-2019, it is overall suspected to be highly susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. Given that ASB is projected to occur beyond the three-generation length period, the final species decline was based on past coral cover loss.

threats:
This species is particularly susceptible to bleaching, disease, predation and other threats, and therefore, population declines are predicted across its entire range. Threats to this species include local dredging and resulting sedimentation (Jones 2016) and bleaching due to climate change (Richards and Rosser 2012). This species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is highly susceptible to bleaching.

This species has a branching growth form and is susceptible to predation by the crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) (Acanthaster planci), which are found throughout the Pacific and Indian Oceans, and the Red Sea. Crown-of-thorns are voracious predators of reef-building corals, with a preference for branching and tabular corals such as Acropora species. Populations of the crown-of-thorns starfish have greatly increased since the 1970s and have been known to remove large areas of coral reef habitat. Increased breakouts of COTS has become a major threat to some species, and has contributed to the overall decline and reef destruction in the Indo-Pacific. The effects of such an outbreak include the reduction of abundance and surface cover of living coral, reduction of species diversity and composition, and overall reduction in habitat area. Crown-of-thorn outbreaks are particularly concerning in coral communities that are recovering from disturbances such as coral bleaching as feeding on remnant survivors and juveniles can further inhibit community recovery (Haywood et al. 2019).

In general, the major threat to Acropora corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching induced mortality, and an increased susceptibility to disease (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2007, Hughes et al. 2017; 2018; 2019). Bleaching can lead to mortality and a reduction in both coral cover and effective population sizes. It also disrupts coral reproduction. Regional coral extinction events following thermally anomalous events are increasingly reported (Sheppard et al. 2020, Muir et al. 2021, Richards et al. 2021). In addition, climate change is predicted to cause an increased severity of ENSO (El Niño/La Niña Southern Oscillation) events and storm intensity, and longer-term changes in ocean chemistry impacting calcification, along with an increase in the severity of flood and fire events impacting coastal catchments areas.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide and a major cause of reef deterioration (Weil et al. 2006). The numbers of diseases and coral species affected, as well as the distribution of diseases have all increased dramatically within the last two decades (Porter et al. 2001, Green and Bruckner 2000, Sutherland et al. 2004, Weil 2004). Coral disease epizootics have resulted in significant losses of coral cover and were implicated in the dramatic decline of acroporids in the Florida Keys (Aronson and Precht 2001, Porter et al. 2001, Patterson et al. 2002). In the Indo-Pacific, disease is also on the rise with disease outbreaks recently reported from the Great Barrier Reef (Willis et al. 2004, Haapkyla et al. 2013), Indonesia (Haapkyla et al. 2007, Subhan et al. 2020), Thailand (Lamb et al. 2014), Marshall Islands (Jacobson 2006), Micronesia (Myers and Raymundo 2009), American Samoa (Work and Rameyer 2005), and the northwestern Hawaiian Islands (Aeby et al. 2006), the Cocos (Keeling) Islands (Preston and Richards 2021), the Maldives (Montano et al. 2015), and the Persian Gulf (Aeby et al. 2020). Increased coral disease levels on the GBR were correlated with increased ocean temperatures (Boyett et al. 2007, Howells et al. 2020) supporting the prediction that disease levels will be increasing with higher sea surface temperatures. As environmental conditions continue to change, it is predicted that conditions on temperate reefs will become favorable for coral diseases and thermodependent bacteria (Bally and Garrabou 2007, Brodnicke et al. 2019) and the geographical range of tropical coral diseases will extend (Vergés et al. 2019).

Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities (Burke et al. 2011). The severity of these combined threats to the global population of this species is not known.

Coral reef monitoring data were also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the 37 subregions of the Indo-Pacific (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered 11 species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 50% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a suspected global level decline of less than 25% since 1989, or over the past three generations.
range:
This species is distributed in the northern and central Red Sea. Despite dedicated survey work, it has not yet been recorded in the Farasan Islands, nor further south in the Kamaran Islands, Yemen. The species may be endemic to the Red Sea (Terraneo et al. 2014).

The depth range is 10-35 m (Terraneo et al. 2014).

Based on clipping the distribution to the WCMC 2018 global coral reef map, the estimated area of occupancy (AOO) is 5,687 km2.
conservationActions: All stony corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. Parts of the species’ range may overlap with marine protected areas.

rationale: This species is widespread and common. Global level, species-specific population data are limited; however, coral reefs have declined globally and are expected to continue rapidly declining due to increasing severe bleaching conditions under temperature stress caused by climate change as well as a variety of other threats. Our species-specific vulnerability traits analysis indicates this species is moderately susceptible to major threats related to coral reef degradation (e.g., disease and bleaching). We applied two analytical approaches involving two different global coral datasets and the species’ distribution map as proxies to infer population decline. Based on global coral cover monitoring data, this species experienced a suspected decline of less than 25% over the past three generations, or since 1989. Based on the projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) conditions via both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios of global climate model data, in combination with the species’ depth range, distribution and bleaching vulnerability, this species is suspected to decline by less than 25% over the next three generations, or by 2050. It is listed as Least Concern. The change in status from the previous assessment reflects updated declines calculated from improved data on modeled coral cover loss and projected date of annual severe bleaching, along with improved knowledge of species traits.
habitat:
This species occurs on shallow reef (generally less than 2 m depth), exposed reef, reef flats and intertidal zones (Z. Richards pers. comm. 2008). Off Kenya, it can occur in generally disturbed or marginal habitat (B. Hoeksema pers. comm. 2008).  

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
This species is bleaching resistant (Kayanne et al. 2002, Richards et al. 2018). The huge Heliopora stands that extend for almost 10 km in Banda Aceh, Indonesia were the most damaged species of all corals due to the earthquake (Foster et al. 2006). This species may outcompete other corals under warm water temperatures (Guzman et al. 2019).

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification. In addition to global climate change, corals are also threatened by disease, and a number of localized threats. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual species is not known.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide with increases in numbers of diseases, coral species affected, and geographic extent (Ward et al. 2004, Sutherland et al. 2004, Sokolow et al. 2009). Outbreaks of coral diseases have damaged coral reefs worldwide with the most widespread, virulent, and longest running coral disease outbreak currently occurring on the Florida Reef Tract and throughout the Caribbean. The disease, stony coral tissue loss disease, has been ongoing since 2014 (Precht et al. 2016) and has devastated affected reefs along Florida (Walton et al. 2018, Williams et al. 2021) and throughout the Caribbean (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2019, Kramer et al. 2019). Numerous disease outbreaks have also occurred in the Indo-Pacific (Willis et al. 2004, Aeby et al. 2011; 2016), Indian Ocean (Raj et al. 2016) and Persian Gulf (Howells et al. 2020). Escalating anthropogenic stressors combined with the threats associated with global climate change of increases in coral disease, frequency and duration of coral bleaching and ocean acidification place coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific at high risk of collapse. 

Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities.
population:
This species is generally common, although it can also be locally rare. The largest stand in the world is thought to be off Ishigaki Island, in southwest Japan (Zann and Bolton 1985). It is known to form large colonies up to 10 km long in Japan and Indonesia (Zann and Bolton 1985, Foster et al. 2006). It is rare in the main archipelago of Fiji, but is considered common near the outlier island of Rotuma, common in Tuvalu, and abundant in Kiribati (Zann and Lovell pers. comm. 2008). This species is dominant in the Marshall Islands, prevalent in Kiribati, and uncommon in Ofu lagoon pools (D. Fenner pers. comm. 2008).

Species-specific, global level population information is limited. However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, Donovan et al. 2021). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends. 
   
Approach 1: Future population trend
The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is little understood and varies by species and locality (Bay et al. 2017, Matz et al. 2020, Logan et al. 2021). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2035 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2039 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2062 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2070 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where the onset of ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0-30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on 1°C of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is more resistant to bleaching. For widespread species, the final estimate of decline was further adjusted by excluding the proportion of cells within its range that were expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 after 2050 (three generation lengths), in order to account for the potential resilience of species to the asynchronous variability of bleaching events that occur across the Indo-Pacific. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Pacific, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in high-latitude reefs (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of less than 25% by the year 2050, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario.

The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered 11 species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 0-20 m and is predominately found at depths less than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered common, overall population is not restricted or highly fragmented, does not occur off-reef, is more resilient to disease, does not recover well from bleaching or disease, has a low susceptibility to crown-of-thorns starfish, is more resistant to bleaching, has an unknown susceptibility to the impacts of ocean acidification (Kornder et al. 2018), did not have >10,000 pieces exported annually in the aquarium trade between 2010-2019, it is overall suspected to be moderately susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 50% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a suspected global level decline of less than 25% since 1989, or over the past three generations.
range:
This species is distributed from the Red Sea, East Africa, Madagascar, Lakshadweep, western Thailand, northwestern Australia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Philippines, Taiwan, Marianas, Bonin, the Ryukyu Islands of Japan, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Papua New Guinea, Bismarck Sea, Solomon Islands, Great Barrier Reef, Fiji, New Caledonia, Tuvalu, Vanuatu, Wallis and Futuna, American Samoa, western Samoa, and throughout the Coral Sea (Zann and Bolton 1985, L. DeVantier and E. Turak pers. comm. 2008). 

The depth range is 0-20 m, but the species primarily occurs from 3-15 m (L. DeVantier pers. comm. 2024).
useTrade: This species is collected for the curio and jewellery trade (dried skeletons give blue colour), and the aquarium trade.
conservationActions:
This non-scleractinian coral is listed under Appendix I and II of CITES. There are no records in the CITES database of exports of non-scleractinians by weight. Parts of this species distribution overlaps with several Marine Protected Areas.

Recommended measures for conserving this species include research in taxonomy, population, abundance and trends, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration action; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management. Artificial propagation and techniques such as cryo-preservation of gametes may become important for conserving coral biodiversity.

Having timely access to national-level trade data for CITES analysis reports would be valuable for monitoring trends this species. The species is targeted by collectors for the aquarium trade and fisheries management is required for the species, e.g., Marine Protected Areas, quotas, size limits, etc. Consideration of the suitability of species for aquaria should also be included as part of fisheries management, and population surveys should be carried out to monitor the effects of harvesting.

rationale: Pennatula aculeata is assessed as Near Threatened. This sea pen species has a wide distribution in the Northeast Atlantic and is found in a broad depth range including many areas susceptible to damage by trawling and other activities. This species slow is growing and has a generation length of approximately 19 years. It is impacted by trawling and bottom contact fishing activity and its population has declined over the last 60 years due to fishing impacts (a period of three generations), particularly in the shallower part of its range where densities are greatest. At most of the depth range, the main method for estimating the population size and extent of this species is via underwater video, and technology with sufficient quality to identify species has only been available in the last 10–15 years. Therefore, it is not possible to quantify directly observed previous population decline, but it is inferred (A2(c)). The extent of damage is also inferred from trawling bycatch, which presents a proxy index for the extent to which specimens are removed from the population (A2(b)). Based on this evidence, the inferred global decline is suspected to be at least 20%. In regions that are not protected from bottom trawling the decline is projected to continue. Since the species is widely distributed at depths from 100 m to 2,300 m across the North Atlantic, it may be unlikely that the total population decline has exceeded 30%, the threshold for Vulnerable (VU), although it has been higher in particular areas (e.g., the Alboran Sea). In regions that are not protected from bottom trawling the ongoing decline will continue into the future.
habitat:
Pennatula aculeata inhabits muddy substrata from the continental shelf to bathyal depths from around 100 to 2,300 m (Langton et al. 1990). It forms dense fields in the Gulf of St Lawrence (Couillard et al. 2021) and possibly in other locations including the Bay of Biscay (e.g., Ruiz-Pico et al. 2017). These assemblages likely play an important role as habitat for early life stages of some fish species (Baillon et al. 2012).

Based on examination of growth rings in P. aculeata (Greely 2022), this species likely reaches maturity at 7 or 8 years. Oogenesis appears to be prolonged and over a duration likely greater than 24 months, with colonies reproducing every other year. The same study estimated that 50% of colonies spawned by age 11–14 years in female colonies, and 8–11 years in male colonies. Estimates of age range from 2 to 21 years, but may be longer (Murillo et al. 2018). An assumed longevity of approximately 30 years indicates an estimated generation length of 19 years.
threats:
Bottom trawling is likely detrimental to sea pen populations, and recovery could be slow given the relative longevity of sea pens and the relative high age at maturity. In the Alboran Sea (Western Mediterranean), a regional Red List assessment estimated that at least 50% of potential habitat had been affected by trawling, with fishing activities still ongoing (Cerrano et al. 2015). Trawling is directly connected to reduction in sea pen abundance in the North Sea (Harrald et al. 2018). There is increasing recognition that trawling is detrimental to sea pens, but conservation efforts vary across the range of this species.

Salmon farming on the coast of Norway is a threat to P. aculeata: field studies have documented reduction in growth and physical degradation of cold water coral areas in proximity to salmon cages (Kutti et al. 2015).
population: There are no published data on population sizes; however, this species can occur in large fields in the Bay of Biscay (Ruiz-Pico et al. 2017) and Gulf of Maine (Langton et al. 1990). The density of sea pens in such fields varied between 0 to 8 per m² in the Gulf of Maine, but could be slightly higher due to their ability to withdraw completely into the sediment (Langton et al. 1990). As the species occurs over a wide range in the Atlantic, the overall population size is therefore likely large. Investigations of reproductive characteristics in the northwest Gulf of St. Lawrence (Couillard et al. 2021) showed that colonies were gonochoric and that there was likely one annual spawning event. Since P. aculeata lives on soft substrates, it is likely subject to trawl damage, particularly in the shallower parts of its distribution where fishing pressure is greater.
range: Pennatula aculeata occurs across the North Atlantic extending from Cape Hatteras to Newfoundland on the western Atlantic margin, from Portugal to northern United Kingdom on the eastern Atlantic margin, also occurring in Iceland and the Mediterranean. This species also occurs on the Azores archipelago (Sampaio et al. 2019).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: Fields of sea pens shallower than 200 m depth are included in the OSPAR threatened and/or declining habitat "Sea pens and burrowing megafauna", while deeper fields (below 200 m) are included in "Coral gardens". However, monitoring in this way lumps multiple vulnerable habitats together and cannot discern declines specifically in P. aculeata. This species cannot be distinguished from Pennatula phosphorea on video data and thus its full distribution and extent are likely not appreciated. Therefore, further research into distribution and occurrence (or not) of P. aculeata in protected areas is recommended. Research into age and other life history parameters would allow a better understanding of the susceptibility and resilience to threats of this species. Research into the impact of ongoing trawling, particularly where the species provides habitat, is required.

rationale: Pennatula phosphorea is assessed as Near Threatened. This sea pen species has a wide distribution in the Northeast Atlantic and is found in relatively shallow-water environments (15–155 m), which are vulnerable to damage by trawling and other activities. The species is impacted by bottom contact fishing and salmon aquaculture, which likely decrease fitness and population density. The decline is projected to continue. It is currently only possible to estimate the population size and extent of this species via underwater video, and technology with sufficient quality to identify species has only been available in the last 10–15 years. Therefore, it is not possible to quantify directly observed previous population decline, but it is suspected (A2(c)). The extent of damage is also inferred from trawling bycatch, which presents a proxy index for the extent to which specimens are removed from the population (A2(b)). In regions that are not protected from bottom trawling the decline is projected to continue. The generation length for this species is estimated at approximately 19 years based on the closely related species P. aculeata. A regional assessment for the Mediterranean listed this species as Vulnerable, based on suspected population decrease of 40% in the last 20 years and continuing decline, and there is evidence of similar decline in the North Sea over a time scale representing three generations for this species (1960s–2020s). These regions are inferred to reflect a global pattern of decline, and the inferred global decline is suspected to be at least 25%. Since the population is mainly found in areas not protected by deep water trawling bans, the global population may reflect similar ongoing rates of decline that will continue into the future.
habitat:
Pennatula phosphorea lives on soft bottom habitats, between 20–700 m, on sandy or muddy bottoms (Grasshoff 1989, Vafidis et al. 1994). Most studies on this species have been conducted in Scotland, where salinity and gravel content were shown to have an influence on its distribution (Greathead et al. 2015). The species was found more likely to occur in areas with low primary productivity in the UK continental shelf and Celtic Seas (Downie et al. 2021).

Pennatula phosphorea grows up to 40 cm in length with approximately half of it protruding above the sediment. As other sea pens, this species can be used as habitat by other species (De Clippele et al. 2015). Growth rates and longevities have not been studied for this species. However, the congeneric species Pennatula aculeata and other cold-water sea pens can have longevities of over 20 years (Murillo et al. 2018; Neves et al. 2015, 2018). Based on examination of growth rings in the congener P. aculeata (Greely 2022), this species likely reaches maturity at 7 or 8 years. An assumed longevity of approximately 30 years indicates an estimated generation length of 19 years.

Female P. phosphorea colonies can maintain a pool of oocytes throughout the year, which are broadcast-spawned during the summer (July and/or August) (Edwards and Moore 2008). Oogenesis and spawning may be related to seasonal cues and annual spawning might be a brief and synchronous event. Mean polyp fecundity increases with colony size, and presence of large oocytes (500 μm) indicate the production of lecithotrophic larvae. These reproduction patterns might not be representative of colonies found at different locations and depths.

Pennatula phosphorea produces blue/green bioluminescence when stimulated, and it can also contract when disturbed (Nicol 1958). Colonies are capable of withdrawing into the sediment (Mackie 1998). Extracts from this species have been found to show narcotic and anorectic properties, acting as feeding deterrents for the octocoral's main predator, the Dover sole Solea solea (Mackie 1998). The bacteria Alphaproteobacteria were observed for the communities associated with both tissues and mucus of P. phosphorea (Porporato et al. 2013).
threats:
Given that Pennatula phosphorea is a sedentary species that lives on soft bottom areas that can be exposed to bottom-touching fishing gear, fishing is one of the threats currently recognised for the species (Murray et al. 2016, Downie et al. 2021, Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2023). Bottom trawling impacts soft-bottom communities including sea pens by decreasing diversity and shifting their trophic structure in fishing areas (Vergnon and Blanchard 2006, OSPAR 2022). Long line fishing also destroys Pennatula phosphorea (Mytilineou et al. 2014).

Pennatula phosphorea has been considered potentially less vulnerable to trawling than other sea pen species, due to its capacity of withdrawing into the sediment (Downie et al. 2021). In the Bay of Biscay and Irish Sea area, populations of P. phosphorea overlap with fishing grounds of the lobster Nephrops norvegicus (Greathead et al. 2005, Le Joncour et al. 2023). A regional Red List assessment estimated that at least 50% of potential habitat had been affected by trawling in the last 40 years, with fishing activities still ongoing (Cerrano et al. 2015). Trawling is directly connected to reduction in sea pen abundance in the North Sea (Harrald et al. 2018). There is increasing recognition that trawling is detrimental to sea pens, but conservation efforts vary across the range of this species. In Scotland, P. phosphorea also overlaps with salmon aquaculture farms (Wilding 2011, Wilding et al. 2012). Other sea pen and coral species show declining growth rates and damage in proximity to salmon cages (Kutti et al. 2015). As for other corals, climate change has the potential to change the range of suitable habitats for the species (Morato et al. 2020), and ocean acidification might affect their calcium carbonate skeletons.
population:
Information on population dynamics for P. phosphorea is not available. Densities can be variable depending on the location and even within a region (Greathead et al. 2007). For example, density reached 7.85 individuals per m² in the Central Fladen NCMPA (Northern North Sea, based on video data, Murray et al. 2016), but colonies were rare in trawl surveys conducted in Norway (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2023).

Pennatula phosphorea is found in areas of bottom-contact fishing activity; however, the population density of this species is negatively correlated with fishing impact (Murray et al. 2016, Downie et al. 2021). The natural undisturbed population density of this species may be very high.
range: Pennatula phosphorea, the species and its varieties, have been reported from European seas, Mediterranean, and both sides of the Atlantic but rarely in the West Atlantic. Specimens of this species have been reported from the Pacific, Indian Ocean, and Antarctica (Williams 1995), but confusion with other species makes the true geographic range uncertain. This assessment is therefore limited to the species found in the North Atlantic.
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions:
Sea pens are indicators of Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems (VME). If P. phosphorea has longevities comparable to those of its congeneric species P. aculeata (i.e., over 20 years in age, Murillo et al. 2018), then recovery from damage could take decades. No conservation sites have been identified specifically to protect the species; however, conservation areas to protect sea pens exist. Sea pens have been reported in several Special Areas of Conservation and they are protected under the ‘Mud in Deep Water Habitat Action Plan’ of the UK Biodiversity Action Plan (UKBAP) (Greathead et al. 2007).

Fields of sea pens shallower than 200 m depth are included in the OSPAR threatened and/or declining habitat "Sea pens and burrowing megafauna". However, monitoring in this way lumps multiple vulnerable habitats together and cannot discern declines specifically in P. phosphorea. This species cannot be distinguished from Pennatula aculeata on video data and thus its full distribution and extent are likely not appreciated. Further research into distribution and occurrence (or not) of P. phosphorea in protected areas is recommended. Research into age and other life history parameters would allow a better understanding of the susceptibility and resilience to threats of this species. Research into the impact of ongoing trawling, particularly where the species provides habitat, is required.

rationale: Anthothela grandiflora is assessed as Least Concern. Fishing with bottom contact gears is identified as the greatest potential threat to this soft coral species, but since A. grandiflora occurs on hard bottom substrates, it is likely less vulnerable to bottom contact fishing than some deep-water corals, and it is unlikely that fishing has a significant impact across its amphi-Atlantic distribution.
habitat: Anthothela grandiflora occurs on a variety of hard substrates. In Baltimore and Norfolk Canyons, USA it was found on isolated rock, rubble, large areas of emergent hard substrate, consolidated sediment or hard pavement, large boulders, and walls and steep slopes comprising rock or consolidated sediment (Brooke et al. 2017). There is no information available on age and growth of A. grandiflora, but like other deep-water corals, it can be assumed to be slow growing and relatively long lived. The reproduction of this species has not been studied.
threats: Bottom contact fishing is a potential threat to this species. As this species inhabits rough and hard substrata, normally considered unsuitable for bottom contact trawling, fishing may pose a lesser risk to this species. Salmon farming on the coast of Norway may be a threat to A. grandiflora; field studies have documented habitat decline within 1 km of salmon farms (Kutti et al. 2015, Maier et al. 2020).
population: The population size of Anthothela grandiflora is not known.
range: Anthothela grandiflora is distributed in the Northeast Atlantic Ocean in deep coastal waters and fjords of Norway and Iceland, down the northeast Atlantic margin at least from Ireland to the Bay of Biscay; in the Northwest Atlantic Ocean in deep waters off the coast of Canada and USA; and in the Southwest Atlantic Ocean off the coast of southern Brazil. It occurs in depths to 1,800 m off the coast of Ireland and in much shallower depths (to 100 m) in northern coastal fjords.
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions:
In the Northeast Atlantic, this species is included in the OSPAR threatened and/or declining habitat "Coral gardens", and colonies occurring below 800 m are protected from bottom trawling across its European range by regulations prohibiting bottom contact trawling below this depth. Many Marine Protected Area (MPA) designations are broadly made to coincide with the occurrence of hard substrate topological features that promote biodiversity and biomass of benthic sessile organisms such as A. grandiflora and, so, this species is likely afforded some protection by those designations.

Further research into the distribution of this species and its overlap with MPAs is recommended. Research into the population size, species-specific growth rates, and other life history traits would lead to a better understanding of the resilience of this species to potential threats.

rationale: Radicipes gracilis is assessed as Least Concern. This is a deep water, cold water species, that has a broad distribution on both sides of the North Atlantic and is locally uncommon. It has been found in fisheries trawling bycatch (Wareham and Edinger 2007) in multiple areas and its populations are proximate to trawl marks on the seabed. The known area of occupancy (AOO) is much less than 2,000 km²; however, the full extent of the species is not well known. The species is regionally assessed as Vulnerable in Norway. There is limited biological and historical information, which limit the ability to infer previous decline or impact on scales of generation lengths for the species. Based on its broad distribution at depths partly protected by trawling bans, it is considered globally Least Concern but additional data could prompt a reassessment.
habitat:
Radicipes gracilis can reach 90 cm in height (Cordeiro et al. 2017). The presence of this species increases local diversity (Grinyó et al. 2022). This species inhabits sandy soft bottoms in cold water (Madsen 1944). In the Northern Atlantic, it inhabits waters with temperatures of 0–7°C (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2015). The species is capable of forming dense stands (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2019). In the Gulf of Cadíz, R. gracilis is abundant on silt sediments in canyon areas and contouritic furrows (Grinyó et al. 2022).

In a 63,000 km² study area off Norway, the total area predicted as suitable habitat for Radicipes meadows was only 391 km², representing just 0.6% of the seafloor (Gonzalez-Mirelis and Buhl-Mortensen 2015).
threats: Radicipes gracilis is impacted by commercial fishing activity. This species has been found in bycatch of both fixed (gillnet and longline) and mobile (otter trawl) fisheries in the Northwest Atlantic ocean (Wareham and Edinger 2007). Radicipes gracilis has been observed near trawl marks off Svalbard (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2022). This species was assessed as Vulnerable on a national Red List within Norway, based on evidence that surveys frequently found habitat fisheries trawl tracks in the area of R. gracilis. This is a significant threat to their occurrence, reducing habitat quality, in addition to having a small distribution area with few localities in Norwegian waters (Tandberg and Mortensen 2021).
population: There is little published data on population size, even though Radicipes gracilis is the most recorded species in this genus of corals (Cordeiro et al. 2017). Radicipes gracilis has been recorded in trawling bycatch (Wareham and Edinger 2007) and inhabits multiple areas in Northern Norway and Svalbard where trawl marks are present, indicating a decline in habitat availability/quality (Buhl-Mortensen 2018, Tandberg and Mortensen 2021). The density of R. gracilis in the North Atlantic (Canada, Davies Strait, South Iceland, and Norway) qualifies it as ‘relatively uncommon’ (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2015). In the Norwegian margin this species lives on sandy-mud bottoms (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2019) and is the most densely occurring species, even with only 2.39 colonies per m² (Gonzalez-Mirelis and Buhl-Mortensen 2015). In Newfoundland the maximum density was similar, with 31 colonies per 10-m transect (Baker et al. 2012). By contrast, a study in the Gulf of Cadíz recorded an average density of 18 colonies per m² or a maximum of 38 colonies per m² (Grinyó et al. 2022).
range: Radicipes gracilis occurs at bathyl depths across the North Atlantic, extending from North Carolina to the Labrador Sea on the western Atlantic margin, and from the Gulf of Cadiz to North of Svalbard on the eastern Atlantic margin, as well as southern Iceland, western Ireland, Eastern Greenland, and the Azores archipelago. At the northern end of its range, north of Svalbard, it is present on the shelf edge between 500 and 700 m (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2022).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: In the Northeast Atlantic, this species is included in the OSPAR threatened and/or declining habitat "Coral gardens", and colonies occurring below 800 m are protected from bottom trawling across its European range and below 1,000 m in Norway by regulations prohibiting bottom contact trawling below this depth. Radicipes gracilis is a Vulnerable Marine Ecosystem (VME) and soft-bottom coral garden/forest indicator species (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2019, Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2017). In the Nordland and Troms areas in Norway, Radicipes sp. meadows are considered habitats of special interest (Gonzalez-Mirelis and Buhl-Mortensen 2015).

rationale: Heteropolypus sol is assessed as Least Concern. It is widely distributed throughout the North Atlantic over a large bathymetric range of 348–4,287 m on soft substrata. Although it is potentially impacted by trawling particularly in the shallower parts of its distribution, it is likely that this is not significant to the overall population size of the species. This species was only described recently and so it would be useful to research its distribution, ecology, and reproductive strategies.
habitat: This species occurs over a wide bathyal depth range on sandy silt, silty sand, and clayed silt (Altuna et al. 2014). Heteropolypus sol is small, with colonies only a few cm high; the colony stalk normally has rootlets. The species name 'sol' refers to the shape of the colony resembling a stylised sun with the expended autozooids around the outer margin.
threats: Bottom trawling is likely to impact Heteropolypus sol as it inhabits soft sediments and cannot retract into the substrate.
population: There is no information on the population size of this species. It was considered the most abundant of the five observed mushroom coral species when they were surveyed offshore Newfoundland, Canada (Altuna et al. 2014), although no information was given on its density or abundance.
range: Heteropolypus sol occurs in soft sediment environments where it anchors directly in the substrate. It is found on both margins of the North Atlantic, from Northeast United States of America, into Newfoundland (Altuna et al. 2014), as far north as southern Iceland and on the southern margin of Ireland. The species occurs on the Mid Atlantic Ridge from the Reykjanes Ridge (Molodtsova 2013) to the Azores archipelago (Molodtsova 2013).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: The majority of records for this species occur in very deep waters below 2,000 m. Within EU waters, legislation prevents bottom trawling deeper than 800 m, which offers protection to this species. In Canadian waters, H. sol may be more vulnerable as it is found on the slope where trawling may be more prevalent. Many of the occurrences for this species fall outside any national jurisdiction and thus may be vulnerable to fishing on the high seas. As this species was only described in the last decade, more research is needed to better understand its distribution and any potential overlaps with Marine Protected Areas (MPAs). More research is recommended on the life history strategies of this species, including but not limited to reproductive strategies, longevity, and growth rates.

rationale: Ceratocaulon wandeli is assessed as Least Concern. This cold water soft coral species is prevalent in large fields in deep water north of Iceland, mainly outside the region of current commercial trawling activity. The species is relatively short and may be able to fully retract into the sediment, which may make it moderately resistant to commercial trawling. Although the area of occupancy (AOO) is smaller than 2,000 km², there is no current evidence for any continuing or projected decline or significant fragmentation of the existing population.
habitat: Ceratocaulon wandeli is a relatively small soft coral, less than 10 cm when fully extended. It lives partly embedded in soft muddy substrates but is also found on hard bottom substrates and can occur attached to cobble or boulders. This species has a very distinctive morphology with a thick cuticular sheath surrounding the stalk of the colony, into which it can fully retract. The species was known from material collected 525–850 m off northern Iceland (Williams 1987), and more recent surveys around Iceland have extended the depth range in both directions to around 200 to >2,000 m deep. Its distribution is restricted to very cold, deep waters, at sea temperatures with an exceptional maximum of 2.5°C but mostly below 0°C in Icelandic waters (Icelandic Benthic Database). The unusual morphology of the species is enigmatic and its position in coral phylogeny is not currently understood (McFadden et al. 2022).
threats: This species could be threatened by bottom contact fishing. Other soft coral species are highly susceptible to trawl damage and in Iceland, where C. wandeli can be abundant, it has been captured as bycatch by trawling in stock assessment surveys. This is a cold water Arctic species that probably cannot tolerate temperatures above ~2.5°C. It is therefore particularly susceptible to threats from ocean warming.
population: Ceratocaulon wandeli has a patchy distribution. It is sometimes recovered in trawl surveys in large numbers, indicating high local population density in northern Iceland, but in other parts of the range it is seldom encountered and known from sparse records.
range: The cold water soft coral Ceratocaulon wandeli is an Arctic endemic species. It is mostly known from bathyal depths from the northern part of Iceland where it can be abundant, with additional records from north of the Faroe Islands. The distribution follows the cold water Iceland-Faroe Slope Jet (Semper et al. 2020) current along a depth contour around 800 m deep. There are also reports of the species from cold water in Atlantic Canada (Watling et al. 2011).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade of this species.
conservationActions: Little information is available specific to Ceratocaulon wandeli. There are no records of this species from within any of the current protected areas around Iceland, where it is best known. However, fisheries effort data from Iceland indicate that most of the records of this species occur outside the areas where there is active commercial trawling and there is no current evidence of bycatch in commercial trawling. Further research into the distribution and occurrence (or not) of this species especially over its entire distribution is recommended. Research into age and other life history parameters would allow a better understanding of the susceptibility and resilience to threats of this species. Research into the impact of ongoing trawling, particularly if/where the species provides habitat, is required.

rationale: Paragorgia arborea is assessed as Near Threatened (NT). This gorgonian species is vulnerable to trawling activity and its population has declined due to fishing impacts, particularly in the shallower parts of its range. A regional assessment for Norway also listed this species as NT and estimated its generation length as 20 years; therefore, the relevant period of three past generations represents a time period of ~1963–2023. It is currently only possible to estimate the population size and extent of this species via underwater video, and technology with sufficient quality to identify species has only been available in the last 10 to 15 years. The extent of damage is also inferred from trawling bycatch, which presents a proxy index for the extent to which specimens are removed from the population (A2(b)); declining frequency in bycatch and the declining size of individuals is evidence of population decline. There is a lack of evidence to conclusively show whether the total population decline has exceeded 30%, the threshold for Vulnerable (VU), although it has been higher in particular locations. The Norwegian regional assessment estimated a 17% regional decline over 60 years based on the frequency of observations of broken colonies, and this rate is likely to be much higher in other areas where the species is not protected by refugia in steep fjords. Based on this evidence, the inferred global decline is suspected to be at least 20%. Paragorgia arborea is slow growing and sessile, and cannot retreat from the threats of bottom-contacting activities and climate change that threaten it throughout its range. It is a brooding species and is sensitive to sediment type, which is controlled by the damage from bottom-contacting activities, meaning it has very low and potentially declining recruitment potential. Population decline is projected to continue.
habitat:
Paragorgia arborea is a large organism and can be a foundation species in coral garden habitats, often representing the early coloniser and, later, the oldest members that structure larger coral areas. Colonies can grow up to 6 m high. The species is restricted to habitats with strong currents including steeply sloping habitats such as marine canyons, growing on mixed hard substrata (cobble or gravel as well as boulder) (Watanabe et al. 2009). It has a broad tolerance for variable slopes compared to some other deep-sea corals (Sundahl et al. 2020).

Food supply is considered to be an important limiting factor that controls distribution and likely influences the substrate selection of new recruits (Lacharité and Metaxas 2013). There is evidence that this species is a brooder (Lacharité and Metaxas 2013). Polyps demonstrate seasonal activity patterns correlated to chlorophyll availability, with a winter dormancy period (Girard et al. 2022, Zuazo et al. 2020). The height of this species may be limited by the size and stability of the attached substratum; colonies on boulders become destabilised when they reach a height of around twice the diameter of the stone (Mortensen and Buhl-Mortensen 2005).

Paragorgia arborea can form dense coral gardens with other species, where P. arborea provides three-dimensional habitat complexity through its large size and branching form. It often grows on scleractinian framework-forming cold water coral reef systems or can form dense forests on steep slopes. It provides shelter and breeding space for numerous other mobile and epibiotic species, including fish and invertebrates. Other associated species include the basket star Gorgonocephalus caputmedusae, which uses P. arborea to gain elevation, and other octocorals such as Primnoa resedaeformis, Paramuricea grandis, Keratoisis ornate and Ptilella grandis.
threats:
Deep sea corals such as P. arborea are threatened by seabed disturbance through activities such as trawling and bottom-touching gear (e.g., long-line fishing), as well as deep sea mining, drilling for oil and gas, or deep sea cables, all of which occur through the entire extent of its global range. Paragorgia arborea is a slow growing species that can live for centuries and its fragile skeleton breaks easily and cannot readily recover (Buhl-Mortensen and Buhl-Mortensen 2005, Sundahl et al. 2020). Damage to P. arborea further impacts other co-occurring species as this species structures the local reef ecosystems.

Salmon farming on the coast of Norway is a threat to P. arborea: field studies have documented reduction in growth and physical degradation of colonies in proximity to salmon cages (Kutti et al. 2015).

Climate change is also likely to impact this species as it is sensitive to temperature: one study has estimated that climate pressures will lead to 99% reduction in available habitats for P. arborea (Morato et al. 2020). Although there may be limited refugia available (Wang et al. 2022), a slow-growing sessile species has limited potential to retreat to other habitats. The skeleton of paragorgid corals is composed of fused magnesium calcite sclerites which can dissolve in carbonate-undersaturated waters making the species vulnerable to the impacts of ocean acidification.
population:
Microsatellite data from one population indicated high variability in a seemingly stable population (Coykendall and Morrison 2015). Variation across populations of this species reflects basin-scale connectivity, with high connectivity across depths within each region. Number of haplotypes are shared across a large scale of distribution, which indicates well connected populations within the species (Herrera et al. 2012).

This species occurs at low densities. Paragorgia arborea broods its larvae and recruitment rates are low. On the Norwegian margin, the population densities vary between 0.15–0.25 colonies per m² on reefs off Norway (Purser 2010). In the Northwest Atlantic, densities are even lower, with 0.009–0.1 colonies per m² (Lacharité and Metaxas 2013).

Growth rates are estimated as around 1 cm per year, and slow after 20 years, meaning that large colonies are hundreds of years old. A regional Red List assessment for Norway calculated the generation time for P. arborea as 20 years (Tandberg and Mortensen 2021) based on the average age of sexually mature individuals (polyps) in a colony (Carpenter et al. 2008), but this is likely a conservative estimate. Colonies are captured as bycatch in trawl fisheries (Mortensen and Buhl-Mortensen 2005), and the species is likely subject to severe damage particularly in the shallower parts of its distribution where fishing pressure is greater.
range: Paragorgia arborea is a large, up to 6-m high, bright pink or white gorgonian coral living in deep water at temperatures from 3 to 8°C in antitropical latitudes. Its range spans between 30° to 70° of the North and South Atlantic and the South Pacific. It generally occurs at depths of 1,000–2,000 m but with many records from continental shelf breaks around 300–500 m, and is also found exceptionally deeper than 3,000 m and at shallower depths up to 40 m in fjords in Norway or British Columbia (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2015).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: In the Northeast Atlantic, Paragorgia arborea habitats below 200 m are included in the OSPAR designation "Coral gardens", and this species is also an indicator species of Vulnerable Marine Ecosystem for ICES / FAO and at national level in several countries where it occurs. This species lives in high current areas that are difficult to sample and monitor. Therefore, the distribution and abundance are not well known. Further research into distribution and occurrence of P. arborea in protected areas is recommended. Research into life history, especially age at maturity of adult colonies, and larval dispersal and recruitment would allow a better understanding of the susceptibility and resilience to threats of this species. Research into the impact and potential for recovery after damage from ongoing trawling, particularly where the species provides habitat, is required.

rationale: Distichoptilum gracile is assessed as Least Concern. This sea pen species has a near global distribution and occurs from 450 m to approximately 3,000 m. Although it is potentially impacted by trawling, particularly in the shallower parts of its distribution, it is unlikely that there is significant global impact on the population size.
habitat: This species inhabits fine muds and silts between 450 to 3,400 m. It is a filter-feeder and is known to be bioluminescent (Williams 2011). There is no published information on its reproduction, growth rates or longevity. Generally, sea pens are gonochoric with a sex ratio of 1:1 (Chia and Crawford 1973).
threats: Bottom trawling is likely detrimental to Distichoptilum gracile, and recovery could be slow due to the low growth rates as known from other sea pens. However, most of the distribution is deeper than current active fishing activities.
population: There is almost no information on the population size of this species, which is mostly known from individual records.
range: This species has a wide distribution with occurrences in the Atlantic as far north as Iceland. It occurs along both east and western North Atlantic margins and has been reported in the Gulf of Mexico. It occurs as far south as South Africa in the southeastern Atlantic Ocean and has been reported to occur off Argentina (Schejter et al. 2018) in the southwest Atlantic. There is a single occurrence in the Indian Ocean, off southwest India (Araya et al. 2018). It occurs in the northwest Pacific, offshore from California and Mexico, and on both sides of the South Pacific, as far south as Chile in the southeast and along eastern Australia in the southwest. The species occurs as far south as New Zealand. It is not known from the Southern Ocean. Despite its wide range, records of Distichoptilum gracile are patchy and with records that may reflect the intensity of deep-water exploration regionally; it is mostly known from countries with well-developed infrastructure and fisheries management organizations, where it is more likely to be recorded.
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: Conservation actions vary regionally. In the EU, bottom trawling is banned below 800 m, protecting individuals that occur below this depth. Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) have been erected to protect deep-sea benthic communities from bottom trawling. However, many MPAs are erected based on the presence of geogenic and biogenic topological features that are known to promote biodiversity and abundance of benthic fauna, and since D. gracile inhabits soft substrates, it may not be protected by those designations. Further research into its population size, abundance, life history, and ecology is required, as is research into the potential threat posed by bottom trawling. A better understanding of how this species overlaps with MPAs would be useful.

rationale: Convexella jungerseni is assessed as Data Deficient. This species is known from only a handful of occurrences in the North Atlantic in the Denmark Strait and from the New England and Corner Rise Seamounts. It is unknown whether the species is endemic to the region or is just more widespread in difficult to explore offshore environments, and research is required to determine this. More research is needed on all aspects of the life history strategies of this species including but not limited to reproductive strategies and fecundity, generation time, growth rates, and longevity to determine its resilience to potential threats. Finally, research into the overall ecology of the species is required.
habitat:
At the Mytilus Seamount, along with sponges, Convexella jungerseni dominated the community at depths greater than 2,800 m and in waters of ~2.75–3°C, where it occurred in areas with basalt pillars and ledges interspersed with sediment, ledges, and piles of rock (Lapointe et al. 2020). Convexella jungerseni was found in low abundance at Yakutat Seamount in ~3.5–4.5°C where the substrate was a botryoidal ledge of thick manganese crust that was covered by pteropod shells in some areas (Lapointe et al. 2020). The type specimen was found in waters at 1.6–3°C in the Denmark Strait (Madsen 1944). The original type specimen was 9.4 cm in length. Nothing is known about the reproductive strategy, growth rate or longevity of the species or of any closely related species.

Another species in the genus Convexella had bioactive compounds with abundant metabolites extracted, hypothesized to have an ecological role in chemical defence or antifouling, which could be of interest for potential biomedical applications (Rojo de Almeida et al. 2010).
threats: Convexella jungerseni occurs on seamounts, which create biodiversity hotspots, causing nearby waters to often be targeted by fisheries. We infer that fishing may be a threat to this species as it is presumed that, like most deep-sea corals, this species is likely to be long lived, slow growing, and has a long generation time. Thus, when damaged, recovery would be extremely slow.
population: There are no published data on population sizes for this species or other species of the same genus.
range: The gorgonian Convexella jungerseni is a deep-sea coral that occurs in the Northwest Atlantic and is known from a handful of records from offshore Iceland, Greenland, and the Mytilus and Yakutat Seamounts in the New England and Corner Rise seamount chain, with the Yakutat seamount being in the High Seas. This species has been reported from a bathymetric range of approximately 1,940–3,000 m.
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: This species is known from only a handful of specimens from the North Atlantic, with some records occurring in areas beyond national jurisdiction. More research is needed on the species’ reproductive strategy, fecundity, growth rate, and longevity to determine its resilience. More research into exploring this species’ distribution is needed to see whether it occurs elsewhere or is endemic to the region. More research into the population size of this species is required to adequately assess any threats to the overall survival of the species.

rationale: Primnoa resedaeformis is assessed as Near Threatened. This gorgonian species known as “Red Tree Coral” is susceptible to fisheries pressure, and while there has been no formal population assessment, there have been documented declines via bycatch records decreasing compared to historical records, as well as negative size selection in some regions (A2(b)). It is not possible to quantify directly observed previous population decline, but it is inferred (A2(c)). A decline in extent can be inferred as the species is common in bycatch from the area. This species is an important source of habitat for commercially important species, so fishing pressure is likely to be an ongoing threat to this species across its range. Furthermore, there are emerging threats to P. resedaeformis habitat from offshore energy development and, in particular, rising temperatures, with certain populations already experiencing temperatures at their thermal maximum. The global population may reflect similar ongoing rates of decline that will continue into the future. The long lifespan and reproductive patterns of this species mean that recovery from these impacts is slow and thus impacts are cumulative. The generation length for this species is estimated at approximately 44 years. Over the relevant period of the last 100 years, the inferred global population declines for this species is suspected to be around 25%.
habitat:
Primnoa resedaeformis occurs on a variety of hard substrates in the northeast Atlantic, from canyon walls to boulders and glacial dropstones to Desmophyllum pertusum reefs. It is one of the most abundant and widely distributed habitat-forming gorgonians in the North Atlantic (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2010). Primnoa resedaeformis provides important habitat for a variety of invertebrate and fish species, including commercially important rockfishes (Krieger and Wing 2002, Buhl-Mortensen and Mortensen 2003, Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2010).

Studies have documented growth rates in P. resedaeformis of 2.6 cm year-1 (Sherwood and Edinger 2009); however, due to fishing pressure, the ages of individuals included in that study are biased towards smaller, younger individuals. Mortensen and Buhl-Mortensen (2005) reported growth of 1.8–2.2 cm year-1 for young colonies and slower rates for older colonies, and age up to 61 years. Similar growth rates and ages up to 80 years have been recorded in the sister species P. pacifica from the Pacific, for which growth rate has been shown to decline with age (Choy et al. 2020).

Primnoa resedaeformis is a gonochoric, broadcast spawning species. It has been shown to have multiple size classes of oocytes, suggesting overlapping reproductive cohorts, and a reproductive cycle that lasts longer than a year. This species can have variable fecundity among individuals. Age at first reproduction could range from 7.6–19.8 years and may be dependent on the sex of the colony, which may have implications for recovery from disturbance (Mercier and Hamel 2011, Fountain et al. 2019). This minimum age at first reproduction and the long life span indicate a generation length of around 44 years for this species.
threats:
This species overlaps with commercially valuable fisheries, meaning that fishing pressure, particularly trawl fisheries, can damage and remove colonies of this species (Husebø et al. 2002). Fishers in Canada have recorded a reduction in bycatch of this species over time (Gass and Willison 2005). The slow growth rate, long lifespan, and relatively high age at maturity, as well as the sex differences in age at maturity can impact the species capacity for recovery.

Salmon farming on the coast of Norway is a threat to P. resedaeformis: field studies have documented reduction in growth and physical degradation of colonies in proximity to salmon cages (Kutti et al. 2015).

This is a cold water species that is found at temperatures of 1–11°C (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2015), and some populations approach the upper thermal quartile for this species (4.5–7.5°C), which puts it at risk for climate change effects in the future (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2015, Fountain et al. 2019). Excess warming has been shown to induce physiological stress in mesocosm studies in this species (Scanes et al. 2018).

Specific populations of this species may also expose it to emerging threats such as offshore energy development (e.g., wind energy development).
