Energy production by offshore wind is forecast to increase to 260 GW or more by 2030 (Musial et al. 2022), and the structures of these platforms may interact with benthic habitats directly (ICF 2020) as well as alter other environmental factors such as hydrodynamics and productivity (Hogan et al. 2023); however, impacts from these potential threats have not been documented at this time.
population: There are no published data on population sizes in Primnoa resedaeformis; however, this species can occur in isolated patches to dense coral gardens. In a number of studies P. resedaeformis was the most abundant species observed (Cairns and Bayer 2005, Gass and Willison 2005, Gordon and Kenchington 2007).
range: Primnoa resedaeformis occurs across the North Atlantic, with records from off Virginia in the western Atlantic to off the coasts of Norway, Sweden, Scotland, Faroe Island, and Iceland in the eastern Atlantic (Cairns and Bayer 2005). This species is limited to northern waters with no records occurring south of Virginia. This species is exclusive to the Atlantic; any records from the Pacific are of the sister species, Primnoa pacifica (Cairns and Bayer 2005).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: The distribution of this species overlaps with designated Habitat Areas of Particular Concern (HAPC), National Monuments, and Marine Protected Area (MPA) zones in the Northeast Atlantic, which may protect it from fisheries impacts in these areas. Further research is required to determine population size trends, provide better understanding on life history, and to better understand the threats from harvesting. Monitoring of habitat trends is required.

rationale: Paragorgia johnsoni currently is relatively sparsely distributed, with occurrence data in the Northeastern and Northwestern Atlantic and isolated populations in Brazil. This species is slow growing and sessile, and cannot retreat from the threats of bottom-contacting activities and climate change that threaten it throughout its range. The long lifespan of this bubblegum coral means that it is likely slow to recover from damage. Bottom trawling continues to occur in some of the supposedly protected areas, where the status of this species' populations also remains unclear. Uncertainty about the current and past global distribution and population status preclude a robust understanding of ongoing impacts, as in regions not protected by current trawling bans the declines is ongoing. Population decline is projected to continue. Only a minority of the range is protected, with a majority subject to potential damage from fishing, and the total range is vulnerable to impacts of climate change. Based on this evidence, the inferred global decline is suspected to be at least 20%. The extent of past damage is inferred from trawling bycatch, which presents a proxy index for the extent to which specimens are removed from the population (A2(b)). There is a lack of evidence to conclusively show whether the total population decline has exceeded 30%, the threshold for Vulnerable (VU), although most of the present habitat is subject to ongoing trawling. Therefore this species is assessed as Near Threatened (A2b).
habitat:
Paragorgia johnsoni was the dominant species in one local population in coral gardens on rocky and lithic substrates of Cavala and Gigante Seamount, Azores between 500 to 650 m depth (Tempera et al. 2013, Morato et al. 2021). Scientific surveys in the Flemish Pass and northeast slope of the Grand Banks off Newfoundland recorded bycatch of P. johnsoni mostly between 1,200 and 1,300 m depth (Murillo et al. 2011). 

There are distinct cream and red-coloured colony morphotypes. Colonies have typical sizes between 40 to 60 cm but can be larger. This species was found with a concave fan-shaped structure oriented towards the current direction, from which there is food intake (Morato et al. 2021). These assemblages represent three-dimensional habitats for associated fauna like lace corals, other gorgonians, and sponges, for which they might play an important role (Tempera et al. 2013).

Bubblegum corals (Paragorgia spp.) have slow growth and long lifespans of decades to centuries and consequently recovery from damage takes a long time. The congener P. arborea was estimated to have a generation length of 20 years, and this is an appropriate proxy for generation length in P. johnsoni.
threats:
Direct human impacts on the seabed such as bottom fisheries, cable and pipeline laying, hydrocarbon drilling, and seabed mining, or indirect human impacts such as climate change and ocean acidification resultant from fossil emissions can target this species (Tempera et al. 2013). As an ecosystem-forming species, impacts on P. johnsoni also impact other associated species. Local fisheries targeting depths below 500 m have captured this species as bycatch in the Azores (COLETA - IMAR/DOP-Uac 2015). Off Newfoundland, this species was one of the main species vulnerable to bottom trawling activity with high biomass reported during scientific surveys (Murillo et al. 2011).

Fishing impact in the Azores has been inferred based on observed filament lines near damaged colonies, and structural damage to corals was greater close to the summit of the seamount, where more fishing occurs (Morato et al. 2021). It can be projected that if local longline fisheries proceed to target greater depths in future, more of the population may be vulnerable to impact.

Modelling of climate change impacts on the closely related species Paragorgia arborea indicated potentially severe declines by 2100 (Morato et al. 2020). Climate change will include increases in sea temperature, and ocean acidification. The skeleton of paragorgid corals is composed of fused magnesium calcite sclerites, which can dissolve in carbonate-undersaturated waters making the species vulnerable to the impacts of ocean acidification.
population: There is limited population information for this species. One population of large specimens of Paragorgia johnsoni was discovered on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge within the Azorean EEZ between 545 to 595 m depth. The density of this population was estimated to have an average of 6.6 colonies per 100 m², with a local maximum around 30 colonies per 100 m² (Morato et al. 2021). Considering the large distribution range of P. johnsoni over the Atlantic and the disjunct distribution records for this species, its overall population size could be very large although it is likely relatively sparsely distributed in most areas.
range: Paragorgia johnsoni occurs across the North Atlantic from Azores to Madeira on the eastern Atlantic margin, and from Newfoundland and Bahamas to Brazil (off Rio de Janeiro) between 545 and 4,152 m depth (Grasshoff 1979, Sánchez 2005, Murillo et al. 2011, Morato et al. 2021). It is part of the lineage with species mostly from the Pacific; therefore, in terms of phylogenetic diversity it is a quite unique species in the Atlantic (Herrera and Shank 2016).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions:
In the Northeast Atlantic, habitats of P. johnsoni below 200 m are included in the OSPAR designation "Coral gardens" (OSPAR Comission 2010); however, as bottom trawling continues to occur in some OSPAR areas, the status of this species' populations remains unclear in these places. This species is also an indicator species of Vulnerable Marine Ecosystem for ICES / FAO “hard bottom coral garden”, and it is part of the EUNIS habitat classification system “A6.11X_PT02: Paragorgia johnsoni on hard substrate” (Tempera et al. 2013).
Within the EU, P. johnsoni is protected from bottom trawling below 800 m, and it seems to sustain minor damage from by-catch on long and handline fisheries (Sampaio et al. 2012). In an evaluation of P. johnsoni at Gigante seamount, Azores, colonies were found to be mostly intact or with minor damage potentially caused by longline fishing lines. OSPAR areas are nonetheless subject to trawling and populations within Marine Protected Areas may still be subject to damage from fisheries. 

Research is needed to understand the distribution and abundance of this species as well as life history information to better understand of the susceptibility and resilience of this species to threats.

rationale: Trachythela rudis is assessed as Least Concern. The species is widespread and likely less susceptible to the impacts of fishing than many other octocorals because of its encrusting nature and preference for hard substrates that are less trawled. Research into its biology and ecology would help assess the potential impact of any future threats.
habitat: This species grows on hard substrates, often carpeting dead coral skeletons, at depths of 500–2,000 m. It is easily identified from video data because of its distinctive deep purple colour; however, its extremely soft tissue makes the species difficult to collect and handle and there are no published studies on the biology of this species.
threats: Fishing with bottom-contact gears is a potential threat to this species. However, the preference of Trachythela rudis for hard substrates, coupled with its encrusting nature, offers some protection from fishing gears.
population: The population size of this species is unknown, but it can occur in high densities at specific locations.
range: Trachythela rudis occurs in the Northwest Atlantic from the northern Gulf of Mexico to Nova Scotia, off Ireland and on the Fangorn Bank in the Northeast Atlantic, off Southeast Brazil (Carvalho et al. 2023), and off New Zealand.
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: There are no specific conservation actions in place for this species, but it likely does occur in protected areas that encompass deep biogenic or geogenic substrate. Research on its population size and ecology would help determine the resilience of this species to potential threats.

rationale: Balticina christii occurs in a fairly limited region of the North Atlantic where fishing activity with bottom trawl is high, and it is at risk of damage from commercial fisheries trawling and other activities that disturb the seabed. The level of global decline cannot be determined for this species based on the data currently available, however decreases to other ecologically similar species have been shown to be substantial across large ranges. Bottom trawling on soft-bottom communities including sea pens has been shown to decrease diversity and shift the trophic structure in fishing areas, and species that are sensitive to disturbance are typically absent from impacted areas. Because of its relatively shallow distribution, B. christii is not protected by trawling bans in deep waters. It is likely that the species has suffered past declines that have been unrecorded. In some regions, over 90% of the available habitat is potentially impacted. Based on currently available data we are unable to define whether this species should be listed as Least Concern or under any category of threat, and currently assess it as Data Deficient. Data regarding the population density and distribution, and/or specific impacts of trawling on local populations could prompt a reassessment.
habitat: Balticina christii lives on soft bottoms in deep photic to upper bathyal depths in the subarctic North Atlantic. It is a suspension feeding sea pen; however, more specific ecology is not known.
threats: This species can be sensitive to direct impacts on the seabed such as trawling, or to other disturbance that changes sediment patterns such as major energy infrastructure construction. Bottom trawling impacts soft-bottom communities including sea pens by decreasing diversity and shifting their trophic structure in fishing areas (Vergnon and Blanchard 2006, OSPAR Commission 2010). Because of the relatively shallow distribution of Balticina christii in most of its range, it is not protected by trawling bans in deep waters in the EU (below 800 m) or Norway (below 1,000 m). Soft bottom communities including sea pens are broadly impacted by trawling, with nearly 100% of the habitat being impacted, and species that are sensitive to disturbance are absent from impacted areas (Pommer et al. 2016). Morphologically similar species are highly susceptible to trawl damage and, although damaged individuals can re-attach to the bottom, suffer high mortality after disturbance (Malecha and Stone 2009). The Norway regional assessment considers the species to have a substantial and stable population (Tandberg and Mortensen 2021), even though many of the species' records are in areas with fishing farms, where the threats are sedimentation and eutrophication.
population: Sampling of this species via oceanographic cruises or as by-catch of longline fisheries typically recovers single specimen records (Iceland Biodiversity Database). Other species of Balticina sometimes form dense fields (e.g., Fuller et al. 2008). It is not known whether B. christii also forms dense fields. Population data for this species are scarce.
range: Balticina christii is a species of sea pen found in the northern part of the Northeast Atlantic, ranging from 110 to 500 m depth. It inhabits soft bottom sediments in areas off the coasts of Norway, north of the United Kingdom, the Faroes, and Iceland.
useTrade: There is no known use or trade of this species.
conservationActions: In the Northeast Atlantic, fields of sea pens shallower than 200 m depth are included in the OSPAR threatened and declining habitat "Sea pens and burrowing megafauna communities", while deeper fields (below 200 m) are included in "Coral gardens". Little information is available specific to Balticina christii. OSPAR considers the status of sea pens and burrowing megafauna communities in the Arctic to be unknown, and in areas slightly further south to be "poor"; OSPAR also considers the status of coral gardens in these areas to be poor (OSPAR 2022). However, the Norway regional assessment considers the species to have a substantial and stable population (Tandberg and Mortensen 2021), even though many of the species' records are in areas with fish farms. Further research into the distribution and occurrence of this species in protected areas is recommended. Research into age and other life history parameters would allow a better understanding of the susceptibility and resilience to threats of this species. Research into the impact of ongoing trawling, particularly if/where the species provides habitat, is required.

rationale: Candidella imbricata is assessed as Least Concern. Fishing with bottom contact gears is identified as the greatest potential threat to this gorgonian species, but since C. imbricata occurs in deeper water (420–2,060 m) and on hard bottom substrates, it is likely that most of the population is less vulnerable to bottom contact fishing than some deep-water corals, and it is unlikely that fishing has a significant impact across its amphi-Atlantic distribution.
habitat: Candidella imbricata inhabits hard substrates on the continental slope at depths of 420–2,060 m. The colonies create unique habitats for the deep-sea polychaetes Gorgoniapolynoe caeciliae and G. pseudocaeciliae, and host ophiocanthid ophiuroids (Eckelbarger et al. 2005, Maxwell et al. 2022, Watling et al. 2011). There is no published information on the reproduction, growth rates, or longevity of C. imbricata.
threats: Bottom trawling is likely detrimental to Candidella imbricata, and recovery could be slow due to the low growth rates as known from other deep-sea corals. This species inhabits rough and hard substrata, normally considered unsuitable for bottom contact trawling, and thus fishing may pose a reduced risk to the species.
population: Candidella imbricata is mostly known from individual records (Morrissey et al. 2022), and there is almost no information on the population size of this species.
range: The gorgonian Candidella imbricata is a deep-sea coral that occurs in a broad range across the North Atlantic, extending along the western Atlantic margin from the north of the United States to the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea, and along the eastern Atlantic margin from Ireland to the Canary Islands. It also occurs around the Azores archipelago and in small patches in the high seas.
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: In the Northeast Atlantic, this species is included in the OSPAR threatened and/or declining habitat "Coral gardens". This species occurs in waters deeper than 400 m, and colonies occurring below 800 m are protected from bottom trawling across its European range by regulations prohibiting bottom contact trawling below this depth. Fisheries management plans also exist for areas of the High Seas in the North Atlantic. Many Marine Protected Area (MPA) designations are broadly made to coincide with the occurrence of hard substrate topological features that promote biodiversity and biomass of benthic sessile organisms such as C. imbricata, and so this species is likely afforded some protection by those designations. Further research into the distribution of this species and its overlap with MPAs is recommended. Research into the population size, species-specific growth rates, and other life history traits would lead to a better understanding of the resilience of this species to potential threats.

rationale: Enallopsammia profunda is endemic to the Northwest Atlantic, occurring over a depth range of 133 to 2,286 m. As with other deep-sea coral species, E. profunda is assumed to be long-lived and slow-growing (generation length of 51.5 years). This species is often found co-occurring with Desmophyllum pertusum reefs, which are currently listed as Vulnerable and have suffered a 30% decline in the last 30 years; where we know D. pertusum reefs have been damaged, it is likely E. profunda has also been impacted. However, based on availability data, there is uncertainty about the current population status. Many recent records of E. profunda occur within a Marine Protected Area (MPA) where bottom trawling is banned, but the full extent of the population distribution is not well understood. As the global decline of Desmophyllum reefs indicates historical declines in E. profunda may have been significant and because the declines may be continuing in regions not protected by current trawling bans, it is inferred that this species has undergone some level of global decline in the last 100 years and may be approaching the threshold for Vulnerable under criterion A2b. It is therefore listed as Near Threatened A2b.
habitat: Enallopsammia profunda is an ahermatypic deep-sea coral that grows on hard substrata, between 130–2,280 m, very often co-occurring with reef forming Desmophyllum pertusum (Reed 2002, Hebbeln et al. 2014). Colonies are dendroid in shape and grow up to 1 m² (Friedwald et al. 2004). There are no empirical studies on the life history characteristics of E. profunda; however, the closely related species E. rostrata is known to be a gonochoric broadcast spawner and has been reported to spawn both continuously throughout the year offshore Brazil (Pires et al. 2014) or once per year offshore New Zealand (Burgess and Babcock 2005). That species is reported to have a high fecundity in excess of 144 oocytes per polyp (Burgess and Babcock 2005). Estimated growth rates of E. rostrata vary between 0.6 to 5 mm per year (Adkins et al. 2004, Houlbrèque et al. 2010), and colonies of E. rostrata have been dated between 100 to 608 years old (Adkins et al. 2004, Houlbrèque et al. 2010).
threats: Bottom contact fishing practices such as trawling are likely detrimental to Enallopsammia profunda, as with other scleractinian corals, due to its brittle skeleton, longevity, and slow growth rates. Damaged colonies and habitat take decades to recover. This species is often found co-occurring with Desmophyllum pertusum reefs, which are currently listed as Vulnerable and have suffered a 30% decline in the last 30 years. Although there is uncertainty about the current population status of E. profunda, this species is likely to have been impacted by fishing activity where we know D. pertusum reefs have been damaged.
population: There is no information on the population size of this species. This species is often found co-occurring with Desmophyllum pertusum reefs, which are currently listed as Vulnerable and have suffered a 30% decline in the last 30 years. Where we know D. pertusum reefs have been damaged, it is likely E. profunda has also been impacted. As the global decline of Desmophyllum reefs indicates historical declines of E. profunda may have been significant, it is inferred that this species' population has undergone around 25% of global decline in the last 100 years.
range: Enallopsammia profunda is endemic to the Northwest Atlantic occurring from offshore Northeast United States to St Lucia and into the Gulf of Mexico.
useTrade: This species is protected by CITES Appendix II.
conservationActions:
This species inhabits hard substrata and co-occurs with the reef forming coral Desmophyllum pertusum. Many MPA designations are broadly made to coincide with the occurrence of hard substrate topological features that promote biodiversity and biomass of benthic sessile organisms, and so a proportion of the species may be protected by those designations. MPAs designated for the protection of reef framework and living D. pertusum reef may include a certain proportion of the population of E. profunda. Records for this species occur in MPAs along the Blake Plateau where bottom trawling is banned, further reducing the risk of significant impact. There are no empirical species-specific studies that provide information on reproductive stages, longevity, generation time, or general ecology of E. profunda. Such habitats are normally considered unsuitable for bottom contact trawling and thus fishing may pose a reduced risk to the species (although many areas of hermatypic deep-sea corals have been damaged by trawling in previous decades).

Research is needed into the population size of this species. The presence of multiple reproductive strategies for this species depending on the region of study indicates that more information is needed on its reproductive strategies worldwide. Research is also needed on life history parameters such as generation length and on the general ecology of the species. Finally, research on the overlap between species occurrence and MPAs is needed to determine what proportion of the population is protected.

All members of the order Scleractinia are included in CITES Appendix II, which includes this species.

rationale: This species is assessed as Least Concern. Gyrophyllum hirondellei has a disjunct but broad distribution across the North Atlantic, at bathyl depths from 721–2,000 m. This sea pen species is protected in part of its range by trawling bans, and it is unlikely that current threats have a significant impact on the global population size.
habitat: Gyrophyllum hirondellei lives on soft bottoms in bathyal depths of the North Atlantic, between 721–2,220 m depth (López-González et al. 2022). It has been found in muddy bottoms as well as in rock, pebble, and gravel bottoms (Tixier-Durivault and D’Hondt 1974).
threats:
This species can be sensitive to direct impacts on the seabed such as trawling, or to other disturbance that changes sediment patterns such as major energy infrastructure construction. Bottom trawling impacts soft-bottom communities including sea pens by decreasing diversity and shifting their trophic structure in fishing areas (Vergnon and Blanchard 2006, OSPAR 2010). Soft bottom communities including sea pens are broadly impacted by trawling, and species that are sensitive to disturbance are absent from impacted areas (Pommer et al. 2016). Morphologically similar species are highly susceptible to trawl damage and, although damaged individuals can re-attach to the bottom, suffer high mortality after disturbance (Malecha and Stone 2009).

The shallower part of the distribution of Gyrophyllum hirondellei is not protected by trawling bans in deep waters in the EU (below 800 m) or Norway (below 1,000 m).
population: Precise population estimates are unknown. Distribution information for this species is based on records from oceanographic cruises or by-catch from longline fisheries, and these commonly comprise single specimen records (Tixier-Durivault and D’Hondt 1974). It appears that G. hirondellei occurs at relatively low density and does not form dense beds or fields of sea pens at bathyal depths in the North Atlantic (Tempera et al. 2013).
range: The species is present in the North Atlantic Ocean from the Faroe Plateau to the Azores (Sampaio et al. 2019) and in the Northwest Atlantic in the Bahamas (López-González et al. 2022).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: Sea pen fields are recognised as Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems and are thus afforded protection under various legislative actions which vary across the world. For example, in the Northeast Atlantic, fields of sea pens deeper than 200 m are included in "Coral gardens". Populations of G. hirondellei in the Azores are protected from trawling through a ban implemented since 2005; however, these populations are still vulnerable to bottom longline and handline fisheries (Sampaio et al. 2012). Gyrophyllum hirondellei occurs at low densities, making potential decline more difficult to assess. Research into age and other life history parameters would allow a better understanding of the susceptibility and resilience to threats of this species. Considering its disjunct distribution in the North Atlantic and variable fishing activity across different regions, research is needed to address appropriate measures to protect G. hirondellei at a local scale.

rationale: Anthoptilum murrayi has a wide distribution, primarily in the North Atlantic Ocean, but extending into the South Atlantic, and the Indo-Pacific. This species is impacted by damage from bottom trawling, which occurs throughout its global range except in a few protected areas, where the status of the species' populations remains unclear. Information on population trends is not available for this sea pen species, in particular data on the potential historical size and extent of the population are lacking. This species is sessile and slow growing, and is likely slow to recover from impacts of bottom-contacting activities that disturb the seabed or damage colonies. Reference data on the prior extent, distribution, and population density are lacking to determine the extent of recent and ongoing decline. In regions not protected by current trawling bans, decline is ongoing and projected to continue, with large fractions of potential habitat degraded or destroyed. Only a minority of the range is protected, with a majority subject to potential damage from fishing. The level of global decline cannot be determined for this species based on the data currently available. Therefore, we are unable to define whether this species should be listed as Least Concern or under any category of threat, and currently assess this species as Data Deficient. Data regarding the population density and specific impacts of trawling on local populations could prompt a reassessment.
habitat:
Anthoptilum murrayi lives on soft bottom habitats, mostly along continental slope areas, from depths of 155–2,500 m. Based on ecological observations of congeneric species, it likely plays an important role in providing habitat for epifauna and juvenile fish (Baillon et al. 2012, 2014).

In Iceland, age estimates for mature colonies were 6–17 years old, and growth rates were slow (0.10–0.17 mm per year; García-Cárdenas and López-González 2022). The species likely lives typically longer than 20 years. Therefore the generation length can be estimated as: Generation length = Age of first reproduction + [ z * (length of the reproductive period) ]. Using z = 0.5 as an appropriate estimate for broadcast spawning species, gives: 6 + [ 0.5 * 14 ] = 13 years.

The animals are gonochoric and apparently occur in a 1:1 sex ratio; they reproduce by broadcast spawning and the large eggs indicate likely lecithotrophic larvae (Pires et al. 2009). The species is highly fecund; however, there may be strong regional differences in fecundity, with a high number of 31,000 ± 5,000 oocytes per colony in Brazil (Pires et al. 2009), but around half that density in Iceland (García-Cárdenas and López-González 2022). Non-feeding larvae limit the potential larval duration and therefore dispersal potential.
threats:
Sea pens such as Anthoptilum murrayi are threatened by seabed disturbance through activities such as trawling and bottom-touching activities, which may occur through the entire extent of its global range. Impacts of fishing gear, particularly trawls, have been documented on various sea pen species and are likely to be similar on A. murrayi, hence fishing is the main threat currently recognized for the species. Soft bottom communities including sea pens are broadly impacted by trawling, with nearly 100% of the habitat being impacted, and species that are sensitive to disturbance are absent from impacted areas (Pommer et al. 2016). Regional assessments of relevant species assemblages have shown that more than 86% of potential habitats in the Greater North Sea and Celtic Sea are physically disturbed, with ongoing fishing pressure that prevents potential habitat recovery (OSPAR 2017).

Multiple colonies of this species can potentially be caught as fishing bycatch in the same tow through trawling. Damage to A. murrayi can further impact other co-occurring species as this species structures the local habitats. Since colonies of this species are slow-growing and can reach 20 years in age (García-Cárdenas and López-González 2022), recovery from breakage caused by trawl impacts could potentially take decades.
population: Anthoptilum murrayi is a sessile species with a patchy distribution. Like other sea pens, it can occur in large, aggregated populations (Pires et al. 2009), but little further detail exists on its population size.
range: This species has been reported from the northeast coast of North America (first recorded in Nova Scotia) and is primarily known from the North Atlantic, with a range extending to southern Iceland, along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (Sampaio et al. 2019), Bay of Biscay (Grasshoff 1981, Molodtsova et al. 2008), and into the South Atlantic, as well as validated records in New Zealand (Cairns et al. 2009). Published records also include distribution off West Africa, the Caribbean, the Indo-Pacific (e.g., Australia, Japan), and the west coast of the United States.
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions:
Sea pen fields are recognised as Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems and are thus afforded protection under various legislative actions which vary across the world. For example, in the Northeast Atlantic, fields of sea pens shallower than 200 m depth are included in the OSPAR threatened and/or declining habitat "Sea pens and burrowing megafauna", while deeper fields (below 200 m) are included in "Coral gardens". Still, bottom trawling continues to occur in some OSPAR areas, and thus the status of this species' populations remains unclear in these areas. No reports on the effect of the conservation efforts in sea pen habitats within the OSPAR agreement are available.

No conservation sites are identified specifically to protect A. murrayi, but conservation areas to protect sea pens exist. For example, one of the conservation objectives of the Laurentian Channel Marine Protected Area (MPA), Canada is to protect sea pens.

rationale: Kophobelemnon stelliferum is assessed as Near Threatened (NT). It has a broad distribution within the Mediterranean and Atlantic regions, mainly found on bathyal muddy bottoms that are largely impacted by trawling activities in both areas, which has a high incidental mortality for this species. It is also found in the Pacific; this assessment is based on data from the Atlantic (its core range). This species is slow growing, with an estimated generation length of 19 years based on data from two ecologically similar species (Funiculina quadrangularis and Pennatula aculeata). Kophobelemnon stelliferum currently occurs in a highly disturbed habitat and evidence indicates that local populations, for example in the Mediterranean basin as well as other regions, have been entirely eradicated in a period representing three generations for this species (1960s–2020s) (A2c). The decline is projected to continue and is likely representative of other declines across the global population. The extent of damage is also inferred from trawling bycatch, which presents a proxy index for the extent to which specimens are removed from the population (A2(b)). Based on this evidence, the inferred global decline is suspected to be at least 20%. In most of its depth range, the main method for estimating the population size and extent of this species is via underwater video, and technology with sufficient quality to identify species has only been available in the last 10–15 years. Therefore, it is not possible to accurately quantify previous population decline, but at least 20% reduction is inferred. Most of the present distribution of Kophobelemnon stelliferum is not protected by trawling bans in deep waters in the EU (below 800 m) or Norway (below 1,000 m).
habitat:
Kophobelemnon stelliferum inhabits soft, muddy bottoms along continental slopes in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. It can retract completely into the sediment (Mastrototaro et al. 2013). It is a characteristic species of bathyal mud and canyons (Carpine 1970) and is considered a common element for Alboran Sea bathyal mud facies (Pardo et al. 2011). In Norway, this species provides important shelter and acts as a hunting base for crustaceans such as Munida spp. (de Clippele et al. 2015).

Sea pens species are generally slow growing and live for several decades (Wilson et al. 2002, Ager 2003). The growth rate of K. stelliferum is very slow, even compared to other similar sea pen species, with radial growth rate around 0.06 mm/year (Greely 2022). The generation length of 19 years is based on comparison with ecologically similar species (e.g. Funiculina quadrangularis and Pennatula aculeata).
threats:
Bottom trawling impacts soft-bottom communities including sea pens by decreasing diversity and shifting their trophic structure in fishing areas (Vergnon and Blanchard 2006, OSPAR 2010). Soft bottom communities including sea pens are broadly impacted by trawling, and species that are sensitive to disturbance are absent from impacted areas (Pommer et al. 2016). In the Alboran Sea (Western Mediterranean), a regional Red List assessment estimated that at least 50% of potential habitat had been affected by trawling, with fishing activities still ongoing (Cerrano et al. 2010). Trawling is directly connected to reduction in sea pen abundance in the North Sea (Harrald et al. 2018).

This small species has some ability to withdraw into the sediment; however, it occurs in relatively high frequency in trawl bycatch, indicating that it is destroyed by bottom-touching fishing activities (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2023). The shallower part of the distribution of K. stelliferum is not protected by trawling bans in deep waters in the EU (below 800 m) or Norway (below 1,000 m). There is increasing recognition that trawling is detrimental to sea pens, but conservation efforts vary across the range of this species. Gear efficiency for direct extraction of sea pens including K. stelliferum is relatively low; however, the incidental mortality is 40–50% based on one year recovery after trawling (Kenchington et al. 2011). The occurrence of K. stelliferum is statistically negatively correlated to fishing intensity (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2016). Sea pens do not occur in natural densities in areas with fishing activity.
population:
There are no published data on population sizes although regional studies have calculated densities. A 1992 study estimated population densities of up to 2.6 colonies per m² in the Porcupine Seabight, south-west of Ireland, with the largest colonies located in the deepest areas (Rice et al. 1992). In the Northwest Atlantic, this species is relatively abundant, with densities of up to 12 colonies per m² (Rowe 1971). In the Mediterranean Sea’s Santa Maria di Leuca coral province, K. stelliferum has a highly patchy distribution and is less dense than in the Atlantic, averaging 0.0154 ± 0.014 colonies per m², though the study’s authors admit the sampling gear used may underestimate abundance (Mastrototaro et al. 2013). In the Mediterranean Sea, the distribution is not well-studied, and information is lacking on genetic flux between Atlantic and Mediterranean populations (Mastrototaro et al. 2013).

The Norwegian regional Red List assessment and Mediterranean regional assessment both listed Kophobelemnnon stelliferum as Least Concern (LC). In Norway this was determined based on the assumption of a permanently reproducing, established population not requiring further conservation effort (Tandberg and Mortensen 2021). In the Mediterranean the assessment explicitly referred to the evaluation based on limited evidence but that the threats were probably underestimated. There is evidence that this species has declined significantly in the Mediterranean: it was previously a common component of fisheries bycatch and is now rarely observed (Bastari et al. 2018, Grinyo et al. 2020). Kophobelemnon is also one of the most common sea pens found in trawling bycatch in Norway (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2023).

Within the genus Kophobelemnon, individual colonies reach sexual maturity with greater colony lengths (25 cm), and gonads are distributed throughout the rachis and the distal part of the peduncle (Rice et al. 1992). Additional information on their biology is poorly known, but individual colonies have separate sexes with a sex ratio of about 1:1 and there is no evidence of seasonal reproduction in the Porcupine Seabight (Rice et al. 1992). No data are available on potential genetic connectivity among different regional populations.
range: Kophobelemnon stelliferum is considered a widespread Atlantic species (Hickson 1916, Ocaña et al. 2000). It occurs from Newfoundland to Georgia on the western North Atlantic margin and from northern Norway to Morocco on the eastern North Atlantic margin. It is present in the Western Mediterranean Sea, extending as far east as the Northern Ionian Sea. It also occurs on the southern part of the Eastern Atlantic margin off Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, and Namibia. The species is also found in the Pacific around New Zealand and Sagami Bay, Japan. Recent surveys have recorded no sea pens in the south-eastern US coasts, even though this is within the range of this species and there are historical records of Kophobelemnon in the region (Brooke and Schroeder 2007).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade for this species.
conservationActions: Fields of sea pens shallower than 200 m depth are included in the OSPAR threatened and/or declining habitat "Sea pens and burrowing megafauna", while deeper fields (below 200 m) are included in "Coral gardens". However, monitoring in this way combines multiple vulnerable habitats and cannot discern declines specifically in K. stelliferum. Further research into the distribution and potential occurrence (or not) of K. stelliferum in protected areas is needed. Research into age and other life history parameters would allow a better understanding of the susceptibility and resilience to threats of this species. Research into the impact of ongoing trawling, particularly where the species provides habitat, is required.

rationale: Funiculina quadrangularis is assessed as Near Threatened (NT). Regional declines over recent decades are estimated at around 40% in the Mediterranean, as well as near total removal in the North Sea, with substantial reductions recorded in the Gulf of Mexico, and other areas in a period representing three generations for this species based on a generation length of approximately 19 years (1960s–2020s) (A2(c)). These regional range reductions likely reflect a global pattern of fishing impacts on coastal shelf regions throughout the range of this species. This is further likely representative of declines across the global population, where it is recorded sometimes in high biomass levels as bycatch from demersal trawl fisheries. The decline is projected to continue. At most of the depth range, the main method for estimating the population size and extent of this species is via underwater video, and technology with sufficient quality to identify species has only been widely available in the last 10–15 years. Therefore, it is not possible to quantify directly observed previous population decline, but it is inferred. The extent of damage is also inferred from trawling bycatch, which presents a proxy index for the extent to which specimens are removed from the population (A2(b)). Based on this evidence, the inferred global decline is suspected to be at least 25% over the past three generations (57 years). It may be unlikely that the total global population decline has exceeded 30%, the threshold for Vulnerable (VU); although it has been higher in particular locations, the species has persisted in the deeper parts of its range. It has been shown that this species could recover well if fishing pressure is removed.
habitat:
Funiculina quadrangularis is found in muddy bottom habitats between 20 and 2,000 m depth (Wright et al. 2015), typically inhabiting shallower habits but with records both shallower and deeper. This species can exceed 200 cm in length though size at maturity is unknown (Greathead et al. 2007), with one quarter of the length embedded in substrate (Gili and Pagès 1987). In general, F. quadrangularis has very specific habitat requirements: soft undisturbed mud and muddy sand (Greathead et al. 2005, Ager and Wilding 2009).

This species is dioecious, with relatively even sex rations. Based on studies in the UK, oocyte production takes place throughout the year; however, gamete maturation and spawning appear to occur in a single season. Sea pens are gonochoric, their sex ratio is 1:1. Reproductive data is unavailable for other regions of the world, but these patterns are consistent with those of other sea pen species, which tend to have high overall fecundity (Edwards and Moore 2009). Studies indicate this species could recover well if fishing pressure is removed, and its global distribution provides a large reservoir population that could facilitate recolonization of impacted areas (Greathead et al. 2007, Pierdomenico et al. 2018, Martinelli et al. 2023).

Sea pens species are generally slow growing and live for several decades (Wilson et al. 2002, Ager 2003). Funiculina quadrangularis is slow growing and long lived, based on comparison with similar species (Greathead et al. 2007) and examination of growth ring (Greely 2022), likely reaching maturity at 6 or 7 years. An assumed longevity of approximately 30 years indicates an estimated generation length of 19 years.

This species cannot retract into the seabed, meaning it does not retract and actively avoid trawl nets, which makes it more vulnerable. However, Eno et al. (2001) found that F. quadrangularis could bend away from lobster creels dropped on them in a passive response to the pressure wave travelling ahead of the pot, and were further able to reinsert into the muddy substrate after being uprooted, provided that the peduncle gained contact with the mud surface.

In many regions, sea pen-dominated communities are considered Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems (VME) and Essential Fish Habitats. These animals provide habitat for early life stages of some fish species (Baillon et al. 2012). Moreover, F. quadrangulis can form "prairies" providing essential habitat for commercially important crustacean species; in the Mediterranean these include Parapenaeus longirostris and Nephrops norvegicus and cephalopods (Eledone cirrhosa, Illex illecebrosus coindetii and Todaropsis eblanae) (Ardizzone 2006).
threats:
Funiculina quadrangularis is a relatively large sea pen species (reaching 200 cm) that typically inhabits shallower habitats and cannot retract into the seabed; these characteristics make it quite vulnerable to trawling. The occurrence of F. quadrangularis is statistically negatively correlated to fishing intensity (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2016).

The occurrence in soft sediments, particularly those in continental shelf zones that overlap with commercial fisheries, mean that disturbance from fisheries, particularly trawl fisheries, are the primary threat to this species (Greathead et al. 2007, Wright et al. 2015, Pierdomenico et al. 2018, Martinelli et al. 2023). Regional studies have documented reduction in population in response to trawl fishery pressure, and the species can be documented in bycatch (NOAA DSCRTP 2016). Damage from trawling eliminates mainly large and reproductively mature colonies (MacDonald et al. 1996).

Funiculina quadrangularis has a long, delicate axial rod, which is unable to withdraw into the sediment and breaks easily through the mechanical damage of bottom touching fisheries. ROV surveys have found large numbers of dead Funiculina in areas of fishing activity, as well as large volumes in bycatch, indicating ongoing impacts of fishing activities that impact the species throughout its range (Buhl-Mortensen et al. 2023).

The species was very common in some localities in the Mediterranean in the 1970s but has now disappeared from areas subject to commercial trawling, for example in France (Fabri et al. 2013), Sicily (Castriota et al. 2001) and Algeria (Tudela 2004). Bottom trawling is widespread in other Mediterranean soft muddy sediments areas producing a strong negative impact on the soft-bottom benthos (Sanchez et al. 2000, Tudela 2004, UNEP/MAP 2012, Vassilopoulou 2012). In New Zealand, bycatch from crustacean trawl fisheries included more than 100 tonnes of Funiculina quadrangularis over a five-year period (2016–2021) recorded by fisheries observers (Anderson et al. 2023). The species is also recorded in bycatch in the East Pacific indicating extensive damage and reduction to those populations in the last 10 years. The species was known from shelf habitats in the Gulf of Mexico in the 1960s and is now absent from that area (Zimmerman et al. 2020).

Salmon farming is also a potential threat to F. quadrangularis: field studies on the coast of Norway have documented reduction in growth and physical degradation of colonies in proximity to salmon cages (Kutti et al. 2015).

The broad distribution of this species may also expose it to emerging threats such as offshore energy development (e.g., wind energy development). Energy production by offshore wind is forecast to increase to 260 GW or more by 2030 (Musial et al. 2022), and the structures of these platforms may interact with benthic habitats directly (ICF 2020) as well as alter other environmental factors such as hydrodynamics and productivity (Hogan et al. 2023). However, impacts from these potential threats have not been documented at this time.
population:
This sea pen species has a global distribution and is known to be a relatively fecund, broadcast spawner. While genetic connectivity across its entire global distribution is undetermined, regional work has indicated high levels of gene flow and high diversity in patchily distributed local populations (Edwards and Moore 2009, Wright et al. 2015). Funiculina quadrangularis occurs in soft sediment habitats worldwide and occurs in beds with moderate density. This species has a scattered and patchy distribution, forming clusters (Gili and Pagès 1987, Ocaña et al. 2000). Mačić et al. (2022) described populations of F. quadrangularis in the South Adriatic Sea between 160 m to 400 m depth with maximum densities of 0.83 colony/m².

Microsatellite-based genetic studies demonstrated high gene flow and high genetic diversity, consistent with the reproductive strategy in this species (Wright et al. 2015). Global genetic structure for this species is unknown, but high levels of gene flow are consistent with a highly fecund, broadcast spawning species. While documented globally, only limited density information for this species is available and available data are biased by past impacts, so global species trends cannot be determined. However, reduction in population has been documented regionally worldwide, often associated with trawl fishing pressure (Pierdomenico et al. 2016, Anderson et al. 2023, Martinelli et al. 2023).
range:
Funiculina quadrangularis is locally common throughout the North Atlantic and Mediterranean and is distributed worldwide (Ager and Wilding 2009). Records for this species occur in all oceanic regions except the Arctic (Wright et al. 2015), with records in over 30 countries. The species occurs across a very broad range of depths, from 20 m to 3,600 m. The majority of records are from depths above 500 m; well documented specimens from deeper depths have been recorded, but eventual genetic work may determine deeper specimens to be a separate species. Although widespread, the range is reduced compared to the potential habitat for this species. Disparity between potential and actual records indicate removal of F. quadrangularis within in the North Sea (Downie et al. 2021).

Surveys in the French Mediterranean reported that this species was rarely observed and confined to deeper canyons (Fabri et al. 2014). Funiculina were historically present in the Gulf of Mexico shelf but are now absent there and found in deeper slope sites that are less impacted by trawling (Zimmerman et al. 2020).
useTrade: There is no known use or trade of this species.
conservationActions:
Fields of sea pens shallower than 200 m depth are included in the OSPAR threatened and/or declining habitat "Sea pens and burrowing megafauna", while deeper fields (below 200 m) are included in "Coral gardens". Species specific conservation efforts have not been established for this species; however, its distribution overlaps with established areas protected from fishing pressure such as regional or nationally designated Marine Protected Areas, Special Areas of Conservation, and Essential Fish Habitat. These areas can act as incidental protection zones. In places where conservation measurements have been implemented and bottom trawling activity decreased, rapid growth in F. quadrangularis population was observed to follow (Martinelli et al. 2023).

While the species has a broad global distribution, local disturbance can cause significant population impacts. A regional assessment for the eastern Mediterranean listed this species as Vulnerable. Protected areas for this species could provide a highly effective conservation measure. Increased research into the global population diversity, life history, reproductive timing, and standing stock is required to clarify regional connectivity, population trends, and conservation needs. Research into the impact of ongoing trawling, particularly where the species provides habitat, is required.

This species inhabits lagoons and commonly co-occurs with Cyphastrea microphthalma (Baird et al. 2017).

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
threats:
In the Solitary Islands, coral cover declined between surveys conducted in 1990 and 2013-2014, but reefs were considered to be in reasonably good condition as of 2014. Causes of this decline are thought to include bleaching events, occasional large subtropical storms and disease outbreaks. The progression of climate change is expected to cause increases in sea surface temperature that will likely severely impact corals in the Solitary Islands in the future, and this is especially concerning since connectivity with coral populations in the Great Barrier Reef is low (Mizerek et al. 2021). 

The coral community of Lord Howe Island experienced severe and unprecedented consecutive bleaching in both 2010 and 2011 during which up to 99% of corals were affected at shallow sites; however, coral cover returned to pre-bleaching levels in three years. Minimal bleaching and mortality was recorded among members of Merulinidae, which includes this species, but the predicted increase in frequency of severe bleaching events will impact even the resilient corals as the isolation of Lord Howe in both high latitude and from other coral populations (e.g., the Great Barrier Reef) are factors that reduce the ability to recover (Dalton et al. 2020).

The general susceptibility of this species to bleaching, coral disease, predation by Acanthaster planci, and recovery from bleaching is unknown. However, the genus Cyphastrea is generally resistant to bleaching (Marshall and Baird 2000, Ralph et al. 2001, Manikandan et al. 2016) with a moderate capacity to recover from bleaching (Hill et al. 2004). The general susceptibility of this genus to predation by the crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci) is low, as other coral species are preferentially targeted (Keesing et al. 2019). Cyphastrea species likely have moderate susceptibility to coral disease as diseases are known to occur within species of this genus, but with less severity than other genera (Aeby et al. 2020).

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of storms, and ocean acidification.

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide with increases in numbers of diseases, coral species affected, and geographic extent (Ward et al. 2004, Sutherland et al. 2004, Sokolow et al. 2009). Outbreaks of coral diseases have damaged coral reefs worldwide with the most widespread, virulent, and longest running coral disease outbreak currently occurring on the Florida Reef Tract and throughout the Caribbean. The disease, stony coral tissue loss disease, has been ongoing since 2014 (Precht et al. 2016) and has devastated affected reefs along Florida (Walton et al. 2018, Williams et al. 2021) and throughout the Caribbean (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2019, Kramer et al. 2019). Numerous disease outbreaks have also occurred in the Indo-Pacific (Willis et al. 2004, Aeby et al. 2011; 2016), Indian Ocean (Raj et al. 2016) and Persian Gulf (Howells et al. 2020). Escalating anthropogenic stressors combined with the threats associated with global climate change of increases in coral disease, frequency and duration of coral bleaching and ocean acidification place coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific at high risk of collapse.

Localized threats to corals include fisheries, human development (industry, settlement, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual species is not known.

Species-specific, global level population information is limited. However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, Donovan et al. 2021). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.     

Approach 1: Future population trend
The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is little understood and varies by species and locality (Bay et al. 2017, Matz et al. 2020, Logan et al. 2021). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2035 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2039 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2062 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2070 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where the onset of ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0-30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on 1°C of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is moderately susceptible to bleaching. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Pacific, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in high-latitude reefs (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of less than 25% by the year 2050, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario. 

Approach 2: Past population trend
Coral reef monitoring data were also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the 37 subregions of the Indo-Pacific (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered 11 species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 0-50 m and is predominately found at depths greater than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered common, overall population is not restricted or highly fragmented, does occur off-reef, is highly susceptible to disease, does or does not recover well from bleaching or disease, has a low susceptibility to crown-of-thorns starfish, is moderately susceptible to bleaching, has an unknown susceptibility to the impacts of ocean acidification (Kornder et al. 2018), did not have >10,000 pieces exported annually in the aquarium trade between 2010-2019, it is overall suspected to be more resistant to threats related to reef degradation. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 20% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a suspected global level decline of less than 25% since 1989, or over the past three generations.

This species is distributed in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, East Africa, Madagascar, the southwest and northern Indian Ocean (Mondal et al. 2019), Persian Gulf, central Indo-Pacific, Australia (the Cocos-Keeling Islands, Christmas Island and from Coral Bay, Western Australia across northern Australia to the Great Barrier Reef and Lord Howe Island), Southeast Asia, southern Japan, East China Sea, China (Xin-Qing et al. 2013), Palmyra Atoll (Williams et al. 2008), oceanic West Pacific, and central Pacific to French Polynesia (Veron et al. 2016, Juszkiewicz et al. 2022).

Approach 1: Future population trend
The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that coral populations may experience near complete mortality and are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022).

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is little understood and varies by species and locality (Bay et al. 2017, Matz et al. 2020, Logan et al. 2021). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells. 

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2038 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2042 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2065 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2083 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. For species where the onset of ASB occurs within 3-generation lengths, the 3-generation reduction is calculated as 80% multiplied by two proportions: (i) the proportion of the species' depth range that is in 0-30 m range, and (ii) for widespread species, the proportion of cells within the species' range that are expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 before 2050 (three generation lengths). We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on 1°C of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is more resilient to bleaching. For widespread species, the final estimate of decline was further adjusted by excluding the proportion of cells within its range that were expected to experience ASB under SSP2-4.5 after 2050 (three generation lengths), in order to account for the potential resilience of species to the asynchronous variability of bleaching events that occur across the Indo-Pacific. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the assumption that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and might decline at a faster rate in some places than species that also occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003), although this is not always the case (e.g., Smith et al. 2016, Frade et al. 2018). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Pacific, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in high-latitude reefs (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). Therefore, this species is suspected to experience a projected global level decline of less than 25% by the year 2050, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario.
